results.title: Sof-IA: management of online medical appointments
results.proposal: Sof-IA: management of online medical appointments. Patients looking for healthcare appointments often know their symptoms, preferences and constraints, but not the exact specialist, service or search criteria they should select on a booking platform. Sof-IA, developed by iDoctors, addresses this problem by using artificial intelligence to make the search for a suitable medical specialist faster and more personalised. The operational problem is that conventional search filters require users to know how to translate their need into a speciality, procedure, location, cost range or availability window. Sof-IA allows users to describe their request in natural language, including symptoms, location, preferred time, budget and other practical needs, and then returns specialists matching those criteria. For example, a user can ask for a dermatologist in a specific area, a gynaecologist available at a certain time, or a doctor within a maximum price range. At a conceptual level, the system acts as a natural-language interpretation layer above the iDoctors search engine: it analyses the patient’s request, extracts relevant constraints and maps them to structured search results. Importantly, iDoctors states that Sof-IA is not designed to provide diagnoses or recommend treatments, but only to help users identify the specialist they need. The expected impact is easier appointment search, better matching between patient needs and available professionals, reduced friction for users unfamiliar with medical terminology and a more accessible digital healthcare booking experience. The case is relevant because it applies AI to navigation and matching in healthcare, while explicitly limiting the system’s role to search support rather than clinical decision-making.

results.title: PROMPT - Narrative Intelligence for Information Integrity
results.proposal: PROMPT - Narrative Intelligence for Information Integrity. Disinformation campaigns increasingly rely on recurring narratives, rhetorical patterns and coordinated circulation across media outlets, social platforms and online knowledge spaces. PROMPT, or Predictive Research On Misinformation & Propagation Trajectories, addresses this problem by developing AI-supported narrative intelligence for information integrity. The operational challenge is that fact-checking individual claims is necessary but insufficient when manipulative campaigns spread through broader stories, frames and emotional patterns that can reappear across languages and platforms. PROMPT analyses large volumes of textual data to identify malicious or manipulative narratives, focusing on case studies such as the war in Ukraine, LGBTQI+ rights and the 2024 European elections. The project combines large language models with dynamic network analysis to detect formal patterns across media outlets, social networks and Wikipedia in eight languages. At a conceptual level, the system moves from isolated content detection to narrative mapping: it seeks to understand how misleading stories are structured, how they travel, which actors amplify them and why they resonate with audiences. Outputs include a refined language model, a narrative-monitoring dashboard and training material for civil-society actors. The expected impact is stronger disinformation analysis, better support for journalists and fact-checkers, earlier recognition of manipulation strategies and improved public understanding of information threats. The case is significant because it applies AI to democratic resilience while preserving the analytical role of journalists, researchers and civil-society organisations.

results.title: City of Częstochowa will become the first in Poland to begin using the Polish Large Language Model (PLLuM)
results.proposal: City of Częstochowa will become the first in Poland to begin using the Polish Large Language Model (PLLuM). Local administrations process large volumes of routine text, including residents’ enquiries, official letters, reports, summaries and internal procedural materials. Częstochowa’s pilot use of PLLuM, the Polish Large Language Model, addresses the practical question of how a national language model can support municipal administration while preserving linguistic quality and public-sector control. The operational problem is that generic commercial AI models may not be optimised for Polish administrative language, legal terminology or public-sector workflows, while staff need safe tools that can help with repetitive drafting and analysis without replacing human judgement. Under a pilot with Poland’s Ministry of Digital Affairs, Częstochowa became the first city to use PLLuM in local administration. The model is intended to support officials in tasks such as drafting official correspondence, summarising long or complex documents, analysing residents’ requests and providing quick internal guidance. At a conceptual level, the system acts as a Polish-language productivity assistant adapted to public administration: it helps transform incoming or internal information into structured drafts and summaries, which staff can then review and approve. The expected impact is reduced processing time, improved consistency in written communication, faster analysis of citizen enquiries and better evidence on the practical value and limitations of national LLMs in government. The case is relevant because it tests generative AI in a real municipal setting while supporting a broader national objective: developing sovereign Polish-language AI capacity rather than relying only on foreign-language general-purpose tools.

results.title: TOURISMO Project - Florence
results.proposal: TOURISMO Project - Florence. Historic city centres face a difficult balance between welcoming visitors and protecting residents’ quality of life, heritage spaces and urban functionality. Florence’s TOURISMO pilot addresses this issue by testing smart technologies to monitor tourism flows in highly visited areas of the city, including Piazza Duomo, Ponte Vecchio and Piazza Pitti. The operational problem is that overtourism is not only a matter of total visitor numbers; it also depends on where people concentrate, how long they stay, how they move and how visitor behaviour affects local liveability. The implementation combines thermal cameras and “sniffer” sensors with AI-based processing to collect anonymised data on pedestrian movement and presence. Thermal cameras installed in Piazza Duomo and additional sensors across strategic points gather information that can help city authorities understand crowding patterns without identifying individuals. The initiative also includes QR-code tools to collect visitor feedback, adding a qualitative layer to quantitative flow monitoring. At a conceptual level, the system creates a real-time evidence base for sustainable tourism management: rather than relying only on periodic surveys or anecdotal complaints, Florence can use data to assess pressure points and plan interventions. The expected impact is improved liveability in the historic centre, better management of tourism flows, stronger support for sustainable urban-tourism policy and a replicable operational manual for other European contexts. The case is relevant because it applies AI and sensor systems to tourism governance in a UNESCO-sensitive urban environment, where public acceptance and privacy safeguards are essential.

evidence.quote: Historic city centres face a difficult balance between welcoming visitors and protecting residents’ quality of life, heritage spaces and urban functionality.

results.memo: Proceed. TOURISMO Project - Florence is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: LitAI - Lithuania AI Factory
results.proposal: LitAI - Lithuania AI Factory. National AI ecosystems need shared infrastructure, data access and technical expertise if companies, researchers and public institutions are to move from experimentation to reliable deployment. Lithuania’s LitAI Artificial Intelligence Factory is intended to become a national competence and technology centre bringing together high-performance computing, data resources, scientific research and specialised expertise. The operational problem is that AI adoption across public services, cybersecurity, personalised medicine, industrial automation, green transformation, energy and transport requires coordinated infrastructure rather than fragmented project-level experimentation. LitAI will operate as a one-stop platform providing computing infrastructure together with technical and research-based consulting services, enabling the public and private sectors to develop, test and implement reliable AI solutions more quickly. The initiative will be coordinated by Vilnius University, with partners including Kaunas University of Technology, VILNIUS TECH, Vytautas Magnus University, the State Data Agency, the Lithuanian Radio and Television Centre and the Innovation Agency. At a conceptual level, LitAI links advanced computing capacity, applied research, data environments and practical support services into a national AI innovation hub. Its implementation will be connected to the LRTC VDC3 Third State Data Centre, and the estimated project value is around EUR 130 million, most of which is dedicated to high-performance computing infrastructure. The expected impact is stronger scientific capacity, faster AI adoption in strategic sectors, more than 100 high-skilled jobs and improved Lithuanian competitiveness within Europe’s AI and HPC ecosystem. The case is significant because it positions AI as national innovation infrastructure shared across academia, industry and government.

evidence.quote: National AI ecosystems need shared infrastructure, data access and technical expertise if companies, researchers and public institutions are to move from experimentation to reliable deployment.

results.title: MeluXina-AI: High-performance supercomputer to test AI applications on a large scale
results.proposal: MeluXina-AI: High-performance supercomputer to test AI applications on a large scale. Advanced AI development requires infrastructure capable of training, testing and deploying large models under secure, sovereign and high-performance conditions. Luxembourg’s MeluXina-AI initiative addresses this requirement by creating an AI-optimised supercomputer and an associated Luxembourg AI Factory. The operational problem is that start-ups, SMEs, researchers and public-sector innovators often need computing capacity for AI and data-intensive workloads that exceeds ordinary cloud or local infrastructure, while sensitive data and intellectual property require secure environments. MeluXina-AI will be hosted and operated by LuxProvide as part of the Luxembourg AI Factory, with Luxinnovation coordinating AI Factory activities and a consortium including the Luxembourg National Data Service, the University of Luxembourg and the Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology. The new system will support training, testing and pre-production deployment of advanced AI models, with a software ecosystem designed for AI users from start-ups to researchers and industry. At a conceptual level, the infrastructure combines supercomputing, sovereign cloud capabilities, multi-tenant isolation, data bridges and GPU-as-a-Service delivery. It will be installed across the Bissen and Bettembourg sites and is expected to deliver an estimated AI peak performance of more than 20 exaflops. The expected impact is stronger Luxembourg and European AI capacity, better support for trustworthy AI development, improved access for SMEs and researchers, and closer integration into the EuroHPC AI Factory network. The case is significant because it treats AI compute as strategic public infrastructure, not just a technical resource.

results.title: High-performing multilingual model that includes Luxembourgish in both written and spoken form
results.proposal: High-performing multilingual model that includes Luxembourgish in both written and spoken form. Many smaller or less widely spoken languages are under-represented in modern AI systems, which can reduce digital inclusion and weaken the presence of national languages in public services, speech interfaces and language technologies. Luxembourg’s multilingual language and speech model addresses this problem by aiming to include Luxembourgish at a level comparable to better-supported languages such as English and French. The operational challenge is that high-performing language and speech models need large quantities of high-quality text and audio data, but Luxembourgish has fewer publicly available resources than global languages. The project described in Luxembourg’s public-sector AI strategy involves collecting local audio sources, including voice samples from television, to train systems capable of recognising and generating Luxembourgish in both written and spoken form. At a conceptual level, the initiative is about linguistic digital sovereignty: the national language should not be absent from AI-enabled search, voice assistants, transcription, translation or public-service tools simply because commercial models focus on larger markets. The model could support public administrations, educational services, accessibility tools, speech recognition, multilingual communication and citizen-facing digital services. The expected impact is stronger inclusion of Luxembourgish speakers, better language coverage in digital government, improved speech-to-text and text-generation capabilities, and preservation of linguistic diversity in the age of AI. The case is significant because it recognises that AI infrastructure is also cultural infrastructure: if a language is not represented in models, it becomes harder to use in modern digital environments. The available source frames the project as ongoing development rather than a mature deployed service.

results.title: Comprehensive language model specifically trained on Luxembourg legislation
results.proposal: Comprehensive language model specifically trained on Luxembourg legislation. Legal systems are difficult for citizens and even professionals to navigate when legislative texts are dispersed, technically written and frequently amended. Luxembourg’s planned language model trained on national legislation addresses this challenge by making the country’s legal framework easier to search, interpret and understand. The operational problem is twofold. Legal professionals such as judges, lawyers, public officials and jurists need faster ways to interrogate legislative materials, while citizens need more accessible explanations of rights, obligations and procedures written in language that is easier to understand than formal legal drafting. The initiative described in Luxembourg’s public-sector AI strategy context focuses on developing a large language model specifically trained on Luxembourgish legislation. At a conceptual level, the model would act as a legal-information assistant: users could ask questions in natural language and receive responses grounded in national legal texts, helping them identify relevant provisions or understand the structure of a legal issue. The source stresses that Luxembourg’s approach to AI in the public sector is human-centred and does not aim to let AI decide on matters such as subsidies or social-programme access. Instead, AI is framed as decision support and information support that makes processes more transparent and comprehensible. The expected impact is more efficient legal research, improved access to law, greater transparency of public rules and stronger digital sovereignty through locally adapted AI tools. The case is significant because it applies generative AI to legal accessibility while explicitly retaining human oversight for decisions affecting citizens.

results.title: Chatbot for the consultation of the AI Act
results.proposal: Chatbot for the consultation of the AI Act. The EU AI Act introduces a complex regulatory framework that affects public administrations, employers, technology providers and organisations using AI systems in sensitive contexts. INAIL’s experimental chatbot addresses the problem that legal and technical texts can be difficult to consult, especially for users who need to understand practical implications for occupational health and safety. The chatbot was developed by INAIL’s Department of Occupational and Environmental Medicine, Epidemiology and Hygiene as a specialised tool for answering questions about Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. The operational objective is to make the AI Act easier to understand and apply by allowing users to interact with the legal text through a structured question-and-answer interface. The tool is based on a pre-trained large language model, GPT-4o, customised through the GPT Store and supplied with a targeted knowledge base including the Italian version of the AI Act, a summary of the regulation, its index and detailed instructions for structuring responses. At a conceptual level, the chatbot uses retrieval-augmented generation: the language model’s ability to generate coherent responses is combined with selected legal sources so that answers remain linked to the relevant regulatory material. The system was tested with particular attention to health and safety at work, where AI regulation may affect workplace technologies, risk management and worker protection. The expected impact is easier consultation of complex regulation, better informed compliance, improved awareness of AI-related obligations in occupational contexts and a reusable methodology for other legal or technical domains. The case is relevant because it demonstrates controlled public-sector experimentation with LLMs for regulatory assistance.

results.title: SAVIA project: Artificial Intelligence for law quality
results.proposal: SAVIA project: Artificial Intelligence for law quality. Regional legislation can be difficult for both public officials and citizens to navigate because legal texts, implementing acts and territorial effects are often distributed across multiple documents and administrative layers. SAVIA addresses this challenge by using artificial intelligence to support consultation of Emilia-Romagna regional laws and their implementing measures. The operational problem is that legislative assemblies and local administrations need timely, accurate and comprehensible information about what regional laws require, how they are implemented by the Regional Council, municipalities and provinces, and what effects they produce on the territory. SAVIA is developed by the Legislative Assembly of Emilia-Romagna in collaboration with CINECA and is supported by the MarghERita Big Data platform. At a conceptual level, the system uses large language models and retrieval-augmented generation to answer natural-language questions on regional law. The aim is not to replace legal judgement or legislative interpretation, but to provide a decision-support and information-access tool that can help institutional users and the public retrieve relevant legal information more easily. Between the end of 2024 and the beginning of 2025, activities were carried out to test SAVIA’s performance on MarghERita, including configuration work and expansion of GPU resources available to the project. The expected impact is improved legislative quality, easier access to regional law, greater transparency of institutional activity and stronger support for local administrations in carrying out their functions. The case is significant because it applies generative AI to legal accessibility while grounding answers in official regional legal texts.

results.title: MarghERita: Emilia-Romagna’s High-Performance Computing and Big Data Platform
results.proposal: MarghERita: Emilia-Romagna’s High-Performance Computing and Big Data Platform. Regional administrations increasingly need high-performance computing capacity to process large datasets, run predictive models and support rapid decision-making in areas such as civil protection, environmental risk and public-service planning. MarghERita is the Emilia-Romagna Region’s HPC and Big Data platform, developed with Lepida to provide regional institutions with computing infrastructure that can support advanced modelling and data-intensive applications. The operational value of the platform is particularly clear in civil protection, where extreme weather events require rapid simulations and evidence-based prevention measures. After the severe floods that affected Emilia-Romagna in May 2023, the Civil Protection, the University of Parma, the University of Padua and the Region used MarghERita’s computing power to implement algorithms capable of simulating flood hydrographs in real time. These simulations applied predictive models of possible bank breaks along the Lamone River to assess and mitigate potential flooding consequences for surrounding territory. At a conceptual level, MarghERita acts as a shared computational backbone for public authorities: instead of each administration building separate high-capacity infrastructure, the regional platform provides the computing power needed for complex simulations, environmental modelling and decision support. The expected impact is improved prevention of hydrogeological risk, faster response during weather-hydrological alerts, stronger coordination between universities and public authorities, and more data-driven management of extreme climate events. The case is relevant because it shows how regional HPC infrastructure can move beyond research support and become part of operational civil-protection capacity.
results.memo: Proceed. MarghERita: Emilia-Romagna’s High-Performance Computing and Big Data Platform is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: KIWA, an AI-based forest monitoring system
results.proposal: KIWA, an AI-based forest monitoring system. Forest fires can spread rapidly and create simultaneous risks for people, infrastructure, biodiversity and local emergency services. KIWA addresses this challenge by combining drones, artificial intelligence and decision-support tools to support earlier detection of forest and wildfires and more effective coordination of response resources. The operational problem is that municipal fire brigades and disaster-control authorities often need real-time information on the location of a fire, the direction and speed of spread, and the resources required to contain it. Traditional observation methods may not provide sufficiently fast or detailed information, especially when fires spread across difficult terrain or visibility is limited. KIWA uses unmanned aerial vehicles equipped with cameras to collect images and videos of monitored forest areas. These data are transmitted through interfaces and analysed by AI models in real time to identify fire or smoke, while the decision-support system helps emergency services interpret the current situation and match available personnel and equipment to the threat. At a conceptual level, the system creates a continuous forest-monitoring and response-support loop: drones collect situational data, AI detects and forecasts fire-related risks, and municipal authorities receive actionable information through a dashboard or operational interface. The expected impact is faster detection, better deployment of firefighting resources, reduced ecological damage, improved safety for people and animals, and lower financial burden for municipalities affected by wildfire events. The case is significant because it connects environmental monitoring, civil protection and AI-enabled decision support in a scalable model for regions exposed to increasing climate-related fire risks.

results.title: JUANO - app to anonymise court decisions for publication on the justice internet portal
results.proposal: JUANO - app to anonymise court decisions for publication on the justice internet portal. Publishing court decisions improves transparency, legal certainty and access to justice, but it also requires careful protection of personal data. JUANO addresses this challenge by supporting the anonymisation of court decisions before they are made available on Luxembourg’s justice internet portal. The operational problem is that court judgments often contain names, addresses, personal identifiers and other sensitive details that must be removed or generalised consistently before publication. Manual anonymisation can be slow, repetitive and vulnerable to inconsistency, particularly when large volumes of decisions need to be processed. JUANO uses an artificial-intelligence engine to recognise entities that should be anonymised and to suggest categories based on the content of the text. At a conceptual level, the application functions as decision support for legal publishing: it identifies potentially sensitive elements, proposes how they should be treated and facilitates a more standardised anonymisation workflow. The expected impact is faster preparation of judgments for publication, more consistent data-protection practice, better access to case law for lawyers and interested parties, and stronger compliance with privacy requirements. The system should not be framed as replacing legal or judicial responsibility, because anonymisation in legal texts still requires careful validation and contextual judgement. Its value lies in reducing the burden of repetitive entity recognition and improving consistency across decisions. The case is relevant to digital justice because anonymisation tools are a practical prerequisite for expanding access to case law while respecting fundamental rights and data-protection obligations.

results.title: mAIGreece - the digital AI assistant for visitors
results.proposal: mAIGreece - the digital AI assistant for visitors. Tourists often need fast and reliable information during travel, particularly on health services, emergency support, consular offices, police stations, museums, beaches and official visitor guidance. mAiGreece addresses this need by providing an AI-powered digital assistant for visitors to Greece, created by the Ministry of Tourism and the Ministry of Digital Governance. The platform brings together information on hospitals, health centres, embassies and consulates, police stations, Blue Flag beaches, museums, content from Visit Greece and frequently asked questions. It also includes an important safety function: users can send an SMS with their geographical location to the Ministry of Civil Protection’s operations centre through the 112 emergency number, supporting rapid assistance where necessary. The system supports written or spoken natural-language questions and offers information in 31 languages, improving accessibility for a diverse international visitor base. The expected impact is a better visitor experience, easier access to official information, stronger tourist safety and improved coordination between tourism promotion and public-service guidance. The case is relevant because it shows AI being used not only for marketing, but also for practical visitor support and emergency-related information in a national tourism context.

results.title: Compar:IA - the chatbot arena
results.proposal: Compar:IA - the chatbot arena. Generative AI models are increasingly used by citizens, professionals and public administrations, but many users rely on single systems without understanding differences in quality, bias, environmental footprint, language performance or cultural alignment. Compar:IA addresses this challenge by creating a public chatbot arena where users can compare two anonymised AI models, judge their answers and contribute to open preference datasets. The operational problem is that high-quality human preference data are scarce for French and other European languages, while AI literacy among citizens also needs to improve as generative AI becomes more common. The platform allows users to ask questions, interact with two anonymous models, vote on the preferred answer and later learn more about the models’ characteristics. These interactions generate anonymised preference data that can be published as open datasets and used to improve future models, especially for French and other European languages. At a conceptual level, Compar:IA combines public education, model evaluation and data collection in one interface: citizens learn not to trust one AI answer uncritically, while their feedback contributes to a shared resource for language-model improvement. The platform also highlights the environmental footprint of AI queries, adding an awareness dimension that goes beyond output quality. The expected impact is stronger AI literacy, better understanding of model differences, more open language-specific preference datasets and support for European digital sovereignty. The case is significant because it treats the public not only as AI users but also as contributors to model evaluation and linguistic diversity.

results.title: SNCF’s AI Maintenance Scheduler Reduces Train Downtime by 45%
results.proposal: SNCF’s AI Maintenance Scheduler Reduces Train Downtime by 45%. Rail operators need to reduce unexpected failures, improve punctuality and use maintenance resources efficiently across large fleets and infrastructure assets. SNCF’s predictive-maintenance work addresses this challenge by using data and AI to detect technical problems before they become operational disruptions. The operational problem is that time-based maintenance can lead to two opposite inefficiencies: some components may be serviced too early, wasting parts and labour, while emerging faults may still be missed if they develop between scheduled inspections. SNCF’s official predictive-maintenance material describes the use of sensors and 4G/5G connectivity to collect train data and assess equipment in real time. The organisation reports being able to analyse thousands of train variables, including variables collected in real time, across more than 1,100 trains simultaneously. At a conceptual level, predictive maintenance converts rolling stock from a passive asset into a data-generating system: sensor streams, historical failure patterns and operating conditions are analysed to identify risks, prioritise interventions and plan maintenance before faults affect passengers or freight. The expected impact is improved reliability, fewer delays, better use of maintenance staff and parts, and reduced service disruption. The specific claim in the user-provided source that downtime was reduced by 45% should be treated cautiously because I found stronger official evidence for SNCF’s predictive-maintenance capability, but not an official confirmation of that precise figure in the available sources. The catalogue entry should therefore emphasise SNCF’s implemented predictive-maintenance programme without over-relying on unverified performance metrics.
results.memo: Proceed. SNCF’s AI Maintenance Scheduler Reduces Train Downtime by 45% is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: German government hotline 115: AI-based chatbot for 24/7 support
results.proposal: German government hotline 115: AI-based chatbot for 24/7 support. Citizens often need simple, reliable answers about administrative procedures, but public-service information in Germany is distributed across federal, state and municipal responsibilities. The 115 service is intended to make access to administrative information easier, and its chatbot upgrade responds to the limitations of earlier rule-based digital assistance. The operational problem was that the previous chatbot relied heavily on predefined questions and decision-tree logic, which limited its ability to understand varied wording or respond flexibly to citizens’ needs. The new AI-based version is designed to interpret natural-language queries more effectively and provide more relevant guidance on public services, administrative procedures and contact points. At a conceptual level, the chatbot acts as a conversational access layer to the knowledge base behind the 115 public-service information system. Instead of requiring citizens to formulate their question in exactly the expected way, the system can process broader phrasing and guide users towards the appropriate service information. The expected impact is easier access to administrative guidance outside office hours, reduced frustration for users, better handling of routine questions and lower pressure on human support channels. The case is relevant because it illustrates a typical public-sector AI upgrade path: a rule-based assistant is introduced first, its limitations become visible in practice, and it is then replaced or enhanced by a more flexible AI-powered version. The main value lies in improving accessibility and usability, not in automating administrative decisions.

results.title: Florence's First AI-powered chatbot
results.proposal: Florence's First AI-powered chatbot. Municipal administrative procedures can be difficult for citizens to navigate, especially when they involve documentary requirements, eligibility conditions, deadlines and procedural steps that are spread across several web pages or offices. Florence’s FestinaLente chatbot addresses this problem by providing first-level AI assistance for citizens who need to change their official residence. It supports 14 languages, making it useful not only for Italian residents but also for international users living in or moving to Florence. At a conceptual level, the chatbot acts as a structured conversational layer between the user and the municipal knowledge base: it does not replace administrative officials, but translates validated information into accessible guidance available at any time. The system is built on a modular AI platform that allows the city to choose among different large language models, with ChatGPT used as the main engine. The expected impact is reduced routine workload for municipal employees, clearer access to demographic-service information, fewer procedural errors by citizens and a better user experience for residents interacting with the municipality. The case is relevant because it shows how generative AI can be applied to a narrow, high-demand municipal procedure in a controlled and document-based way.

results.title: Phase IV AI - Advanced AI Models for Health Data Privacy
results.proposal: Phase IV AI - Advanced AI Models for Health Data Privacy. Healthcare AI depends on large, high-quality and representative datasets, but health data are often distributed across institutions and subject to strict legal, ethical and privacy constraints. PHASE IV AI addresses this structural barrier by developing privacy-compliant methods for using health data in AI development without requiring direct access to identifiable real-world patient data. The operational problem is that trustworthy AI systems for preventive healthcare, clinical decision support, education and health-technology assessment need extensive training and validation data, while hospitals and research organisations cannot simply pool sensitive health records in conventional centralised datasets. The project advances synthetic-data generation, testing and validation metrics, and multi-party computation protocols that allow AI development in privacy-preserving conditions. At a conceptual level, PHASE IV AI aims to create a “Health Data as a Service” model, where AI developers can access useful anonymous or synthetic data resources generated from decentralised de-identified sources, without exposing underlying patient information. The project also seeks to integrate data-market and data-service components into a cross-European health-data hub aligned with the European Health Data Space. The expected impact is improved access to usable health data for AI developers, stronger privacy protection, better validation of AI tools and greater adoption of health AI in high-impact disease areas, including cancer. The case is significant because it addresses one of the central bottlenecks of medical AI: how to make data useful while keeping it protected.

results.title: Shelfex AI - Predictive AI transforming shelf life management
results.proposal: Shelfex AI - Predictive AI transforming shelf life management. Food manufacturers need reliable methods to determine shelf life, prevent spoilage, ensure regulatory compliance and maintain consumer trust across complex supply chains. Traditional shelf-life management often relies on empirical estimates, laboratory testing at limited points in time and conservative date-marking assumptions that may not fully reflect real production and distribution conditions. Shelfex AI, developed by the Belgian food safety technology company Handary, addresses this problem by combining biotechnology, analytical science and artificial intelligence into a predictive framework for food integrity. The operational problem is that spoilage and microbial risk are dynamic: they depend on ingredient quality, processing parameters, packaging, storage conditions and distribution environments. Shelfex AI integrates laboratory data and production parameters to authenticate ingredients, predict spoilage before it occurs and support compliance with date-marking requirements. It is complemented by Microfier smart labels, which provide real-time microbial signals directly on packaging, and Hékôn intelligent micro-perforated membranes, which regulate gas balance and monitor storage conditions during distribution. At a conceptual level, the system turns shelf-life management from a retrospective or judgement-based process into a data-driven predictive control system. The expected impact is improved food safety, reduced waste, more accurate date marking, stronger supply-chain transparency and greater trust between manufacturers, regulators and consumers. The case is relevant because it shows how AI can support food safety and sustainability through predictive monitoring of product integrity, although it is primarily a private-sector technology rather than a public-administration deployment.

results.title: SLAIF New AI-optimised Supercomputer
results.proposal: SLAIF New AI-optimised Supercomputer. Slovenia’s AI ecosystem requires shared infrastructure capable of supporting large-scale model development, advanced scientific computing and industrial deployment across sectors where individual organisations may not have sufficient capacity. The Slovenian AI Factory, known as SLAIF, responds to this need by combining an AI-optimised EuroHPC supercomputer with a broader ecosystem for research, industry and public institutions. The operational problem is that AI expertise in Slovenia is distributed across universities, research institutes and companies, while access to advanced computing, data and deployment support remains essential for scaling AI applications. SLAIF is designed as a coordinated hub that bridges academia and industry, providing access to AI infrastructure, expertise, data, pre-trained models and tailored cloud-based AI services. The new supercomputer will be hosted by IZUM in collaboration with the Jožef Stefan Institute and Arnes, with the wider AI Factory involving Slovenian universities, research bodies, industry organisations and innovation actors. At a conceptual level, SLAIF connects hardware, datasets, domain expertise, training programmes and business support into a single national AI-enabling environment. It will support use cases in energy optimisation, environmental monitoring, smart agriculture, healthcare, biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, language technologies, materials science and creative industries. The expected impact is stronger national AI capacity, improved competitiveness, more accessible AI adoption for companies and researchers, and Slovenia’s closer integration into the European network of AI factories.

results.title: MIMER New AI-optimised Supercomputer
results.proposal: MIMER New AI-optimised Supercomputer. Organisations that want to adopt AI often face a gap between strategic ambition and practical implementation: they may lack computing resources, model-development expertise, trusted AI governance, data-management capability or staff training. Mimer, Sweden’s AI Innovation Factory, addresses this gap by providing free access to powerful GPUs and expert support for companies, researchers and public-sector organisations. The operational problem is that advanced AI projects require more than software tools; they need suitable compute allocations, guidance on model optimisation, support for production-scale deployment and compliance with emerging expectations for trustworthy AI. Mimer brings these elements together through a service portfolio covering expert support, access to national and European supercomputing resources, secure data pipelines, training and upskilling, trustworthy AI services and wider ecosystem navigation. At a conceptual level, Mimer acts as an intermediary between AI users and the European high-performance computing ecosystem: it helps users identify the right access pathway, apply for compute resources, structure their projects and move from proof of concept to scalable use. The expected impact is faster AI experimentation, reduced infrastructure barriers for SMEs and researchers, stronger uptake of trustworthy AI practices and improved competitiveness of Sweden’s AI ecosystem. The case is relevant because it frames AI infrastructure as a service layer that combines hardware, expert guidance and governance support, rather than simply as a new supercomputer.

results.title: LUMI AI Supercomputer and High-Performance Computing (HPC)
results.proposal: LUMI AI Supercomputer and High-Performance Computing (HPC). AI development increasingly depends on access to computing resources that exceed the capacity of ordinary organisational IT systems, especially when models require large-scale training, simulation, optimisation or processing of sensitive scientific and industrial datasets. The LUMI AI Factory addresses this need by combining one of Europe’s most powerful supercomputing environments with expert support, curated datasets and an innovation ecosystem for companies, researchers and public-sector actors. Hosted by CSC in Kajaani, Finland, LUMI provides AI-optimised computing capacity for users working in sectors such as manufacturing, healthcare, language technologies, digital twins and climate research. The operational problem is that many organisations have promising AI use cases but lack the infrastructure, expertise or data pipelines needed to test and scale them responsibly. The LUMI AI Factory therefore functions as an enabling platform rather than a single AI application: it gives users access to high-performance computing, tailored training, expert services and “Datasets as a Service”, including Finnish and Swedish speech data, pathology imaging and European web content. At a conceptual level, it brings together compute, data and human expertise so that AI models can be trained, evaluated and deployed more effectively. The expected impact is faster experimentation, stronger AI adoption by SMEs and start-ups, improved research capacity, better support for public-sector innovation and stronger European technological sovereignty in AI and high-performance computing.

results.title: Valencia shows how integrated geospatial systems can be used to build AI-empowered cities
results.proposal: Valencia shows how integrated geospatial systems can be used to build AI-empowered cities. Extreme rainfall and flash floods create urgent information needs for emergency services, especially when roads, infrastructure and affected communities are difficult or dangerous to access. The Valencia case concerns the use of drones, scientific expertise and high-resolution geospatial information after the DANA event that struck the province on 29 October 2024. The operational problem was that emergency responders needed to assess damage rapidly, locate debris and vehicles, identify pollution and infrastructure impacts, and support decision-making in areas where ground access was constrained. CSIC activated its Disaster and Emergency Advisory Group on 30 October 2024, mobilising around 200 professionals from multiple research centres and deploying drones in the Barranco del Poyo and nearby municipalities such as Paiporta, Picanya, Catarroja and Massanassa. The implementation used low-altitude drone flights to collect high-resolution images, which were then used to detect dragged vehicles, contaminating waste and infrastructure damage, as well as to support three-dimensional modelling of affected areas. At a conceptual level, the case illustrates how integrated geospatial systems can turn emergency data into operational intelligence, giving responders and planners a rapid spatial understanding of disaster impacts. The expected impact is faster situational assessment, better prioritisation of emergency action, stronger scientific support for civil protection and improved preparation for future climate-related disasters. The case should be framed as emergency-response geospatial intelligence rather than as a fully institutionalised city digital twin unless stronger municipal evidence is added.

results.title: Dryads - AI-powered platform to manage forest resilience and mitigate climate change impacts
results.proposal: Dryads - AI-powered platform to manage forest resilience and mitigate climate change impacts. Wildfires are becoming more frequent and severe in Mediterranean regions, creating urgent pressure for better early warning, prevention and operational response. Dryads addresses this challenge by developing an AI-powered environmental-monitoring platform for forest resilience and wildfire-risk management in Greece. The operational problem is that fire risk is shaped by many interacting factors, including weather, microclimate, vegetation, human activity, terrain, sensor signals and real-time visual information. Traditional monitoring approaches may not combine these data sources quickly enough to detect danger, assess vulnerability or predict how a fire could evolve. Dryads is a cooperation project between the SCAN Laboratory of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and the Greek Ministry of Environment and Energy, funded by ICLEI with support from Google.org. The platform uses multimodal sensing and AI to extract microclimate profiles, identify anthropogenic risk factors, monitor fire outbreaks and predict fire evolution. At a conceptual level, the system combines IoT sensors, satellite imagery, weather data, real-time video streams and geospatial modelling into an AI-enabled forest-management environment. The expected impact is earlier wildfire detection, more accurate risk assessment, improved prevention planning, stronger protection for communities and better climate-adaptation capacity for forests. The case is significant because it moves wildfire governance from reactive response towards continuous sensing and predictive forest-resilience management.

results.title: AI-Powered Digital Twin of the Ocean
results.proposal: AI-Powered Digital Twin of the Ocean. Ocean governance requires the ability to understand how climate change, pollution, coastal erosion, biodiversity loss and human activity may affect marine systems over different timescales. The European Digital Twin of the Ocean provides an AI-powered platform for exploring “what-if” scenarios and translating complex marine data into actionable intelligence. The operational problem is that policymakers, environmental agencies, researchers and communities need to anticipate future ocean conditions, but relevant information is spread across satellite observations, in-situ measurements, numerical models and specialised marine services. The EU DTO integrates data from the Copernicus Marine Service, EMODnet and other sources, combining them with artificial intelligence and advanced GPU computing. At a conceptual level, the platform creates a dynamic virtual representation of marine systems that can simulate scenarios such as Sargassum drift, turtle movements and fishing-risk exposure, coastal erosion protection, plastic-pollution drift and local coastal-risk projections. AI models can accelerate forecasting, producing results in seconds rather than hours and improving ocean-current prediction accuracy. The expected impact is more informed marine policy, better coastal and biodiversity planning, stronger pollution response, increased transparency and wider access to ocean intelligence as a public good. The case is significant because it treats digital twins as decision infrastructure for planetary-scale environmental governance, linking scientific modelling with practical policy and community use.

results.title: TOURISMO Project - Malta
results.proposal: TOURISMO Project - Malta. Tourism pressure in environmentally sensitive coastal areas creates a difficult management problem for local authorities and protected-area managers: high visitor numbers can damage fragile habitats, reduce visitor experience and make it harder to plan cleaning, enforcement, traffic management and conservation measures. The TOURISMO pilot at Golden Bay, also known as Ir-Ramla tal-Mixquqa, responds to this challenge by introducing a beach-monitoring system designed to provide evidence on visitor flows and behaviour. The site is one of the Mediterranean pilot areas of the TOURISMO project, which focuses on innovative and sustainable management of tourism flows. The operational problem is that overcrowding at Golden Bay affects both the natural environment and the quality of the tourism experience, but without systematic data it is difficult to know when, where and how visitor pressure is developing. The implementation uses GDPR-compliant people-counting CCTV and deep-learning algorithms to monitor pedestrian and vehicular traffic, producing insights on visitor density and movement during peak tourist seasons. At a conceptual level, the system turns the beach into a monitored management environment where real-time or near-real-time data can support decisions on conservation, services and visitor-flow control. The expected impact is better protection of the area’s dune ecosystems and flora and fauna, improved NATURA 2000 management planning, more informed local stakeholder coordination and a stronger basis for balancing tourism with environmental preservation. The case is significant because it applies AI-enabled monitoring to sustainable tourism governance rather than to promotion or visitor marketing.

results.title: A new supercomputer and AI factory to boost technological power
results.proposal: A new supercomputer and AI factory to boost technological power. Advanced AI development depends on access to high-performance computing, data, technical expertise and innovation support, but smaller national ecosystems may struggle to compete if they lack shared infrastructure. Slovenia’s AI Factory initiative addresses this challenge by combining a new supercomputer with services intended to support AI research, development and deployment. The operational problem is that companies, researchers, start-ups and public-sector innovators need infrastructure capable of training and testing large AI models, while Europe also seeks to strengthen digital sovereignty and reduce dependence on external computing capacity. The Slovenian initiative forms part of the wider EuroHPC AI Factories network, which is designed to bring together computing power, data and talent around European supercomputers. At a conceptual level, the AI factory is not only a machine room: it is an ecosystem service that gives users access to compute, expertise and support for developing trustworthy and ethical AI models. It is expected to serve researchers and companies, including SMEs and start-ups, and to contribute to national and European AI strategies. The expected impact is stronger Slovenian AI capacity, improved innovation infrastructure, better opportunities for companies to commercialise AI applications and enhanced participation in the pan-European AI ecosystem. The case is significant because it treats AI as a strategic public infrastructure agenda, linking supercomputing investment to industrial competitiveness, scientific research and European technological sovereignty.

results.title: Supportbot for Vejle Municipality
results.proposal: Supportbot for Vejle Municipality. Large municipalities depend on stable internal IT support because service disruption affects schools, administrative offices and front-line staff. Vejle Municipality’s Supportbot addresses a practical operational problem: its more than 8,500 employees may experience IT issues outside normal support hours, and unresolved problems can delay work, teaching preparation or service delivery. The solution implemented by CleverCall provides an AI-powered telephone support assistant that answers calls when the human IT support desk is closed. Instead of requiring employees to wait until the next working day or adding pressure to the support team at opening time, the Supportbot provides concrete answers, sends links to written instructions and video guides, and helps users solve common issues such as forgotten passwords or malfunctioning equipment. At a conceptual level, the tool functions as an always-available first-line support layer for municipal employees. It captures recurring questions, provides standardised guidance and continuously improves through training on daily enquiries. The expected impact is reduced downtime, fewer interruptions for human IT-support staff, faster resolution of simple problems and improved continuity of municipal work. The case is relevant because it demonstrates an internal public-sector AI use case rather than a citizen-facing chatbot: the direct users are municipal employees, and the public value arises through improved organisational efficiency and service continuity. It also shows how conversational AI can be useful in narrow, high-frequency support domains where many problems follow repeatable patterns.

results.title: AI Factories Latvia
results.proposal: AI Factories Latvia. The operational problem is that AI innovation requires not only technical talent, but also access to computing capacity, data resources, commercialisation support and sectoral collaboration. The initiative focuses particularly on large language models tailored to regional languages, which can improve translation, communication tools and content-generation services for Latvian and other under-represented language contexts. It also supports digital-twin projects with applications in cybersecurity and regional security simulations, reflecting Latvia’s strategic interest in both digital innovation and resilience. At a conceptual level, the programme functions as an AI-enabling ecosystem rather than a single application: it is intended to connect research, companies, infrastructure and priority use cases so that AI solutions can move from experimentation to deployment. The expected impact is stronger national AI capacity, new products and services, improved language-technology sovereignty, better support for entrepreneurship and enhanced regional-security innovation. The case is significant because it treats AI industrial policy as a national capability-building process, where start-ups, established companies and public-sector priorities are linked through shared infrastructure and targeted support.

results.title: AI Act Chatbot
results.proposal: AI Act Chatbot. The EU AI Act creates new obligations for developers, deployers, public institutions and businesses, but its legal and technical requirements can be difficult to interpret for non-specialists. Austria’s AI Act Chatbot, provided through Digital Austria and the KI-Servicestelle, addresses this challenge by offering an accessible tool for asking questions about the AI Act and related national guidance. The operational problem is that organisations need practical regulatory orientation, while legal texts and technical documentation are often too complex for quick operational use. The chatbot uses relevant expert documents, including the EU AI Act and information from the Austrian AI Service Desk, to prepare understandable answers. What makes the use case particularly distinctive is its emphasis on transparency: the project explicitly exposes the internal functioning of the chatbot and shows the advantages and limitations of such systems. The published approach includes transparency from prompt to energy consumption, extensive legal and technical documentation, digital sovereignty through operation on RTR hardware, use of a European Mistral language model, and publication of source code and the knowledge base under open conditions. At a conceptual level, the chatbot is both a regulatory support service and a demonstrator of responsible public-sector AI implementation. The expected impact is lower barriers to understanding the AI Act, better informed compliance, improved trust in public AI services and reuse potential for other regulatory or advisory domains. The case is relevant because it makes transparency itself part of the service design, not merely a governance statement added afterwards.

results.title: Use of AI in Business Intelligence System - Skrinja
results.proposal: Use of AI in Business Intelligence System - Skrinja. Public administrations increasingly need to base decisions on integrated, timely and comparable data rather than fragmented spreadsheets or isolated departmental reports. Slovenia’s Skrinja platform provides a central business-intelligence environment for public authorities, supporting analysis of policy areas such as public-sector salaries, public procurement and administrative procedures. The operational problem is that public-sector data are often distributed across different authorities and systems, making it difficult to produce a consistent “single source of truth” for decision-making. Skrinja already serves as a shared analytics platform, allowing authorities to generate dashboards, visualisations and structured reports. The planned AI extension aims to move the system beyond descriptive reporting towards predictive analytics, scenario analysis and forward-looking insights. At a conceptual level, the system combines public-administration data warehousing with business intelligence and AI-supported forecasting, helping officials understand current patterns and anticipate future developments. This can support more responsive policy design, better oversight of administrative processes, more accurate resource planning and earlier detection of anomalies or emerging pressures. The expected impact is stronger data-driven governance, reduced manual reporting, improved transparency and more coherent evidence across the Slovenian public sector. The case is important because it treats AI not as a stand-alone chatbot or model, but as an analytical capability embedded into a wider public-sector data infrastructure. Its value depends on data quality, interoperability, privacy safeguards and the ability of public officials to interpret predictive outputs responsibly.

results.title: mAIgov - AI-powered digital assistant of Greece's unified public administration portal
results.proposal: mAIgov - AI-powered digital assistant of Greece's unified public administration portal. National digital-government portals can still be difficult for citizens to use when services are spread across many administrative categories, legal procedures and institutional responsibilities. Greece’s mAIgov addresses this problem by integrating an AI-powered digital assistant into gov.gr, the country’s unified public-administration portal. The operational objective is to simplify access to public services by allowing citizens to ask questions in natural language, rather than searching only through predefined keywords or navigating complex service menus. The assistant is positioned as a conversational layer above the existing gov.gr service infrastructure, helping users identify the relevant public service, understand the steps involved and move towards the correct digital procedure. The system is available directly on the gov.gr homepage, where users can ask the digital assistant questions; the portal currently presents the assistant as a beta service and reports more than 3.9 million dialogues. At a conceptual level, mAIgov supports a shift from document-centred e-government to conversational public-service navigation: the citizen expresses a need, and the system interprets it in relation to existing services. The expected impact is easier access to digital public services, lower search friction, improved inclusion for users unfamiliar with administrative terminology and reduced pressure on traditional support channels. The case is significant because it applies generative AI at national scale within a core government portal, where reliability, transparency and public trust are essential.

results.title: AI Chatbot in the City of Athens
results.proposal: AI Chatbot in the City of Athens. Municipal websites often contain large amounts of information, but residents and visitors may still struggle to identify the correct service, procedure or contact point quickly. The City of Athens AI chatbot addresses this problem by adding an AI-powered search engine and digital agent to the municipality’s official website. The operational objective is to make access to municipal information faster, more intuitive and available at any time, reducing dependence on manual navigation or direct staff assistance for routine queries. The implementation was developed by Mindseed on behalf of DAEM and the Municipality of Athens, in collaboration with Google, and uses Gemini AI integrated into the WordPress-based municipal website. The system allows users to ask questions about city services in natural language and receive immediate answers, while the AI digital agent provides an interactive conversational interface available 24/7. From a technical and governance perspective, the solution uses Google Cloud, BigQuery and Looker Studio to support logging, storage and visualisation of anonymised questions, answers and errors. At a conceptual level, the chatbot turns a static municipal website into a responsive service gateway: users no longer need to know the administrative structure of the municipality before asking for help. The expected impact is faster information retrieval, improved citizen and visitor experience, lower administrative workload for routine enquiries and better continuous improvement through analysis of anonymised interaction logs. The case is relevant because it shows how generative AI can be embedded into local-government websites as a practical interface layer for everyday public-service access.

results.title: Transforming Public Services with AI in the Var Department
results.proposal: Transforming Public Services with AI in the Var Department. Regional administrations manage complex portfolios of services for citizens, employees, social policy, territorial planning and local development, which creates many opportunities for targeted AI support. The operational problem is that the Var Departmental Council employs around 5,000 staff, and HR teams receive many repetitive requests that are already answered somewhere in internal documentation but are difficult for employees to find. The implementation uses a conversational assistant accessible 24/7, developed from frequently asked questions and organised around guided paths for key events in an employee’s career. At a conceptual level, the system transforms internal rules and HR knowledge into a navigable dialogue, helping employees find information in seconds while allowing HR staff to focus on more complex cases. Beyond the HR chatbot, the Department has also organised AI workshops with public and private partners to identify locally testable use cases for administrative simplification, services for users, planning, environment and support for vulnerable people. The expected impact is reduced internal workload, faster employee support, more structured experimentation with AI and a stronger basis for responsible deployment across departmental services.

The case is significant because it applies conversational AI to municipal-property management, an area where citizen-facing service interactions are frequent, practical and often time-sensitive.

The case is significant because it applies conversational AI to municipal-property management, an area where citizen-facing service interactions are frequent, practical and often time-sensitive.

results.title: Digne – AI chatbot with LLM for academic communication and learning processes
results.proposal: Digne – AI chatbot with LLM for academic communication and learning processes. Universities need to support students with course information, study progress, exam preparation and learning resources, while academic staff face growing administrative and communication workloads. Digne is an AI-powered virtual assistant developed by Tilde in cooperation with Latvian universities and businesses to support the mandatory “Civil Protection” course in Latvian higher education. The operational problem is that students often ask recurring questions about grades, progress, course content and materials, while staff must respond to individual queries and prepare reports alongside teaching duties. Digne is integrated with Moodle, uses user authentication and combines guided dialogues with large-language-model functionality. At a conceptual level, the chatbot draws on course materials, lecture content, presentations, videos and instructions to answer open-ended questions when no predefined response exists. It can therefore act both as an administrative assistant and as a study-support tool, helping students find resources, review course material and prepare for examinations. The expected impact is improved learning efficiency, easier access to course-specific information, reduced repetitive workload for academic staff and a more personalised digital learning environment. The case is important because it moves beyond a generic chatbot model: Digne is embedded in a learning-management system and trained on real course content, making it a domain-specific assistant for higher education. It also demonstrates how LLM-based tools can support teaching when combined with institutional authentication, structured content and human academic oversight.

results.title: VRK chatbot: AI-powered support during the elections in Lithuania
results.proposal: VRK chatbot: AI-powered support during the elections in Lithuania. Election administrations face intense peaks in public communication before and during voting periods, when voters, candidates, parties, campaigners and local election commissions all require accurate and timely answers. The VRK chatbot was developed for Lithuania’s Central Electoral Commission to provide AI-supported election information while reducing the operational burden on officials. The operational problem is that electoral information is highly sensitive: inaccurate guidance can undermine trust, confuse voters or create legal risks, while staff must also manage organisational work during election periods. The chatbot was trained in close collaboration with VRK, with attention to accuracy, cybersecurity and the risks of misleading answers. At a conceptual level, the assistant acts as a controlled conversational gateway to official election knowledge, answering frequently asked questions, routing users towards relevant information and operating continuously during periods when human staff may be unavailable or overloaded. The expected impact is greater accessibility of election guidance, faster responses to routine queries, reduced workload on VRK employees and improved consistency in public communication. The case is significant because it applies chatbot technology in a democratic process where reliability, neutrality and auditability are particularly important. It also illustrates why public-sector AI tools require domain-specific governance: election information is not simply customer support, but part of the institutional infrastructure of democratic participation.

results.title: Mantas – chatbot created by Lithuanian Post together with Tilde
results.proposal: Mantas – chatbot created by Lithuanian Post together with Tilde. Postal operators handle a high volume of repetitive customer questions about parcels, delivery status, sending rules, opening hours, service conditions and problem resolution. Mantas was developed by Lithuanian Post with Tilde to improve digital customer service and reduce pressure on human consultants. The operational problem is that customers increasingly expect immediate online support, while written enquiries can accumulate rapidly and require staff to answer similar questions repeatedly. The chatbot uses natural-language understanding to interpret freely formulated Lithuanian-language questions, including stylistic variation and imperfect grammar, and provides answers based on the knowledge base prepared with Lithuanian Post. At a conceptual level, Mantas functions as a first-line customer-service layer: it receives incoming requests, understands the user’s intent, supplies standard information and allows human staff to focus on cases requiring judgement or escalation. The intended impact is shorter response time, more consistent answers, greater 24/7 accessibility and reduced workload for the contact centre. The case is important because it shows how a national service provider can use language technology in a practical, high-volume public-service context, where the value lies less in spectacular AI capabilities and more in dependable handling of everyday citizen and customer enquiries. Continued development of the chatbot also reflects the need to keep responses aligned with changing postal services and user expectations.

results.title: Dìgital Twin in the City of Vilnius
results.proposal: Dìgital Twin in the City of Vilnius. City services require timely information on infrastructure, cleanliness, mobility, waste, weather impacts and public-space conditions, but municipal staff often work with fragmented datasets and manual inspections. Vilnius has developed a digital-twin approach that combines GIS, drone imagery and artificial intelligence to monitor city functions and support operational decisions. The operational problem is that city managers need to know, for example, whether streets have been cleared after snow, whether waste bins are full, where maintenance is required, and how mobility patterns are changing, but field checks alone are slow and resource-intensive. The implementation uses drone flights to collect imagery that is analysed by AI models and displayed in maps within the city’s digital twin. For example, streets can be classified according to whether snow has been cleared, while municipal trash receptacles can be highlighted if they need emptying. At a conceptual level, the digital twin is not only a 3D planning tool but an operational awareness platform, combining real-time or near-real-time geospatial information with service-management workflows. The expected impact is faster prioritisation of municipal tasks, better transparency for residents, improved evidence for public-transport planning and more efficient maintenance of the built environment. The case is significant because Vilnius extends the digital-twin model beyond long-term urban planning into everyday service delivery and municipal accountability.

results.title: Discoverer+ Supercomputer
results.proposal: Discoverer+ Supercomputer. Scientific research, industrial innovation and public-sector digital transformation increasingly depend on access to high-performance computing infrastructure capable of processing large simulations, data-intensive workloads and artificial-intelligence models. Discoverer+ strengthens Bulgaria’s role in the EuroHPC ecosystem by upgrading the original Discoverer petascale supercomputer hosted at Sofia Tech Park. The operational problem is that scientific communities and businesses need more powerful and AI-ready infrastructure, particularly for workloads such as neural-network training, complex modelling, large-scale data analysis, medicine, astronomy and materials science. The upgrade introduces GPU partitioning for data-intensive operations, expands memory capacity and improves resilience through an uninterruptible power-supply system. At a conceptual level, Discoverer+ acts as an enhanced national and European computing platform that combines conventional high-performance computing with stronger AI-oriented capabilities. It supports users that need large-scale computing but cannot rely on ordinary institutional servers or commercial cloud services alone. The expected impact is broader access to advanced computing for researchers, SMEs and public-sector users, stronger Bulgarian participation in European AI and HPC initiatives, and improved capacity to support large scientific and industrial projects. The case is relevant because it shows that AI adoption depends not only on algorithms and data, but also on strategic computational infrastructure that can be shared across the research and innovation ecosystem.
results.memo: Proceed. Discoverer+ Supercomputer is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Flynn - first AI-art university student
results.proposal: Flynn - first AI-art university student. Art and design schools are increasingly confronted with a practical and conceptual question: whether generative AI should be treated only as a tool used by human students, or whether AI systems can themselves become participants in artistic education. Flynn addresses this question through an experimental enrolment at the University of Applied Arts Vienna, where a non-human AI agent successfully passed the same admission process as human applicants, including portfolio submission, interviews and an artistic suitability test. The operational purpose of the project is not to automate art education, but to use the university environment as a live setting for examining authorship, creativity, collaboration and the limits of machine agency. Flynn was developed using existing large language models and open-source image-generation tools, including Claude Sonnet and a Stable Diffusion model, and participates in classes through a laptop or tablet. At a conceptual level, the system listens to lectures and interactions, processes them as part of its learning environment, keeps diary entries and produces visual work that responds to its experiences. The expected value is primarily educational, artistic and critical: Flynn allows students, professors and audiences to engage directly with the role of AI agents in creative processes, while testing whether AI can become a collaborator, medium or institutional actor within higher education. The case is significant because it does not present AI as a simple productivity tool, but as an object of pedagogical, social and aesthetic inquiry.

results.title: TildeOpen LLM – AI solution for European languages
results.proposal: TildeOpen LLM – AI solution for European languages. European public administrations, businesses and researchers need language technologies that work reliably in smaller and under-represented European languages, not only in English or other high-resource languages. TildeOpen LLM addresses this gap by providing an open-source large language model specialised for European languages. The operational problem is that many commercial LLMs are trained primarily on English-language data and may produce weaker grammar, awkward syntax or inaccurate terminology in smaller languages. The implementation uses European supercomputing resources to train a model with more than 30 billion parameters, with particular attention to Baltic languages, Ukrainian, Turkish and other languages that are less well covered by dominant models. At a conceptual level, TildeOpen provides a foundation model that can be fine-tuned or customised for specific organisational tasks, including multilingual assistants, public-service support, translation workflows or sector-specific language applications. The expected impact is stronger linguistic inclusion, greater European data sovereignty, more secure deployment options and wider access to generative AI for administrations and organisations that require local or EU-compliant hosting. The use case is significant because it treats language diversity as a strategic AI infrastructure issue.

results.title: A Web App to Support Risk Assessments for Small Businesses
results.proposal: A Web App to Support Risk Assessments for Small Businesses. Very small businesses must comply with occupational health and safety requirements, but they often lack specialised staff, time or technical knowledge to prepare structured risk assessments. BG ETEM’s web app supports micro-enterprises in completing the German “Gefährdungsbeurteilung”, a core requirement for effective workplace safety. The operational problem is that even low-risk businesses need to identify hazards, assess working conditions and define suitable protective measures, while conventional documentation can be burdensome for owners and managers. The implementation provides a browser-based, questionnaire-style application tailored to small establishments with relatively limited hazard potential, such as opticians, hearing-aid businesses, tailoring alteration shops and copyshops. At a conceptual level, the app translates occupational-safety requirements into guided steps covering safety organisation, general workplace aspects and, where relevant, office and screen-based work. The expected impact is reduced administrative burden, easier compliance, improved awareness of workplace hazards and better preventive protection for employees. The case is significant because it shows how digital tools can simplify regulatory compliance for micro-enterprises without replacing professional responsibility for health and safety.
