results.title: Municipality Welcome Manager (L2B2 Service Robot) in Ludwigsburg
results.proposal: Municipality Welcome Manager (L2B2 Service Robot) in Ludwigsburg. Visitors to municipal service offices often need orientation before reaching the correct desk, department or waiting area, especially in buildings where multiple citizen services are delivered. Ludwigsburg introduced L2B2 as a speaking service robot in the entrance area of its citizen office, making it the first German municipality to use this type of welcome robot in a city administration. The objective was to provide first information and guidance for citizens visiting the service department while demonstrating how robotics could support public-facing administration. The implementation uses a mobile robot that welcomes visitors, moves autonomously through corridors and accompanies them to relevant departments. At a conceptual level, the robot combines speech interaction, indoor navigation, visitor guidance and service information. It does not make administrative decisions or process applications; its role is to reduce uncertainty at the first point of contact and provide a visible, interactive guide within the municipal building. The expected impact is improved visitor experience, faster orientation, reduced routine guidance burden on staff and public familiarity with service robotics. Public material describes strong media and citizen interest, and the robot’s name was chosen through a public call, giving the project a participatory communication dimension as well as a technical one.
results.memo: Proceed. Municipality Welcome Manager (L2B2 Service Robot) in Ludwigsburg is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: eTranslation: Machine translation for public administrations
results.proposal: eTranslation: Machine translation for public administrations. European public administrations need to exchange information across many languages, but manual translation can be too slow or expensive for routine documents, datasets, forms and digital services. eTranslation provides the European Commission’s machine-translation service for EU institutions, public administrations, academia, SMEs, NGOs, Digital Europe Programme projects and other eligible users. The objective is to make multilingual public-sector communication faster and more accessible while relying on infrastructure aligned with European institutional needs. The implementation uses neural machine translation built on the EU’s long history of professional translation and is available both through a web interface and machine-to-machine APIs. At a conceptual level, the service receives text, documents or integrated system requests, translates them across official EU languages and selected associated languages, and returns raw machine translation that can be used for understanding, publication support or professional refinement. Public systems can integrate the API directly into services, such as portals that need to translate metadata or user-facing content across multiple languages. The expected impact is reduced translation turnaround, greater multilingual accessibility, easier cross-border public-service delivery and more efficient reuse of public data. Current Commission material presents eTranslation under AI-based multilingual services in the Digital Europe framework and confirms that both web pages and APIs are available for machine-to-machine access.

evidence.quote: The implementation uses neural machine translation built on the EU’s long history of professional translation and is available both through a web interface and machine-to-machine APIs.

results.title: Detection of mowing events on grasslands from Sentinel-data
results.proposal: Detection of mowing events on grasslands from Sentinel-data. Agricultural payment agencies must verify whether farmers comply with land-management requirements, but manual on-the-spot checks are costly, time-consuming and difficult to scale nationally. Estonia’s Agricultural Registers and Information Board applied satellite-data analysis to automate detection of mowing events on grasslands, supporting compliance checks for agricultural subsidies. The operational problem is that mowing is one of the conditions for receiving certain government grants, yet field inspections can only cover a limited sample of parcels. The implementation uses time series from Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical imagery, allowing the system to observe vegetation changes over the growing season even under frequent cloud cover. A deep-learning model with a reject option detects likely mowing events and can flag uncertain cases for further attention. At a conceptual level, the system converts satellite observations into a national monitoring layer for agricultural practice: changes in vegetation and surface characteristics indicate whether a field has probably been mown. The expected impact is fewer unnecessary field inspections, earlier reminders to applicants, better compliance monitoring and more efficient use of administrative resources. Public case records describe Estonia’s system as the first nationwide automated monitoring system for agricultural practices in the EU, operational from 2018, with reported mowing-detection accuracy of around 85%.

results.title: A unique artificial intelligence system now directs Ülemiste City drivers to available parking spots
results.proposal: A unique artificial intelligence system now directs Ülemiste City drivers to available parking spots. Large business districts can lose time, capacity and user satisfaction when drivers circulate looking for parking spaces without reliable real-time information. Ülemiste City introduced an AI-powered smart parking system to guide drivers directly to available spaces and reduce the uncertainty of parking in a busy urban campus. The implementation combines cameras, AI video analysis, signposts, LED displays and a web interface. Instead of relying on individual in-ground sensors for every bay, the system analyses camera feeds to estimate occupancy and communicate availability to drivers. At a conceptual level, computer-vision models detect vehicles and available spaces, aggregate occupancy information and distribute it through digital displays or interfaces so that drivers can decide where to go before entering or circulating through parking areas. The expected impact is shorter parking-search time, improved use of available capacity, lower unnecessary vehicle circulation and better experience for employees and visitors. The supplier, Pixevia, describes the underlying smart-parking technology as using precise mapping from security cameras, with one camera able to cover up to around 100 parking spots, and information on available places delivered to displays or applications.

results.title: Natural language processing for Land Registry documentation in Sweden
results.proposal: Natural language processing for Land Registry documentation in Sweden. Land-registry authorities manage large collections of historical legal documents, including handwritten records that can be difficult to search, interpret and reuse in modern digital workflows. The Swedish Land Registry used natural language processing to handle land-registry requests more efficiently by extracting and structuring information from low-quality handwritten documentation. The operational problem was that staff received many requests from citizens for information about properties, but older records were difficult to process because image quality and resolution were poor and handwriting recognition was challenging. The implementation first pre-processed handwritten documents to improve input quality, then used handwritten text recognition to extract text. A neural network then applied word corrections and associations to complete sentences where the recognition process missed words, after which an AI model highlighted key features such as locations, names and summaries. At a conceptual level, the system combines image pre-processing, handwritten text recognition, neural language correction and information extraction. The expected impact is faster handling of citizen requests, reduced manual search effort, better access to historical property information and more time for case handlers to focus on urgent decisions.
results.memo: Proceed. Natural language processing for Land Registry documentation in Sweden is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Management of the emergency at Hospital Gemelli - Rome
results.proposal: Management of the emergency at Hospital Gemelli - Rome. Major hospitals faced exceptional operational pressure during the COVID-19 emergency, requiring rapid decisions on intensive-care capacity, ward planning, patient pathways and resource allocation. Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Agostino Gemelli IRCCS used SAS analytics to support management of the emergency by transforming clinical and organisational data into actionable insight. The practical problem was that many important data relating to COVID-19 patients were unstructured, particularly information contained in clinical notes and hospital documentation, while managers and clinicians needed timely intelligence on patient flows, complications and expected organisational impact. The implementation used SAS analytics, visual analytics and text-mining techniques to extract information from unstructured clinical data, support prediction of intensive-care demand, understand possible medical complications and plan hospital operations. At a conceptual level, the system combines data integration, text mining, predictive analytics, dashboards and operational planning. Its expected impact was faster access to clinical information, better forecasting of admissions and hospitalisation needs, more efficient resource allocation and support for personalised patient pathways. SAS describes Gemelli as using its solutions to predict ICU admissions, understand medical complications, plan ward work and manage COVID-19 vaccine administration.

results.title: Reporting issues in public space
results.proposal: Reporting issues in public space. Cities receive large volumes of reports about waste, broken infrastructure, unsafe traffic situations, nuisance and maintenance issues, and the value of such reporting depends on routing each case to the correct municipal team. Amsterdam’s public-space reporting system allows residents to submit issues online, by phone or through external applications. The earlier approach depended heavily on users choosing the right category from many drop-down options, which could lead to errors and delays because the municipality has many service departments and categories. The implementation uses an algorithm within the Signals reporting system to recognise relevant words and phrases in the user’s description, infer the likely category and support routing to the responsible department. At a conceptual level, the system applies natural-language processing or keyword-based text classification to citizen-submitted reports, then links the classification to municipal workflow allocation. This reduces the administrative burden on the person making the report and improves the chance that the case reaches the correct team quickly. The expected impact is faster processing, fewer misrouted reports, less manual reclassification and better responsiveness in public-space management.
results.memo: Proceed. Reporting issues in public space is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Automated parking control
results.proposal: Automated parking control. Managing scarce parking space in a dense city requires regular enforcement, reliable permit checks and a process that can cover large numbers of parked vehicles without excessive manual patrol effort. Amsterdam uses automated parking control to determine whether parked vehicles have the right to occupy paid parking spaces, either because a fee has been paid through a parking meter or app, or because the vehicle has a valid parking permit. The implementation uses scan cars equipped with cameras and automatic number-plate recognition to identify licence plates and check them against relevant payment and permit systems. At a conceptual level, the scan car captures the plate, converts it into machine-readable data, checks the data against back-office records and flags cases where no valid parking right appears to exist. Human procedures can then verify and handle enforcement actions where needed. The expected impact is more efficient street-parking enforcement, better compliance with parking rules, reduced fraud and improved turnover of parking spaces. The system operates at large scale: Egis reports that Amsterdam’s on-street parking service uses ANPR to monitor more than six million vehicles per month.

evidence.quote: The expected impact is more efficient street-parking enforcement, better compliance with parking rules, reduced fraud and improved turnover of parking spaces.

results.memo: Proceed. Automated parking control is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: KRATID - Detecting traffic anomalies and incidents of the Estonian data exchange layer (X-Road)
results.proposal: KRATID - Detecting traffic anomalies and incidents of the Estonian data exchange layer (X-Road). Digital government depends on reliable data exchange between public institutions, and Estonia’s X-Road is a critical infrastructure layer for secure communication between public and private-sector systems. KRATID uses machine learning to monitor traffic patterns in the Estonian data exchange layer and detect anomalies or possible incidents. The operational problem is that very large numbers of exchanges take place through X-Road, making it difficult for human administrators to identify unusual behaviour, technical faults or unexpected changes in service use manually. The implementation compares current data-exchange behaviour with previous periods and searches for differences that may indicate an error, abnormal usage or another event requiring attention. At a conceptual level, the system combines traffic monitoring, anomaly detection, historical pattern comparison and human review. If the system cannot determine whether an observed situation is erroneous or permitted, a user still decides how to interpret the signal. The expected impact is stronger operational awareness for the Information System Authority, faster detection of incidents, better guidance for X-Road users and more resilient digital public infrastructure. The use case should be separated from other Estonian AI examples sometimes listed in the same source, such as job matching, land-mowing detection or police traffic deployment; the core KRATID case concerns X-Road anomaly and incident detection.

results.company: Finnish Government Shared Services Centre for Finance and HR
results.title: Palkeet - RPA Project
results.proposal: Palkeet - RPA Project. Shared service centres handle large volumes of repetitive finance and HR tasks where accuracy, consistency and processing speed are essential. Palkeet, the Finnish Government Shared Services Centre for Finance and HR, introduced robotic process automation to automate routine business processes across public administration support services. The operational problem was that tasks such as purchase-invoice validation, supplier-register maintenance and other administrative checks required structured but repetitive work by staff. The implementation used UiPath software robots, alongside other tools where appropriate, to model and execute automated workflows. At a conceptual level, RPA bots log into existing systems, follow predefined process rules, validate data, move information between applications and flag exceptions for human review. This approach allowed Palkeet to automate without immediately replacing all underlying legacy systems. The expected impact is higher productivity, improved processing quality, fewer manual errors, faster throughput and better use of staff time for expert work. The project is recognised as one of the first major RPA implementations in the Finnish public sector and formed part of a wider government digitalisation agenda. UiPath’s case material states that Palkeet began considering RPA in spring 2015 and became one of the first Finnish organisations to foresee its benefits, while Palkeet remains an active shared-services provider in Finnish government.
results.memo: Proceed. Palkeet - RPA Project is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Dashboard to Explore state spending in Finland
results.proposal: Dashboard to Explore state spending in Finland. Open procurement data can strengthen public accountability only if citizens, companies and analysts can understand what the government is buying and from whom. Finland’s Explore State Spending service, Tutkihankintoja.fi, provides a public dashboard for examining government purchase-invoice data, including spending by procuring organisation, supplier and category of goods or services. The operational problem was that e-invoicing data from the state system was not originally categorised according to a standard procurement taxonomy, making it difficult to search, compare or analyse. Hansel piloted a machine-learning solution to automatically categorise state e-invoicing data according to the United Nations Standard Products and Services Code taxonomy. At a conceptual level, the system takes invoice-level procurement data, classifies spending into meaningful procurement categories and makes it searchable through a public web interface. This enables users to explore areas such as ICT procurement, administrative services, equipment or transport-related purchases. The expected impact is greater transparency, easier spending analysis, better procurement oversight and improved data quality for public buyers. Other AI-enabled analysis is also used internally for procurement authorities. Current sources confirm that the portal remains online and that Hansel continued expanding the service by adding new organisations in 2023.

evidence.quote: At a conceptual level, the system takes invoice-level procurement data, classifies spending into meaningful procurement categories and makes it searchable through a public web interface.

results.memo: Proceed. Dashboard to Explore state spending in Finland is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Sentilo BCN - Plataforma de Sensors i Actuadors de Barcelona
results.proposal: Sentilo BCN - Plataforma de Sensors i Actuadors de Barcelona. Smart-city services depend on the ability to collect, share and reuse information from many heterogeneous sensors and urban systems without creating isolated vertical platforms. Barcelona City Council developed Sentilo as an open-source sensor and actuator platform to support its smart-city strategy and provide a reusable infrastructure layer for real-time urban data. The practical challenge was to connect diverse devices, applications and legacy systems in a way that was open, interoperable and scalable across city domains. The implementation provides a cross-platform architecture through which sensors and actuators can publish and consume data, allowing different applications to reuse information from the same urban infrastructure. At a conceptual level, Sentilo acts as a middleware layer between physical devices and smart-city applications: sensors send data to the platform, applications subscribe to relevant streams, and the city can manage urban information through open standards and shared interfaces. This avoids fragmented one-purpose solutions and supports integration across environmental monitoring, mobility, public space, energy and other municipal services. The expected impact is improved interoperability, lower integration cost, stronger reuse of urban data and a larger ecosystem of cities and companies using free software. Current sources describe Sentilo BCN as providing real-time information on Barcelona and confirm that Sentilo remains available as open-source software with public documentation and code repositories.

evidence.quote: At a conceptual level, Sentilo acts as a middleware layer between physical devices and smart-city applications: sensors send data to the platform, applications subscribe to relevant streams, and the city can manage urban information through open standards and shared interfaces.

results.memo: Proceed. Sentilo BCN - Plataforma de Sensors i Actuadors de Barcelona is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Predictive maintenance for wind farms
results.proposal: Predictive maintenance for wind farms. Wind-power operators need to minimise unplanned downtime because failures in turbines can reduce energy production, increase maintenance costs and require costly intervention in remote or difficult-to-access sites. This predictive-maintenance service applies machine-learning techniques to support more efficient management of wind-power assets, with the objective of anticipating failures before they cause stoppages or major damage. The operational problem is that wind turbines generate large volumes of sensor and operational data, but maintenance decisions often depend on identifying weak signals before they become visible through conventional inspection. The implementation uses a software system that processes machinery, sensor and production data to estimate component health, detect abnormal patterns and forecast the risk of specific failures. At a conceptual level, the system combines IoT or machine data, historical failure records, predictive algorithms, alerts, maintenance planning and reporting. This allows maintenance teams to schedule targeted interventions, prioritise high-risk assets and avoid unnecessary preventive work where a component remains healthy. The expected impact is lower downtime, reduced maintenance cost, improved production efficiency and better quality of asset-management decisions. AIMonitoring’s current Predeep platform describes AI-supported predictive maintenance, integration with 4.0 machinery, IoT sensors and databases, automatic alerts, maintenance planning and reported average results such as reduced downtime and maintenance costs, although those performance figures are supplier-reported.

results.title: SARI (Automatic Image Recognition System)
results.proposal: SARI (Automatic Image Recognition System). Facial images can be important investigative material when police need to compare a person shown in a photograph or video with people already recorded in law-enforcement databases. SARI, the Automatic Image Recognition System, was introduced in Italy for the Ministry of the Interior and the Central Anti-Crime Directorate of the State Police. The system is supplied by Parsec 3.26 S.r.l. and is structured around two components: SARI Enterprise and SARI Real-Time. SARI Enterprise supports retrospective identification by comparing a facial image already available to investigators with images in police databases of previously photo-recorded individuals. SARI Real-Time, by contrast, was designed to recognise people from a watch list through camera feeds. At a conceptual level, the technology combines biometric feature extraction, facial matching, image comparison and investigative review. Its operational value lies in helping officers narrow searches, identify possible matches and accelerate investigations where visual evidence is available. However, the two components raise different legal and ethical issues: retrospective matching for investigative purposes is different from real-time public-space recognition, which requires stronger safeguards because of its surveillance implications. The system should therefore be understood as an investigative-support tool whose outputs require human validation and legal control, not as an autonomous identification or enforcement mechanism. Current public material most clearly confirms knowledge of SARI Enterprise as the facial-recognition system used by Italian law enforcement for after-the-fact investigative identification.

results.company: CSI Piemonte (Inhouse ICT of Regione Piemonte)
results.title: AI Autonomation -  Automatic classification tools and integration with Robot Process Automation (RPA)
results.proposal: AI Autonomation -  Automatic classification tools and integration with Robot Process Automation (RPA). Public administrations receive large volumes of email and document-based requests that must be routed to the correct office before any substantive work can begin. CSI Piemonte developed an AI Automation prototype to combine automatic classification tools with Robotic Process Automation, using the regional car-tax management service as a concrete test case. The operational problem was that emails arriving in public-service channels required manual reading, categorisation and forwarding, creating delays and repetitive workload. The implementation uses text classification to sort incoming emails according to their content and direct them to the relevant offices. Where the content and process conditions allow, the system can also trigger RPA workflows so that routine responses or administrative actions are handled automatically. At a conceptual level, the solution combines natural language processing, classification models, workflow routing and robotic process execution. The expected impact is faster email handling, fewer manual sorting tasks, improved consistency of routing and greater capacity for staff to focus on exceptions or complex cases. The use case is framed by CSI Piemonte as research and development work from 2019, centred on a prototype for the regional vehicle-tax service. It demonstrates how relatively narrow administrative processes can be automated by pairing AI classification with process automation rather than trying to replace entire services.
results.memo: Proceed. AI Autonomation -  Automatic classification tools and integration with Robot Process Automation (RPA) is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: PRE-VIEW - Identification of international crisis
results.proposal: PRE-VIEW - Identification of international crisis. Foreign ministries need early signals of instability so that diplomatic, stabilisation and humanitarian responses can be planned before crises escalate. Germany’s Federal Foreign Office uses PRE-VIEW, short for Prediction, Visualization, Early Warning, as a data-analytics tool to support crisis early warning and stabilisation planning. The operational problem is that political, social, economic and conflict-related developments produce large volumes of open data, but analysts need structured insight rather than unfiltered information. The implementation analyses publicly available data on current trends and conflicts, then produces maps, infographics and trend analyses for officials working on international stabilisation and crisis engagement. At a conceptual level, PRE-VIEW combines data collection, machine-learning or AI-supported processing, conflict indicators, geospatial visualisation and analyst-facing dashboards. The system helps civil servants understand how a conflict or political situation is evolving and what developments may require attention. Its outputs support, rather than determine, decisions about next steps in foreign-policy and stabilisation work. The expected impact is earlier identification of emerging risks, better situational awareness, more evidence-based crisis engagement and stronger prioritisation of preventive action. The case fits within the broader international field of AI-supported crisis early warning, where specialised models and integration into decision processes are increasingly emphasised.
results.memo: Proceed. PRE-VIEW - Identification of international crisis is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.company: the Zentral- und Ansprechstelle Cybercrime (Contact Office for Cyber Crime, ZAC NRW)
results.title: AI to combat child pornography online
results.proposal: AI to combat child pornography online. Investigations into child sexual abuse material impose a severe workload and psychological burden on investigators, who may need to review large numbers of harmful images while identifying victims, suspects and links between cases. North Rhine-Westphalia’s cybercrime contact office, ZAC NRW, collaborated with Microsoft and researchers to explore AI-supported analysis methods for this investigative context. The operational objective was to reduce manual exposure to harmful material and accelerate the identification of relevant evidence, while complying with strict rules on data protection and child protection. The implementation used software to anonymise or protect data before analysis, with cloud-based algorithms examining images, detecting illegal content indicators and supporting comparison with profiles or known material. At a conceptual level, the system combines content classification, face or feature matching, secure data handling and investigative review workflows. The technology is intended to support police and prosecutors by triaging and structuring evidence, not to replace human legal assessment or investigative responsibility. The expected impact is faster case analysis, reduced psychological strain for officers, better detection of recurring victims or perpetrators and more efficient allocation of specialist investigative resources. Public material from North Rhine-Westphalia describes the work as a research cooperation at ZAC NRW using AI analysis methods to combat child sexual abuse material.

results.title: The Youth Guarantee Support System (YGSS) to identifying young people not in education or employment
results.proposal: The Youth Guarantee Support System (YGSS) to identifying young people not in education or employment. Young people who are not in education, employment or training can be difficult for municipalities to identify early, especially when information about education, work, residence and social support is held in separate registers. Estonia’s Youth Guarantee Support System helps municipal case managers identify residents aged 16–26 who may need support to return to education or enter the labour market. The objective is to turn existing administrative data into an outreach mechanism for youth support, while keeping the intervention anchored in municipal casework. The implementation works through the STAR social-services and benefits information system. Twice a year, municipalities that have joined the programme can receive a list of young people registered in their locality who appear, based on data from multiple registers, to be in a NEET situation and potentially in need of help. At a conceptual level, the system combines register-based screening, local-authority access controls, case-manager review, youth contact and consent-based follow-up. Young people can restrict analysis, and where support proceeds, they are contacted and asked to complete a survey before individual assistance is planned. The expected impact is earlier identification of unsupported youth, more proactive municipal outreach, better targeting of employment and education services, and stronger prevention of long-term exclusion. Current European and Estonian policy sources continue to describe youth-guarantee support and NEET-targeted measures as active policy areas.
results.memo: Proceed. The Youth Guarantee Support System (YGSS) to identifying young people not in education or employment is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: BOSCO - Distribution of financial aid
results.proposal: BOSCO - Distribution of financial aid. Energy-price vulnerability requires public authorities to determine quickly and consistently whether households qualify for financial support with electricity bills. BOSCO was introduced in Spain by the Secretary of State for Energy to help electricity suppliers assess eligibility for the bono social eléctrico, a social tariff that reduces bills for eligible consumers. The stated rationale was to simplify the process for applicants and make eligibility checking more efficient for reference electricity suppliers. The implementation is an automated decision-support or rule-processing system that checks whether applicants meet legal and regulatory conditions for the social tariff. At a conceptual level, BOSCO translates eligibility rules into software logic, receives or verifies applicant information and returns an outcome that determines whether the supplier can apply the discount. The expected administrative benefit was faster processing, standardised eligibility checks and reduced burden on utility companies. However, the system became controversial after reports that eligible applicants were wrongly denied support. Civio investigated the problem and requested access to the source code to understand the causes. In 2025, Spain’s Supreme Court ordered the administration to provide access to the BOSCO code, making the case a major example of algorithmic transparency in public-service decision-making. Its significance therefore lies both in welfare automation and in the legal debate over accountability for automated public decisions.

results.title: Detecting 'unknown' companies with environmental risk
results.proposal: Detecting 'unknown' companies with environmental risk. Environmental supervision depends on knowing which businesses operate in a municipality, what activities they carry out and whether those activities may create inspection or permitting risks. Eindhoven’s use case focused on mapping “unknown” companies that could pose a potential environmental risk by using data more intelligently. The operational problem is that companies may be invisible to inspectors because records are incomplete, activities change, addresses are inconsistent or information is distributed across multiple administrative sources. This creates the risk that environmentally relevant businesses are not prioritised for supervision or included in the appropriate regulatory process. The implementation uses data matching and analytical screening to identify companies that may fall outside established inspection lists but show characteristics associated with environmental risk. At a conceptual level, the system combines business-register information, location data, sector classifications, permit or enforcement records and risk indicators to generate candidate companies for further human review. The expected impact is better coverage of environmental supervision, earlier detection of potentially risky activities, more efficient targeting of inspections and improved data quality in municipal environmental registers. The system should be understood as a prioritisation and discovery tool: it does not determine guilt or non-compliance, but helps inspectors find entities that may require attention. Public case material records the project as an Eindhoven initiative to make otherwise hard-to-find companies visible through smarter data use.

results.title: Intelligent traffic control systems (I-VRI's) - Better traffic flow
results.proposal: Intelligent traffic control systems (I-VRI's) - Better traffic flow. Urban traffic intersections must balance the needs of private vehicles, buses, emergency services, cyclists and pedestrians while reducing congestion and improving journey reliability. In Gelderland, existing traffic lights at eight intersections in Arnhem and Velp were replaced with intelligent traffic-control systems, or iVRIs, to support better traffic flow. The objective was to move beyond fixed or locally reactive signalling by using digital information from road users and connected systems. The implementation uses mobile data and vehicle-to-infrastructure communication so that road users and traffic-control installations can exchange information. Buses and emergency services can receive priority when approaching an intersection, while other road users may receive up-to-date information about routes and speed advice. At a conceptual level, iVRIs combine connected traffic-light controllers, data exchange standards, road-user messages, priority rules and adaptive signal control. This allows the intersection to respond more dynamically to current traffic conditions and to support policy priorities such as public transport reliability or emergency response. The expected impact is smoother traffic flow, reduced waiting times, better journey predictability and more efficient use of existing road infrastructure. Dutch public portals continue to provide national visibility on iVRI deployments, while Gelderland’s own public material refers to implementation and execution documents for the Arnhem and Velp iVRIs.

results.title: Infobox criminal and unexplained assets (iCOV)
results.proposal: Infobox criminal and unexplained assets (iCOV). Financial crime investigations often require analysts to understand relationships between people, companies, assets, income, transactions and public records that are dispersed across different authorities. The Infobox Crimineel en Onverklaarbaar Vermogen, known as iCOV, provides Dutch public partners with data-driven reports that support the detection and disruption of money laundering, tax evasion, fraud and unexplained wealth. The operational problem is that individual agencies may each hold partial information, while criminal financial structures often exploit fragmentation between enforcement, tax, customs, labour and supervisory bodies. The implementation is a formal cooperation between public organisations, including the Public Prosecutor’s Office, National Police, Tax Authorities, Customs, FIOD, Financial Intelligence Unit and several inspection and investigative services. At a conceptual level, iCOV combines authorised data access, risk indicators, analytical models and reporting formats to generate insight into assets, income relationships, companies and suspicious patterns. The system is not a fully autonomous enforcement mechanism; its outputs support investigation, prosecution and asset recovery by giving professionals a richer picture of potential criminal or unexplained wealth. The expected impact is faster financial investigation, improved targeting of asset-confiscation work, stronger inter-agency cooperation and more effective action against organised financial crime. Current public information describes iCOV as an active cooperation that helps partners through data-driven reports, including practical examples of use by investigation and prosecution services.

results.title: Geniq -  reports wait times
results.proposal: Geniq -  reports wait times. Mental-health providers need accurate and current information on waiting times because delays affect access to care, referral choices, planning, accountability and communication with patients and commissioners. Geniq was developed for Dutch mental-health institutions as a reporting and analytics capability that calculates, analyses and reports waiting times so that managers and operational teams can maintain an up-to-date view of service accessibility. The practical problem is that waiting-time data can sit across electronic client records, intake processes, treatment-planning systems and reporting obligations, making it difficult to produce consistent insight without manual extraction and reconciliation. The implementation uses data-processing and reporting functionality connected to the care-administration environment, allowing institutions to calculate waiting-time indicators, analyse patterns and generate reports for internal management or external accountability. At a conceptual level, the system transforms operational registration data into structured management information, helping organisations distinguish where delays arise, which pathways are under pressure and where additional capacity or process changes may be needed. The expected impact is better planning of clinical capacity, faster identification of bottlenecks, stronger compliance with waiting-time transparency requirements and more informed dialogue with referrers, insurers and patients. In the wider Dutch mental-health context, reliable waiting-time insight remains important because national regulators continue to emphasise the need for dependable data on the scale and development of GGZ waiting times.

results.title: Chatbot Poseidon - Municipality of Palaio Faliro
results.proposal: Chatbot Poseidon - Municipality of Palaio Faliro. Residents and visitors to a municipality often need quick answers about local services, procedures, facilities, events and community resources. Poseidon was introduced as a virtual assistant on the Municipality of Palaio Faliro’s digital portal to make municipal information more accessible through an automated conversational channel. The operational problem is common in local government: useful information may exist online, but users do not always know where to find it, which department is responsible or which procedure applies to their situation. The implementation uses a chatbot interface embedded in the municipal website, allowing users to ask questions and receive automated guidance rather than navigating only through static pages. At a conceptual level, the system recognises common municipal-service queries, retrieves or maps the relevant information and directs users towards appropriate content or service pathways. The expected impact is faster access to municipal information, fewer routine enquiries for staff, better availability outside office hours and improved user experience for people interacting with the municipality online. The chatbot’s function is primarily informational and navigational: it does not replace formal applications, permits or administrative decisions, but provides a more convenient first point of contact. The case fits into Palaio Faliro’s wider digital-service approach, where municipal online channels are used to improve citizen support and access to local services.

results.proposal: Chatbot - Lad Va. The Rural Support Service of Latvia introduced the LAD virtual assistant to make information about agricultural and rural support services easier to access online. The operational problem is that the agency provides a large number of services, while its users often work seasonally and may need answers when consultants or regional offices are not available. The implementation uses an AI-powered chatbot that answers general enquiries and helps users navigate support programmes, rural development measures, funding opportunities and administrative procedures. At a conceptual level, the assistant interprets a user’s question, maps it to the relevant institutional information and provides guidance in conversational form. It reduces the need for users to search across many pages or contact staff for routine questions. The expected impact is quicker access to information, reduced workload for agency employees, better support for applicants and improved accessibility of rural-support administration. The chatbot also helps standardise answers in a service area where rules, deadlines and funding conditions can be complex. Its role is informational and navigational, supporting users before formal application, assessment or decision-making processes take place.

results.title: Use of Public Lighting System to Deploy a Comprehensive Smart City Platform
results.proposal: Use of Public Lighting System to Deploy a Comprehensive Smart City Platform. Public lighting is one of the most extensive forms of urban infrastructure, making it a strong foundation for smart-city services when it is connected, centrally managed and technically scalable. Paris used its public-lighting system as the basis for a citywide smart-city platform, with the aim of reducing energy consumption, improving public safety and creating infrastructure that could support future digital services. The operational problem was not limited to lighting: the city needed a networked urban grid that could minimise environmental impact while also enabling new functions across the public realm. The implementation modernised and connected the lighting grid, transforming it from a standalone utility into a smart-city-ready infrastructure layer. At a conceptual level, connected lighting points can provide power, location, communication and mounting capacity for additional sensors, actuators or urban services. This makes it easier to scale future applications without rebuilding infrastructure from scratch. The expected impact is lower electricity consumption, better maintenance, improved user experience, enhanced public-space safety and a reusable platform for other smart services. The case is important because it treats lighting not simply as an energy-efficiency target, but as a strategic physical and digital backbone for urban innovation.

results.company: Technology Foundation Berlin and the Berlin University of Applied Sciences (HTW)
results.title: COMo - CO2 monitoring in publicly accessible indoor spaces
results.proposal: COMo - CO2 monitoring in publicly accessible indoor spaces. Publicly accessible indoor spaces such as cultural venues, educational buildings and hospitality settings needed practical ways to manage air quality during the pandemic, when ventilation was closely linked to infection-risk reduction. COMo used carbon dioxide concentration as a proxy indicator for indoor air quality and aerosol accumulation, helping operators understand when rooms needed ventilation. The initiative built on the earlier Clair Berlin work and focused on connected sensors that could collect, process and publish CO₂ readings from indoor environments. The implementation combined networked CO₂ sensors, an Internet of Things platform, data processing and public visualisation. At a conceptual level, sensors measured indoor air conditions, transmitted readings to a digital platform, and converted them into actionable information for operators and visitors. Facility managers could use the information to decide when to ventilate, while visitors could consult published data before entering a space. The expected impact was more objective management of indoor air, improved confidence in public venues, better infection-prevention behaviour and a replicable model for low-cost environmental monitoring. The value of the case lies in translating an invisible risk factor into visible, operational information that could support everyday decisions without requiring specialist technical knowledge from building users.
results.memo: Proceed. COMo - CO2 monitoring in publicly accessible indoor spaces is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Talk with Arianna - the chatbot of the Italian National Institute for Social Security
results.proposal: Talk with Arianna - the chatbot of the Italian National Institute for Social Security. Citizens using INPS digital services often need immediate help with access credentials before they can complete personal procedures online. Arianna was designed as a virtual assistant dedicated to questions about the INPS PIN, a credential historically used to access services on the institute’s website. The operational problem was that users frequently needed guidance on how to request, manage, recover or understand their PIN, and these recurring enquiries could generate avoidable pressure on help desks and service channels. The implementation uses a conversational chatbot interface that allows citizens to interact through a guided dialogue rather than searching manually across support pages. At a conceptual level, the assistant recognises the user’s question, connects it to the relevant support content and provides a direct answer or orientation on the next step. The expected impact is faster access to credential-related information, reduced repetitive support requests, improved usability for citizens and a more efficient first level of digital assistance. Although the use case is narrow, it is significant because identity and access management are preconditions for many welfare and social-security services. By making support available continuously and in a conversational format, Arianna helped reduce friction at a critical entry point to INPS online services.

results.title: Virtual Assistant based on generative AI at INPS
results.proposal: Virtual Assistant based on generative AI at INPS. Citizens using social-security services often struggle to find the correct information among many pages, circulars, administrative messages and service sheets, especially for complex benefits such as pension schemes. INPS began experimenting with a generative-AI virtual assistant to improve search and orientation on its website. The objective is to allow users to ask follow-up questions conversationally after searching for a service, receiving clearer explanations and guidance without having to interpret multiple documents independently. The implementation uses a large language model through Microsoft Azure and OpenAI technologies, integrated into the INPS digital environment. In the first experimental area, the assistant supported questions on the “Opzione Donna” pension measure, drawing from service pages, circulars, messages and internal acts. At a conceptual level, the system combines retrieval of institutional knowledge sources with conversational generation, maintaining dialogue context so that users can ask additional questions and receive more precise answers. The expected impact is improved accessibility of social-security information, more intuitive navigation of INPS services, reduced friction for citizens and better use of institutional documentation. The assistant is designed as an information and orientation tool, not as a decision-maker on eligibility or benefits. Its significance lies in the movement from traditional keyword search towards conversational access to complex public-administration knowledge.

results.title: "INPS risponde" - Optimised management of web requests to Customer Service
results.proposal: "INPS risponde" - Optimised management of web requests to Customer Service. Digital customer-service channels can become inefficient when many requests must be handled twice: first by a front-line operator and then again by a specialist office. INPS Risponde receives large numbers of online requests from citizens seeking clarification on services, rules and individual procedures. The operational challenge is to distinguish simple requests that can be handled at first level from complex ones that require second-level intervention, thereby reducing unnecessary handovers and response delays. INPS developed an AI decision engine upstream of the customer-service process to assess the complexity of incoming web requests. At a conceptual level, the system analyses the text of a citizen’s request, identifies topic and complexity signals, and recommends whether the request can be treated by first-level support or should be routed to a specialised operator. The expected impact is faster response time for citizens, fewer duplicate handling steps, improved workload distribution and more efficient use of expert staff. The use case is closely related to INPS’s broader strategy of applying natural language processing to high-volume citizen communication channels while preserving human responsibility for substantive responses. The online INPS Risponde service itself remains a key channel for submitting and monitoring requests for information, clarifications and case updates.
results.memo: Proceed. "INPS risponde" - Optimised management of web requests to Customer Service is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Classification and automatic sorting of CEMs at the Italian National Institute for Social Security (INPS)
results.proposal: Classification and automatic sorting of CEMs at the Italian National Institute for Social Security (INPS). Certified email is one of the main channels through which Italian citizens communicate with INPS, including for pensions, disability, unemployment and other welfare matters. The volume and sensitivity of these messages create a major operational burden because staff must read each message and any attachments, understand the subject, identify the relevant service area and forward the case to the appropriate office. INPS developed an in-house AI system to classify and sort certified emails automatically while keeping data within INPS data centres to meet confidentiality and GDPR requirements. The implementation initially experimented with open-source GPT-2 and then moved to BERT, using transformer-based natural language processing to classify email content and attachments. At a conceptual level, the model analyses unstructured citizen communications, assigns them to relevant welfare-service categories and supports routing to the correct territorial or functional unit. Its expected impact is faster communication handling, reduced manual triage, shorter response times and major savings in administrative working days. The system also demonstrates the value of keeping sensitive public-service AI inside institutional infrastructure when the data include personal and welfare-related information. INPS reports that the project was included in IRCAI’s global Top 10 AI projects supporting the Sustainable Development Goals, and public technology-watch material describes the growth in certified emails from 3 million in 2019 to more than 6 million in 2023.

The operational objective is to improve access to municipal information by offering immediate guidance through an online chat available across the council’s web environment. The implementation uses a chatbot or virtual-assistant interface that supports navigation, answers common questions and can connect users with personalised assistance where appropriate. At a conceptual level, the assistant interprets the user’s question, retrieves relevant municipal information and directs the user towards the appropriate service page, procedure or support channel. The expected impact is faster access to public information, reduced pressure on physical and telephone help centres, improved service availability outside office-based interaction and a more user-friendly digital front door for Madrid’s municipal administration. The value of the system lies in navigation and orientation: it helps citizens locate the right process or information but does not replace formal administrative decisions or case-specific assessment. results.title: AI for anonymisation of court decisions
results.proposal: AI for anonymisation of court decisions. Publishing court decisions improves transparency, legal certainty and access to case law, but it requires careful protection of personal data, addresses, parties and other identifying information. Austria’s Federal Ministry of Justice developed AI-supported anonymisation to prepare court decisions for publication in the Legal Information System. The operational challenge is that manual anonymisation is time-consuming and must preserve the comprehensibility of the case while removing or masking information that could identify individuals or organisations. The implementation analyses decision documents, extracts metadata, recognises natural and legal persons, detects addresses and identifies the roles of actors within the case. It then supports anonymisation of personal data while aiming to maintain the legal and factual intelligibility of the decision. At a conceptual level, the system combines named-entity recognition, role detection, document analysis, metadata extraction and rule-guided anonymisation. Its expected impact is reduced manual workload, faster publication of case law, more consistent anonymisation and wider access to legally relevant decisions. The tool is especially valuable where courts produce large volumes of decisions and where publication depends on balancing transparency with privacy obligations. OECD material describes Austria’s Federal Ministry of Justice as implementing a comprehensive project to automate anonymisation of court decisions, with goals including efficiency, reduced manual effort and broader publication of anonymised decisions.

results.title: AI for digital file management
results.proposal: AI for digital file management. Digital court files require consistent structure, accurate metadata and reliable separation of documents, particularly when legacy paper files are scanned in bulk or when incoming documents arrive in different formats. Austria’s Federal Ministry of Justice developed AI-supported digital file management to ensure that unstructured documents are processed uniformly and that metadata can be adopted automatically. The operational problem is that court staff must often separate individual documents from scanned batches, identify first pages, classify attachments and maintain a coherent digital file structure. The implementation supports detection of first pages after bulk scanning, separation of submissions and supplements, document description, classification, harmonisation of document titles and intelligent creation of file structures, including tables of contents. It can also support object-oriented views, such as grouping documents related to a particular party. At a conceptual level, the system combines document segmentation, classification, metadata extraction, title harmonisation and digital-case-file structuring. The expected impact is more consistent electronic files, lower manual effort, easier navigation for judges and court staff, and stronger quality in the transition from paper-based to digital workflows. In legal administration, this matters because document organisation directly affects searchability, procedural efficiency and the ability of professionals to understand the case file quickly. The system is best understood as a support layer for digital file management, not as a tool that interprets legal merits or influences case outcomes.

results.title: AI for analysing incoming mail
results.proposal: AI for analysing incoming mail. Courts receive large volumes of incoming documents through electronic communication channels, scanned files and structured or unstructured submissions, creating a substantial administrative burden before a case can even be processed. Austria’s Federal Ministry of Justice developed AI-supported incoming-mail analysis to automate routing and classification tasks that would otherwise require court staff to read, interpret and manually allocate documents. The implementation analyses input documents, extracts metadata, identifies file numbers or other identifiers and recognises procedure types where no file number is available. It can also support intelligent allocation, file creation, assignment to the appropriate case or organisational unit, categorisation of scanned documents and preparation of proposed document descriptions or names. At a conceptual level, the system combines document classification, metadata extraction, entity or identifier recognition and workflow-routing rules. Its role is administrative: it turns incoming material into structured, actionable information for court systems and staff. The expected impact is faster handling of incoming judicial documents, fewer manual routing steps, improved consistency in document registration and reduced administrative workload in court offices. This type of tool is particularly useful in digital justice environments because delays or errors at the intake stage can affect all later case-management processes. The Austrian justice framework presents such AI applications as support functions that do not replace or influence judicial decisions.

results.title: AI-based tool for monitoring cultivated land in Lithuania using Copernicus Sentinel data
results.proposal: AI-based tool for monitoring cultivated land in Lithuania using Copernicus Sentinel data. Agricultural paying agencies must verify compliance with Common Agricultural Policy requirements across very large areas, but manual field inspections can be slow, expensive and disruptive for both administrations and farmers. Lithuania’s National Paying Agency worked with Geomatrix UAB and iTree Lietuva to use Copernicus Sentinel data and machine-learning methods for monitoring farm activities and land use during the agricultural season. The objective was to assess subsidy-related conditions more quickly and accurately, giving the agency an evidence base for checking claims and supporting more efficient distribution of CAP funds. The implementation developed SAGRIS, a Sentinel-based agriculture information service, and CAPCON, a CAP control service. These tools process Sentinel-1 and other satellite data to detect and classify land-cover and agricultural activity patterns relevant to subsidy control. At a conceptual level, the service combines Earth-observation imagery, pre-processing workflows, machine-learning classification, parcel-level monitoring and integration with paying-agency information systems. This allows checks to be carried out during the farming season rather than relying only on retrospective or sample-based inspections. The expected impact is faster compliance assessment, reduced need for on-site control, improved administrative efficiency and better targeting of follow-up checks. The case demonstrates how Copernicus data can be operationalised inside national agricultural administration, turning satellite observation into a practical tool for public funding governance.
results.memo: Proceed. AI-based tool for monitoring cultivated land in Lithuania using Copernicus Sentinel data is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: E-health 4.0, chatbots at the service of diagnostic units
results.proposal: E-health 4.0, chatbots at the service of diagnostic units. Healthcare facilities faced extraordinary pressure during the COVID-19 emergency, especially where citizens needed preliminary symptom guidance and hospitals had to manage information demand at scale. Through collaboration between Microsoft and INAIL, Italian healthcare organisations were able to use the Healthcare Bot solution free of charge to create digital assistants for self-assessment of coronavirus symptoms. The initiative supported facilities such as Spallanzani, San Giovanni Addolorata Hospital and ASL Napoli 3 Sud, giving them a rapid way to deploy online symptom-checking and orientation tools. The implementation used a healthcare chatbot configured for COVID-19 self-assessment, allowing users to answer questions about symptoms and receive guidance through the healthcare provider’s portal. At a conceptual level, the service translated triage and public-health information into a conversational workflow, supporting preliminary risk orientation and directing users towards appropriate next steps. Its expected impact was reduced pressure on phone lines and diagnostic units, faster information access for citizens, and more consistent communication from healthcare organisations. The service did not replace medical evaluation; it provided a first layer of digital interaction at a time when health systems needed to reserve human capacity for urgent or complex cases. The use case demonstrates how a reusable cloud-based bot platform could be rapidly adapted to emergency public-health needs.

results.title: Against the infection comes Minerva, a "robot" invented by an engineer from Noci (IT)
results.proposal: Against the infection comes Minerva, a "robot" invented by an engineer from Noci (IT). The early pandemic period generated intense demand for reliable information, while misinformation and rapidly changing rules made it difficult for citizens to know which guidance to follow. Minerva was created as a chatbot intended to share information about coronavirus using data drawn from the Italian Ministry of Health website. The objective was to provide a simple digital assistant that could answer recurring questions and direct users towards official public-health information. Although described publicly as a “robot”, the use case was essentially a conversational information service rather than a physical robot or clinical diagnostic tool. The implementation relied on an automated interface that processed user queries and returned relevant content based on official sources. At a conceptual level, the system acted as a bridge between citizens and institutional information, reducing the need to search manually through government webpages and helping standardise the messages received by users. Its expected impact was faster access to trusted information, improved public awareness and reduced confusion during a period of high uncertainty. The case was connected to a specific emergency context and should be interpreted as a lightweight crisis-communication tool rather than a long-term health-service platform. Its value lay in rapid deployment, official-source orientation and accessibility for users seeking immediate guidance.

results.title: Artificial intelligence "Wuhan model" at the biomedical campus in Rome
results.proposal: Artificial intelligence "Wuhan model" at the biomedical campus in Rome. During the early COVID-19 emergency, hospitals needed rapid tools to support diagnosis and monitoring of pneumonia from lung imaging, especially when clinical pressure was high and radiology teams faced urgent triage demands. Campus Bio-Medico University Hospital in Rome acquired an imaging system originally used in Wuhan to assist with early diagnosis and monitoring of COVID-19 pneumonia. The objective was to help radiologists interpret lung CT scans more quickly and consistently, while supporting clinical assessment rather than replacing specialist judgement. The implementation used an artificial-intelligence system trained to analyse chest CT images and identify patterns associated with COVID-19 pneumonia. Public reporting described a response reliability of 98.5% in around 20 seconds, and the system was tested successfully on anonymised patients by radiologists at the Rome hospital. At a conceptual level, the software processes CT image data, identifies relevant lung abnormalities and provides a rapid diagnostic support output for clinicians. The expected impact was faster radiological triage, improved monitoring of disease progression and better allocation of clinical resources during pandemic peaks. Its longer-term significance lies in demonstrating how emergency deployment of image-analysis systems can support hospital workflows, although public sources describe this primarily as a COVID-era installation and test rather than an enduring, general diagnostic platform.

results.proposal: Bobbi -  Berlin administration. Berlin’s chatbot Bobbi was introduced as an additional channel alongside the ServicePortal and the 115 citizen hotline, helping residents obtain quick answers to administrative questions at any time. The objective was not to replace existing service channels, but to provide a convenient first point of contact for common concerns, especially when users wanted immediate orientation rather than a telephone conversation. The implementation used a conversational interface connected to administrative information from Berlin’s public-service ecosystem. At a conceptual level, the chatbot interpreted user questions, matched them with relevant service descriptions or procedural information, and directed citizens towards the correct administrative pathway. Its expected impact was faster access to information, reduced pressure on human service channels, improved availability outside hotline hours and a more user-friendly digital front door for the city administration. The use case also illustrates the role of municipal chatbots in large metropolitan administrations, where the volume and variety of citizen requests make navigation support valuable. Bobbi was best understood as a supplementary digital assistant: useful for standard questions, but dependent on escalation or redirection where individual circumstances required human assessment.

Its expected impact was to reduce unnecessary pressure on health services, help citizens understand their situation, and provide a rapid channel for standardised information during the first wave of the pandemic. The open-source character also allowed the tool to be reused or examined by other actors. The service should not be understood as a substitute for medical diagnosis; its role was to provide preliminary orientation during an emergency, when demand for health information was exceptionally high and official communication needed to scale quickly.

The use case is strongly linked to the exceptional conditions of the pandemic, when speed of deployment, channel accessibility and operational relief were more important than building a long-term administrative assistant. It demonstrates how regional governments used lightweight conversational tools to manage sudden surges in public-service demand.

results.title: SUVE - Chatbot for questions about the emergency situation and the coronavirus
results.proposal: SUVE - Chatbot for questions about the emergency situation and the coronavirus. During the COVID-19 emergency, citizens needed quick, consistent and accessible answers to frequently asked questions about restrictions, services and official guidance. Estonia’s SUVE chatbot was introduced across the websites of several government agencies to provide automated responses in Estonian and English, reducing pressure on public-service channels and helping users find reliable information from official sources. The operational problem was typical of the pandemic period: public rules changed rapidly, citizens repeatedly asked similar questions, and government agencies needed to maintain a single, trustworthy information layer while avoiding overload on call centres and staff. The implementation used an automated conversational interface able to answer frequently asked questions about general services and the emergency situation. At a conceptual level, the chatbot connected user queries to curated government information, allowing citizens to receive immediate guidance through agency websites without navigating multiple pages or waiting for human assistance. Its expected impact was faster access to public information, reduced administrative burden, greater consistency of answers and improved communication during a fast-moving crisis. Because SUVE relied on official sources and supported both Estonian and English, it also helped reach residents and foreign users who needed emergency information. The case illustrates how conversational automation can be rapidly deployed for crisis communication when public demand is high and information needs are repetitive.

results.title: AI Robort Judge for small claims in Estonia
results.proposal: AI Robort Judge for small claims in Estonia. Small-claims procedures can absorb judicial time even when the amounts involved are relatively low and the dispute is mainly documentary. Estonia’s proposed “robot judge” was intended to explore whether low-value civil claims, initially under €7,000 and focused on contract disputes, could be processed more efficiently through automated support. The objective was to reduce backlogs for judges and court clerks while preserving the possibility of appeal to a human judge. The implementation concept was that parties would upload documents and relevant evidence, after which the system would analyse the material and issue a decision or recommendation. At a conceptual level, such a tool would require structured digital submissions, document analysis, legal-rule modelling, case classification and clear procedural safeguards for review and appeal. The expected impact would be faster processing of routine small claims, lower administrative burden and improved access to justice for simple disputes. However, many details remained unresolved, including legal responsibility, procedural fairness, transparency and the appropriate boundary between automation and adjudication. Later legal commentary suggests that Estonia has long used semi-automatic procedures for small claims, but public evidence of a fully operational autonomous AI judge remains limited. The use case should therefore be treated as an exploratory justice-automation initiative rather than a confirmed deployed judicial decision-maker.

results.title: Smart Dementia project
results.proposal: Smart Dementia project. Dementia care requires balancing safety with personal freedom, because residents may benefit physically and mentally from moving around, while care teams must manage risks linked to disorientation or wandering. The Smart Dementia project at Tante Louise uses eHealth technology to give people with Alzheimer’s disease more freedom inside and outside nursing-home settings. The operational objective is to support professional risk assessment: care teams decide how much freedom each resident can safely have, and the technology helps them monitor whereabouts when additional safeguards are needed. The implementation combines a wristwatch, mobile app, sensor technology and GPS-based location tracking, allowing nurses and authorised staff to locate a resident if necessary. At a conceptual level, the device collects location data, communicates it to relevant caregivers and supports a personalised care arrangement rather than imposing uniform restrictions. The expected impact is greater autonomy for residents, improved confidence for staff and families, and longer preservation of physical and mental activity. The project also demonstrates how personal health data can support more precise and individualised care, while raising obvious requirements around consent, proportionality and data protection. Its value lies in using technology as a supportive layer around professional judgement, not as a substitute for person-centred dementia care.

results.title: SegnalaCI - Transparent management of citizen reports about City status
results.proposal: SegnalaCI - Transparent management of citizen reports about City status. SegnalaCI provides the Municipality of Genoa with a digital channel for managing citizen reports on urban problems, such as road damage, waste collection issues or other maintenance needs affecting the city. The administrative challenge is to ensure that reports from residents are received, assigned to the competent office, resolved and communicated back to the citizen in a transparent and traceable manner. The stakeholders include residents, municipal departments, technical offices, maintenance teams, city administrators and service managers responsible for urban quality. The objective is to improve the management of citizen feedback and use the resulting information to support better staff and resource planning. The implementation allows the administration to take charge of a report, notify the relevant office, manage the intervention and inform the citizen of the outcome once the procedure is completed. Machine-learning techniques are used to process the data gathered through reports and provide a smart dashboard for city administrators. At a conceptual level, the system combines citizen-report intake, workflow routing, notification mechanisms, data classification, dashboard analytics and planning support. The expected impact is more transparent handling of local problems, quicker assignment of issues to responsible units, improved communication with residents and better evidence for allocating municipal resources. By analysing recurring reports and operational needs, the municipality can move from reactive case handling towards more informed urban-service management.

results.title: i-Territory – Intelligent Modeling of Territorial Access to Services of General Interest
results.proposal: i-Territory – Intelligent Modeling of Territorial Access to Services of General Interest. Ensuring equitable access to services of general interest—such as healthcare, education, transport, and administrative services—remains a major challenge in territories affected by demographic change and geographic disparities. The i-Territory initiative, promoted by AMA, seeks to improve how public authorities understand and plan territorial service accessibility. Stakeholders include central and local administrations, regional planners, and service providers. The objective is to support evidence-based territorial planning that reduces inequalities and improves service coverage. The initiative relies on the integration of geospatial data, demographic statistics, service location data, and mobility information into territorial analysis models. These models simulate accessibility scenarios, identify underserved areas, and assess the impact of policy options such as service relocation or new infrastructure. The system is designed to interoperate with public-sector data platforms and geographic information systems, enabling scenario analysis rather than operational decision automation. Public documentation positions i-Territory as an enabling framework and pilot rather than a fully deployed national system. Its value lies in improving analytical capacity, supporting more transparent planning decisions, and helping administrations anticipate territorial needs, even though large-scale operational adoption has not yet been publicly confirmed.
