results.title: Katowice Intelligent Monitoring and Analysis System (KISMiA)
results.proposal: Katowice Intelligent Monitoring and Analysis System (KISMiA). Urban safety services need to monitor public spaces effectively and coordinate responses across different operational units, but conventional video surveillance can become difficult to manage when large numbers of cameras produce continuous streams of footage. Katowice Intelligent Monitoring and Analysis System (KISMiA) addresses this challenge by integrating video management, video analytics and operational support into a single monitoring environment for the Municipality of Katowice. The system is built around three components: a Video Materials Management System, a Video Analytics Component and an Operational Support Component. The video management system administers the video data supplied to the platform, while the analytics layer, based on IBM Intelligent Video Analytics, continuously analyses streams and generates descriptive information from each camera. The operational support component is designed to provide the right people with the right information, helping them coordinate actions and follow results. The main integration point is the IOC platform, which gathers all system elements and supports coordination with other integrated systems, including IVA and VMS. With 260 cameras currently in the system, KISMiA enhances the city’s ability to detect relevant events, manage situational information and support decision-making by public services. Its expected impact is faster operational awareness, improved coordination, more effective use of video data and stronger support for urban safety management.
results.memo: Proceed. Katowice Intelligent Monitoring and Analysis System (KISMiA) is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Resident's Virtual Advisor
results.proposal: Resident's Virtual Advisor. Residents searching for municipal information can struggle to find the correct answer on public administration websites when procedures, forms and official notices are dispersed across many pages. The service responds to the need to optimise customer-service processes for a large user base, including administrations and thousands of customers who require quick and reliable information. Rather than asking residents to navigate the website independently, the system simulates a conversation with a real person and leads the user to the appropriate answer. The technological implementation belongs to the field of intelligent customer-interaction solutions and uses artificial-intelligence mechanisms integrated with sound and video functions. At a conceptual level, the advisor interprets user queries, identifies the most relevant BIP content and presents guidance through a conversational interface. The service is available online, improving access beyond traditional office interactions. The expected impact is faster information retrieval, reduced pressure on municipal staff, more intuitive use of public information resources and greater consistency in how residents are directed to official answers. For Wrocław, the solution supports a more accessible and user-oriented model of digital municipal administration.

results.title: Wroclaw Intelligent parking system
results.proposal: Wroclaw Intelligent parking system. Residents and visitors often lose time searching for parking spaces in busy urban areas, while municipalities lack precise and timely information on parking availability at street level. Wroclaw Intelligent parking system addresses this problem by developing a prototype that collects data from multiple sources, including sensors and cameras, to estimate the likelihood of finding a free parking space in the area towards which a driver is travelling. The operational objective is to reduce uncertainty for road users and improve the management of scarce parking capacity in the city. The system focuses on recognising how many spaces are occupied or available in a given street area, transforming dispersed observations into information that can be used by residents. Its technological implementation combines physical sensors, camera-based detection and data-processing components that analyse occupancy signals and generate parking-availability estimates. As part of the project, a mobile application is planned to show users both the travel time to a car park and the availability of spaces. The expected impact is a better user experience for drivers, reduced unnecessary circulation in search of parking, more efficient use of available spaces and potentially lower congestion and emissions in dense areas. For the municipality, the system can also provide valuable data for parking policy, infrastructure planning and traffic-management decisions.

results.title: Wroclaw Intelligent lighting system
results.proposal: Wroclaw Intelligent lighting system. Cities need to modernise lighting poles so that they do more than illuminate streets, especially where existing infrastructure can support new data services for mobility, safety and urban planning. Wroclaw Intelligent lighting system is a research project aimed at combining the basic function of lighting poles with additional functions designed for residents and municipal management. The operational problem is that traditional street-lighting infrastructure often represents a costly but underused urban asset, while authorities require better data on pedestrian, cyclist and vehicle flows to understand how public space is used. The project therefore adds new sensing and analytical capabilities to lighting infrastructure. Devices installed on selected poles count pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles, including the identification of vehicle types. At the same time, the lighting itself has been replaced with LED luminaires that can adjust light intensity to external conditions. The technological implementation combines traffic-counting devices, adaptive LED lighting and infrastructure-level monitoring, creating a platform that supports both illumination and data collection. The expected impact is improved energy efficiency, better adjustment of lighting to real-world conditions and richer information on mobility patterns in the city. For Wrocław, the system provides a practical testbed for multifunctional urban infrastructure, helping the municipality explore how existing assets can support safer, more responsive and more evidence-based local services.
results.memo: Proceed. Wroclaw Intelligent lighting system is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Smart lighting in urban space
results.proposal: Smart lighting in urban space. Urban residential areas require lighting that improves safety and liveability while limiting electricity costs and making better use of existing infrastructure. Smart lighting in urban space in Wrocław responds to this challenge through the installation of remotely controlled LED lighting in the WUWA 2 estate. The case focuses on replacing conventional lighting with a more flexible system that can adjust to changes in movement and local conditions, rather than maintaining the same level of illumination throughout the night. The implementation combines LED technology with a remote-control system and traffic-sensitive operation, enabling the lighting intensity to change when the system detects variations in use of the space. This supports safer movement for residents, pedestrians and other users while reducing unnecessary electricity consumption during periods of lower activity. A further technical feature is the permanent power supply to street-lighting circuits, which creates opportunities to use lighting infrastructure for additional urban services. These may include electric-vehicle charging or internet provision, turning lighting poles into multifunctional public assets. The expected impact is lower energy expenditure, improved safety and comfort in the estate, and greater flexibility in how urban infrastructure is used. For the municipality, the project also demonstrates how lighting networks can become a platform for broader smart-city services.
results.memo: Proceed. Smart lighting in urban space is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Ioom Intelligent lighting system
results.proposal: Ioom Intelligent lighting system. Municipalities need street-lighting systems that reduce energy use and maintenance costs while still providing safe lighting conditions for pedestrians, drivers and public-space users. Ioom Intelligent lighting system addresses this requirement through centralised street-lighting control based on motion sensors and sensors that analyse weather conditions. The service context is local infrastructure management, where lighting must respond to changing levels of movement, visibility and safety need rather than operating only according to fixed schedules. In the current model, each lamp can be individually controlled and monitored, allowing the responsible authority to define different switching times and lighting behaviours for specific locations. The implementation combines connected luminaires, sensor data, central management software and remote monitoring of lighting parameters. Lamps near pedestrian crossings can be activated earlier and switched off later than surrounding lights, increasing visibility in areas where road-safety risks are higher. Continuous technical monitoring also enables faster detection of failures and supports earlier planning of maintenance work. The expected results include significant energy savings, reduced interruptions in lighting operation, shorter response times when faults occur and lower maintenance costs through better planning. The wider public value is a more adaptive and safety-oriented lighting service that uses local conditions to guide infrastructure operation.
results.memo: Proceed. Ioom Intelligent lighting system is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: AI-based timetables
results.proposal: AI-based timetables. Public transport authorities need timetables that reflect real operating conditions, because planned travel times that do not match actual journey patterns can reduce punctuality and passenger confidence. AI-based timetables in the Municipality of Poznań supports the creation of more accurate timetables by using historical data collected from vehicles after completed services. The operational problem is that public transport schedules are often affected by traffic conditions, route characteristics, time of day and recurring delays, and manually adjusting timetables may not fully capture these patterns. The software enables historical trip data to be projected onto timetable planning, allowing planners to analyse how long vehicles actually take on specific route sections. Its technological implementation applies statistical analysis to vehicle data from completed journeys in order to determine optimal travel times for individual sections. By identifying recurring deviations between planned and actual performance, the system helps create schedules that are better aligned with observed conditions. The expected impact is improved punctuality, more realistic timetable planning, better use of vehicle and driver resources, and a more reliable passenger experience. For the municipality, the system provides a stronger evidence base for transport planning and helps shift timetable design from assumption-based scheduling towards continuous improvement based on operational data.
results.memo: Proceed. AI-based timetables is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Gliwice & Poznan Integrated Public Transport Management System - ITS
results.proposal: Gliwice & Poznan Integrated Public Transport Management System - ITS. Growing cities need to manage traffic, public transport, emergency movements, parking and traveller information in an integrated way, because fragmented systems can reduce punctuality, safety and network efficiency. Gliwice & Poznan Integrated Public Transport Management System brings together several intelligent transport functions to improve mobility management in the municipalities of Gliwice and Poznań. The case addresses multiple operational objectives: giving green-light priority to public transport, prioritising emergency-service vehicles at signalised intersections, informing drivers through road information systems, supporting road users through a mobile application and expanding traffic measurement points with vehicle identification. The technological implementation includes traffic-light priority systems, variable message signs showing journey times, video analytics for intersection monitoring, sensors or detection systems for free parking spaces, meteorological monitoring and pre-selection vehicle weighing at city inlets in Gliwice. Video analytics can automatically inform operators about dangerous road incidents, while traffic and weather data support better management of urban mobility conditions. The expected impact is improved punctuality of public transport, faster emergency-vehicle passage, better information for drivers, stronger incident detection, more efficient parking guidance and improved enforcement of vehicle-weight rules. Overall, the integrated system supports safer, more predictable and more data-informed urban transport management, while giving municipal authorities a broader operational picture of mobility across the city.

results.title: Lupine Intelligent lighting system
results.proposal: Lupine Intelligent lighting system. Municipalities must provide safe and reliable street lighting while limiting energy consumption, maintenance costs and response times when failures occur. Lupine Intelligent lighting system introduces centralised control of street lighting based on motion sensors and sensors that analyse weather conditions, allowing the municipality to adapt lighting more precisely to local needs. results.title: Monitoring of a Water Treatment Station
results.proposal: Monitoring of a Water Treatment Station. Municipal water operators need accurate and continuous information on flow, pressure, intake operations and distribution volumes to maintain reliable supply and detect losses within the network. This use case in the Municipality of Kartuzy addresses this need by introducing monitoring for the local water treatment plant and the associated water-supply system. The operational problem is that insufficient visibility over network parameters can make it harder to control the amount of water sent into the system, identify abnormal losses or regulate intake operations efficiently. The case focuses on measuring flow rate, monitoring network pressure, controlling and regulating intake activity, and balancing the volume of water distributed through the network. The technological implementation relies on sensors and monitoring equipment installed across key points of the treatment and distribution process. These devices collect operational measurements and transmit them to management systems that allow staff to observe conditions, compare distributed volumes and identify potential inefficiencies or losses. The resulting information supports more precise operational control and better evidence for maintenance or intervention decisions. The expected impact is improved reliability of water supply, faster identification of pressure or flow anomalies, better control of water intake and distribution, and stronger capacity to detect water losses. For the municipality, the system contributes to more efficient utility management and a more transparent view of essential water infrastructure.

results.title: Intelligent Management Systems
results.proposal: Intelligent Management Systems. County-office buildings require coordinated management of security, utilities, technical infrastructure and room equipment, yet these systems are often operated separately, making monitoring and optimisation more difficult. This Intelligent Management Systems in the Municipality of Płońsk brings together a range of building-management functions within the County Office to improve control, efficiency and operational reliability. The case responds to the need for a more integrated approach to public-building management, covering access control, external roller shutters, monitoring, water and electricity consumption, PIAPs, IT networks, an intelligent conference room and the fire-protection system. The technological implementation consists of interconnected building-management systems that enable centralised monitoring and control of different technical installations. Sensors, controllers and digital interfaces can be used to gather information on building conditions, resource use and system status, while management software supports supervision and operational decisions. By integrating these functions, the administration can obtain a clearer view of how the building performs and respond more quickly to faults, security issues or inefficient consumption patterns. The expected impact includes improved energy and water management, stronger security, more efficient use of office infrastructure, better continuity of building operations and reduced manual effort for technical staff. In organisational terms, the project supports the modernisation of local-government facilities and provides a more resilient foundation for public administration services delivered from those buildings.

results.title: Virtual Clerk - Assistance with search for information
results.proposal: Virtual Clerk - Assistance with search for information. Municipal offices that serve large numbers of residents and beneficiaries must provide clear procedural information quickly, even when enquiries concern many different services, administrative routes and eligibility conditions. Virtual Clerk helps the Municipality of Chorzów optimise service processes for hundreds of thousands of beneficiaries by offering an intuitive digital channel for finding information about the office and the procedures it manages. The operational challenge is that citizens often need guidance outside office hours or may not know where to look for the correct administrative information, while staff can spend considerable time responding to repetitive enquiries. The system uses artificial intelligence to support natural and user-friendly searches across institutional information. At a conceptual level, it interprets user questions, identifies the relevant procedural content and returns guidance in a form that is easier to access than navigating multiple static pages or contacting the office directly. The service is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, improving accessibility for users who need information at different times. Its impact is faster access to public-service information, reduced friction for beneficiaries, lower pressure on front-office staff and more consistent communication on municipal procedures. For the municipality, Virtual Clerk contributes to a more modern, scalable and citizen-oriented model of administrative service delivery.

results.title: Water management SR - Predicting of water levels
results.proposal: Water management SR - Predicting of water levels. Water authorities need to manage treatment plants and water levels proactively, because delayed detection of operational issues can affect service reliability, maintenance planning and the ability to respond to changing environmental conditions. The Water management system supports Hoogheemraadschap De Stichtse Rijnlanden, Tauw and HAL24K in applying data science to complex water-management challenges. The case focuses on improving how real-time operational data can be used to understand conditions at water treatment plants and anticipate changes in water levels, rather than relying only on periodic checks or reactive maintenance. The technological implementation is based on HAL24K’s Dimension data-intelligence platform, demonstrated through the use of live sensor data. At a conceptual level, the platform collects and processes streams from sensors installed in water-management infrastructure, enabling the analysis of current conditions, anomalies and trends relevant to maintenance or level management. Predictive models can use these data to support earlier identification of risks and more timely operational decisions. The expected impact is more efficient maintenance, faster detection of emerging problems, better use of real-time information and improved capacity to manage water systems proactively. For the responsible organisations, the value lies in strengthening operational resilience, reducing avoidable interventions and creating a more data-driven basis for water-level control and treatment-plant management.

results.title: Amsterdam City Archive - Handwritten Text Recognition for eabling searches on old handwritten texts
results.proposal: Amsterdam City Archive - Handwritten Text Recognition for eabling searches on old handwritten texts. The Amsterdam City Archive holds millions of scans of historical handwritten documents that are valuable for research and public This initaitves aim to make these archival materials more discoverable by automatically converting handwritten scans into text transcriptions. The operational challenge is that manual transcription of such large volumes would be extremely time-consuming, while image-only records limit the ability of researchers, citizens and archivists to search across complete texts. The initiative involves Aincient B.V., Picturae, Sioux Technologies, Islands of Meaning and the Amsterdam City Archive, combining archival expertise with specialist technology providers. The implementation uses Handwritten Text Recognition to analyse scanned handwritten pages and generate machine-readable transcriptions. Natural language processing is then used to support further interpretation, structuring and searchability of the resulting text. At a conceptual level, the system identifies handwriting patterns, converts them into textual output and enables full-text search across materials that were previously far less accessible. The impact is a major improvement in archival discovery, faster access to historical information, reduced dependence on manual indexing and greater reuse of cultural-heritage collections. By making complete handwritten texts searchable, the project strengthens public access to Amsterdam’s documentary heritage and supports more scalable digital-archive services.

results.title: Smart sensor waste containers
results.proposal: Smart sensor waste containers. The Municipality of Rotterdam needs to keep neighbourhood waste collection reliable and clean while avoiding both overflowing containers and unnecessary collection trips to bins that are not yet full. This use case addresses this operational problem by installing sensors in waste containers to measure filling levels and support more efficient collection planning. In dense urban areas, conventional waste collection based on fixed routes or schedules can result in two opposite inefficiencies: waste accumulating beside overcrowded containers when emptying is too late, and staff time and vehicle kilometres being wasted when containers are emptied too early. The system uses “filling degree meters” that transmit the status of containers every hour, providing regular information on how full each bin is. This data is made available to collection teams, and drivers can use a tablet to see which route should be taken next. The technological implementation combines sensor-based monitoring, data transmission and route-support tools that translate container-level information into operational guidance for waste-collection services. The expected impact is cleaner public space, fewer complaints about overflowing containers, more efficient use of collection vehicles and reduced unnecessary driving. For waste-management staff, the system improves day-to-day planning by showing where intervention is actually needed. For the municipality, it supports a more responsive and resource-efficient approach to urban waste services.
results.memo: Proceed. Smart sensor waste containers is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Smart decision aid - Determining if a case is a scam or not
results.proposal: Smart decision aid - Determining if a case is a scam or not. The National Internet Reporting Centre receives around 42,000 reports of buying and selling fraud every year, yet in approximately 10,000 cases a police officer later determines that the reported situation does not constitute a criminal offence. Smart decision aid helps address this mismatch by supporting the initial assessment of online fraud reports and providing direct feedback to the person submitting the report. The operational challenge is that police capacity can be absorbed by reports that require review but do not meet the legal threshold for criminal investigation, while citizens still need clarity on what has happened and what they can do next. Developed within the National Police Lab Artificial Intelligence, the decision aid assists in determining whether a reported buying or selling incident is likely to be a scam. The system uses information entered by the declarant and applies decision-support logic, potentially combining rule-based criteria and data-driven indicators derived from previous reports, to assess whether the case fits known fraud patterns. When the situation does not appear to be a criminal offence, the tool can provide an alternative action perspective to the user. The impact is faster clarification for citizens, reduced unnecessary workload for police officers, better triage of internet-fraud reports and more consistent initial handling of cases. It also supports more efficient use of investigative capacity for reports that are more likely to require police action.

results.title: Smart enforcement cameras - Enforcement of drivers driving through red road crosses
results.proposal: Smart enforcement cameras - Enforcement of drivers driving through red road crosses. Road authorities and enforcement bodies need to prevent drivers from ignoring red crosses above closed lanes, because such violations create serious safety risks for road workers, emergency responders and other road users. Smart enforcement cameras were tested by the Public Prosecutor’s Office and Rijkswaterstaat along the A28 motorway near Amersfoort to detect and reduce these violations. The operational problem is that a red cross indicates that a lane must not be used, often because of incidents, roadworks or traffic-management measures, yet manual enforcement is difficult and dangerous on high-speed roads. The pilot uses smart cameras positioned along the motorway to identify vehicles that continue driving through lanes marked with a red cross. Technically, the system combines camera-based monitoring with automated image analysis to capture relevant evidence, including vehicle passage in relation to the active lane-control signal. The data can then support enforcement processes, subject to verification and applicable legal safeguards. The purpose is not only to sanction non-compliance, but also to increase deterrence and promote safer behaviour around closed lanes. The expected impact is fewer red-cross violations, improved protection for road personnel and road users, better enforcement coverage on motorways and stronger compliance with traffic-control measures. The pilot also demonstrates how digital enforcement tools can complement existing road-safety policies where direct human monitoring is impractical.
results.memo: Proceed. Smart enforcement cameras - Enforcement of drivers driving through red road crosses is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Smart Cameras - Analyzing road situations
results.proposal: Smart Cameras - Analyzing road situations. Rijkswaterstaat needs to manage traffic flow on busy roads safely and efficiently, particularly when decisions such as opening or closing rush-hour lanes must be taken quickly and with reliable situational awareness. Smart Cameras support road operators by enabling cameras to interpret traffic conditions and assist with operational decisions on the road network. The problem is that conventional camera monitoring depends heavily on human observation, which can be demanding when many road sections must be supervised simultaneously and when traffic conditions change rapidly. The initiative, involving Rijkswaterstaat, the Innovation Centre and ViNotion, focuses on smart cameras that can “read” the road situation and thereby make the management of rush-hour lanes faster, easier and safer. The implementation uses camera images and computer-vision techniques to detect relevant traffic conditions, such as the presence of vehicles, congestion, incidents or lane availability. These outputs can be integrated into traffic-management processes to support decisions on whether a rush-hour lane can be opened or should be closed. The technology therefore adds an analytical layer to existing camera infrastructure, helping operators interpret visual information more consistently. The expected impact includes faster operational responses, improved safety when changing lane status, reduced workload for traffic-control staff and smoother traffic flow. By enhancing the use of visual data, the solution strengthens real-time road management and supports a more efficient transport network.
results.memo: Proceed. Smart Cameras - Analyzing road situations is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Excess Material Exchange (EME)
results.proposal: Excess Material Exchange (EME). Organisations that generate residual materials often lack efficient mechanisms to identify potential reusers, assess the value of surplus flows and close material loops across sectors. Excess Material Exchange (EME) addresses this problem by creating a digital trading platform where supply and demand for excess materials can be matched at scale. The initiative involves organisations such as ProRail, Schiphol and other public and private actors seeking to reduce waste and improve circular-economy performance. The operational objective is to move residual materials away from disposal or low-value treatment and towards productive reuse by making information about available materials more visible, comparable and actionable. The technology implementation relies on artificial intelligence to read, interpret and structure data on material streams, including information on composition, availability, quality, location and potential applications. Matching algorithms then identify possible links between suppliers and buyers, including combinations that may not be obvious through manual brokerage. The platform’s intelligence lies not only in listing materials, but also in actively bringing together parties whose residual flows and needs may align. The expected impact is faster matching, greater scalability in circular-material exchange, reduced transaction costs and improved resource efficiency. For participating organisations, EME can support waste reduction, lower procurement or disposal costs, and contribute to broader sustainability and circular-economy objectives.
results.memo: Proceed. Excess Material Exchange (EME) is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.company: Ministry of Social Affairs and Employment
results.title: Digital assistant for answering Parliamentary questions
results.proposal: Digital assistant for answering Parliamentary questions. Policy officials must often answer Parliamentary questions under time pressure, while ensuring that responses are accurate, well-evidenced and consistent with publicly available information. Digital assistant for answering Parliamentary questions supports the Ministry of Social Affairs and Employment by helping policy staff search public sources more efficiently during the preparation of answers. The operational problem is that relevant information may be dispersed across documents, websites, policy files and other open sources, making manual retrieval slow and increasing the risk that important material is missed. The assistant is intended to strengthen the preparatory phase of drafting by accelerating information discovery and supporting staff in identifying relevant public evidence. From a technological perspective, the system functions as a search and retrieval tool that can scan public sources, interpret user queries and return potentially relevant material for policy officers to review. Depending on its configuration, such a tool may use natural language processing to understand questions, rank information by relevance and help structure the evidence base for a draft response. It does not replace the judgement of officials or the political and legal checks required before an answer is submitted. Its impact lies in reducing research time, improving consistency in source use, supporting more complete answers and allowing staff to focus more of their effort on analysis, drafting quality and institutional coordination.

results.title: Algorithm Impact monitor bridge openings
results.proposal: Algorithm Impact monitor bridge openings. The Province of South Holland must manage the movement of both road traffic and shipping across a region where bridge openings can create delays, congestion and competing demands between transport modes. The smart bridge addresses this challenge by using digital monitoring and predictive analytics to support more informed bridge-operation decisions across an infrastructure portfolio that includes more than 100 bridges. The initiative forms part of South Holland’s wider work on smart shipping and focuses on linking up-to-date road-traffic information with live shipping information, so that the impact of bridge openings can be better understood and anticipated. In the project “impact monitor bridge openings”, the province has taken an important step towards predicting traffic intensities around several key bridges. The technological implementation combines sensor-based data collection, traffic information and algorithmic analysis, including Long Short-Term Memory neural networks designed to forecast traffic conditions up to 21 minutes ahead. These models are suited to time-series prediction because they can learn from sequential patterns in traffic behaviour and bridge-operation data. The reported correlation-efficient accuracy of 60–80% indicates that the approach can provide useful short-term forecasts for operational planning. The main value is improved anticipation of congestion, better coordination between road and waterway mobility, more evidence-based bridge management and a stronger basis for reducing disruption while keeping both transport networks accessible and safe.
results.memo: Proceed. Algorithm Impact monitor bridge openings is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: The Refinery: AI in investigation support
results.proposal: The Refinery: AI in investigation support. Police investigators need to process and interpret increasing volumes of information from multiple sources, including case files, operational records and digital evidence, without losing sight of relevant patterns or connections. The Refinery: AI in investigation support is a data-analysis facility developed by the Dutch National Police to enhance investigative capabilities and help officers work with complex information environments. The operational challenge is that valuable links between cases, suspects, events or pieces of evidence may remain hidden when data are fragmented across systems or too extensive to review manually. The platform enables investigators to access, interpret and visualise large volumes of police data drawn from diverse sources. Its implementation combines data integration, analytical tooling and AI-driven methods that support the detection of patterns, relationships and connections within investigative material. At a conceptual level, the system can help structure heterogeneous datasets, identify associations and present results through visual interfaces that make complex information easier to understand. The tool is intended to assist investigative judgement rather than automate final decisions. Its impact lies in faster analysis, improved situational awareness, better detection of links across cases and more effective use of available police data. For the Dutch National Police, The Refinery strengthens investigative capacity, supports evidence-led policing and provides a scalable analytical environment for complex criminal investigations.

results.proposal: Improve data quality with AI - Machine learning to improve the data quality of registrations. This enables the municipality to move from ad hoc data-quality checks towards more continuous monitoring. results.title: Case Law Engine
results.proposal: Case Law Engine. Prosecutors and legal researchers face significant information-management challenges when preparing criminal cases, as relevant case law, procedural material and hidden connections may be dispersed across large and complex legal datasets. Case Law Engine was developed by LexIQ for the Dutch Public Prosecution Service to reduce research time and improve the quality of case preparation. The Public Prosecution Service had explored how advanced digital tools could support daily working procedures, particularly where professionals need to search, analyse and draw insights from criminal-case information. The tool, also described as a “Jurisprudentierobot”, supports prosecutors and researchers in identifying relevant case law, understanding patterns and making better use of information during preparation. Its implementation combines machine-learning algorithms with intuitive search functions, data visualisations and analytical features that help users navigate large volumes of legal and case-related data. Rather than replacing legal judgement, the system provides indications, connections and possible outcome-related insights that professionals can assess within their own legal reasoning. The impact is reduced time spent on manual research, better handling of information overload and improved ability to detect relevant or previously hidden information. For the Public Prosecution Service, the tool offers business value by strengthening preparation quality, supporting consistency and enabling staff to approach criminal-case analysis in a more structured and evidence-informed way.

The broader operational objective is to move from uniform or purely rule-based selection towards more refined risk identification, allowing the administration to focus attention where available data suggest a higher probability of non-compliance or recovery opportunities. One example is Dynamic Monitoring, which links outstanding receivables to possible sources of redress, such as wages, cars, real estate or other assets, and generates lists of claims where new recovery options may be available. The implementation combines machine-learning methods with administrative tax data, inspection histories and feedback loops from previous control results. Models are progressively refined as additional outcomes become available, improving their capacity to identify relevant risk patterns. The potential impact is more efficient allocation of inspection and recovery resources, faster identification of actionable cases and improved use of existing administrative data. At the same time, such systems require careful governance to ensure transparency, legality, non-discrimination and appropriate human oversight in tax decision-making.

results.title: Tree Monitor - Detecting illegal logging
results.proposal: Tree Monitor - Detecting illegal logging. Regional authorities responsible for environmental protection need reliable methods to identify tree loss and possible illegal logging across large territories where field inspections alone may be slow, selective or reactive. Tree Monitor gives the Province of Gelderland an additional monitoring tool for detecting potential illegal felling by comparing satellite images from different years. Operational since December 2017, the system helps authorities locate areas where trees appear to have disappeared and visualises these changes on a map. The objective is to improve the detection of irregular tree removal and support more targeted follow-up by enforcement or environmental-management teams. The implementation uses Earth observation data, with satellite imagery analysed across time to identify changes in vegetation cover. At a conceptual level, image-comparison techniques detect differences between historical and more recent satellite data, highlighting locations where tree cover has declined. These outputs can then be reviewed by officials and used to prioritise inspections or further investigation. The initiative involves the Province of Gelderland, NEO and Wageningen Environmental Research, combining public environmental responsibilities with specialist geospatial expertise. The main impact is broader territorial coverage, faster identification of potential illegal logging, better targeting of field checks and stronger evidence for environmental enforcement. It also demonstrates how satellite-based monitoring can support nature protection and land-use oversight at regional level.

results.title: Anti-cheat software for exams

Anti-cheat software for exams refers to the use of Proctorexam by several Dutch higher education institutions, including the University of Rotterdam and other universities, to monitor students during online tests. The operational challenge is to detect possible cheating in a digital setting where invigilators cannot physically observe candidates, but where fairness, equal treatment and the reliability of qualifications remain essential. The software enables remote surveillance through a student’s webcam, microphone and web browser, allowing examination behaviour and the digital environment to be monitored during the assessment. Its technical implementation combines online proctoring functions with automated or semi-automated detection of behaviours that may be classified as suspicious, such as unusual movements, browser activity or environmental signals. The system can flag students for further review, rather than necessarily determining misconduct on its own. The expected benefit for institutions is greater capacity to run remote examinations while maintaining oversight and reducing manual invigilation constraints. However, the use of such systems also raises important concerns around privacy, proportionality, transparency and student trust, meaning that its operational value depends strongly on governance safeguards, review procedures and clear communication with candidates.

The impact has been to facilitate and accelerate metadata production, improve the usability of the State’s photographic resources and enable better exploitation of the media library’s content across government. The use case delivers administrative efficiency, strengthens information management and supports more consistent reuse of public visual records.

results.title: Intelligence Emploi
results.proposal: Intelligence Emploi. Intelligence Emploi was introduced within Pôle emploi as a transformation initiative aimed at accelerating the return to sustainable employment. The use case addresses a central labour-market challenge: employment services must support large numbers of jobseekers with different profiles, skills, barriers and career objectives, while also responding to employer demand and changing labour-market conditions. Public employment counsellors need tools that help them identify relevant opportunities, personalise support and prioritise interventions without reducing the quality of human guidance. The objective is therefore to strengthen Pôle emploi’s capacity to help people move into stable work more quickly and effectively. The AI implementation acts as a lever within employment-service processes, using available labour-market, jobseeker and vacancy-related data to support matching, guidance and decision-making. At a conceptual level, models may analyse profiles, skills, employment histories, job offers and contextual indicators to identify suitable pathways or opportunities for users. These outputs can help advisers provide more tailored support and improve the relevance of recommendations made to jobseekers. The expected impact is faster return to sustainable employment, better targeting of support measures, improved efficiency for counsellors and greater personalisation of public employment services. For the administration, the use case supports a more data-driven service model while preserving the role of employment professionals in guiding complex individual transitions.

results.title: Targeting establishment inspection - refine targeting of establishments for inspections
results.proposal: Targeting establishment inspection - refine targeting of establishments for inspections. The General Directorate of Food of the French Ministry of Agriculture and Food developed this use case to improve the targeting of inspections in establishments that sell or deliver food directly to consumers, including restaurants, catering businesses and distributors. Food-safety inspection authorities must allocate limited inspection resources across a large and diverse population of establishments, where risks may vary depending on hygiene practices, customer experience, operational conditions and previous signals. Traditional targeting methods may not fully capture emerging problems or recent consumer concerns, particularly where relevant information appears first in public feedback channels. The objective of the use case is to refine the prioritisation of establishments to be inspected by using additional evidence from online consumer reviews. The AI component analyses reviews published on online platforms to identify signals that may suggest possible food-safety or hygiene concerns. Natural language processing can be used to detect relevant terms, patterns of complaints or sentiment linked to establishments, which can then inform inspection planning alongside existing administrative data and regulatory criteria. The system is intended to support, not replace, professional judgement by inspectors. Its expected impact is a more risk-informed allocation of inspection capacity, earlier identification of establishments requiring attention, better use of publicly available feedback and improved protection of consumers through more targeted food-safety controls.
results.memo: Proceed. Targeting establishment inspection - refine targeting of establishments for inspections is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: ASN: better use of the data contained in follow-up letter of inspections
results.proposal: ASN: better use of the data contained in follow-up letter of inspections. The French Nuclear Safety Authority, ASN, developed this use case to improve how inspection knowledge is exploited in the regulation of nuclear installations. Following the Fukushima accident of 11 March 2011, ASN requested operators on 5 May 2011 to undertake complementary safety assessments of their installations, reinforcing the importance of systematic oversight and evidence-based inspection practices. A major operational challenge was the large volume of information contained in around 20,000 inspection follow-up letters. These documents include observations, recommendations and signals that may be relevant for identifying recurring issues or emerging trends, but manual analysis at this scale is demanding and limits the ability of inspectors to detect patterns across time, sites and themes. The objective was to transform unstructured inspection correspondence into structured information that could support inspectors in their work. The AI solution applies text-analysis techniques to inspection follow-up letters in order to detect weak signals, extract relevant information and identify statistical trends. At a conceptual level, the tool processes regulatory documents, organises their content and makes recurring themes more visible to inspection teams. Its value lies in providing a ready-to-use decision-support capability, improving the exploitation of accumulated inspection evidence, reducing time spent on manual document review and strengthening ASN’s ability to identify cross-cutting safety issues across the nuclear sector.
results.memo: Proceed. ASN: better use of the data contained in follow-up letter of inspections is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Safe Spotter - AI platform to detect and transmit data of an accident
results.proposal: Safe Spotter - AI platform to detect and transmit data of an accident. Safe Spotter was developed for the Municipality of Monserrato as part of a broader effort to create an innovative and sustainable smart-city model focused on citizen protection and territorial management. The use case responds to a critical road-safety challenge: when traffic accidents occur, emergency response depends on the rapid availability of reliable information on what happened, where it happened and which vehicles may be involved. Delays or incomplete information can affect the ability of public authorities and emergency services to intervene effectively. The objective is therefore to strengthen the municipality’s capacity to govern road safety by detecting accidents automatically and transmitting essential data quickly. The AI platform uses an advanced network of cameras and sound sensors installed on intelligent street lights. The sound sensors are designed to recognise noises associated with traffic accidents and activate a directional camera when a relevant event is detected. The system then collects Minimum Safe Data, including images or videos, time, location, vehicle direction and registration number. This information can be transmitted to support situational awareness and response coordination. The expected impact is faster accident detection, improved evidence for emergency intervention, stronger monitoring of road-safety events and better protection of citizens. The use case also demonstrates how urban lighting infrastructure can be repurposed as a platform for smart public-safety services.

results.company: Helsinki Region Environmental Services Authority HSY
results.title: Sewage - Improving Sewage Pipe Network predicting sewer blockages
results.proposal: Sewage - Improving Sewage Pipe Network predicting sewer blockages. Helsinki Region Environmental Services Authority HSY implemented this use case to improve the maintenance of a sewage network extending over more than 3,000 kilometres. Sewer blockages create operational, environmental and service-continuity risks, as they can lead to local disruptions, emergency interventions, overflow incidents and higher maintenance costs. Traditional sewer cleaning often relies on fixed schedules or reactive responses after problems occur, which may not direct resources towards the sections most likely to fail. HSY therefore sought a more targeted approach to preventive maintenance, enabling cleaning teams to focus on drain ranges where the risk of blockage is highest. The AI solution, Smartvatten Neuro, predicts possible blockages by analysing sewage-network data and identifying pipe sections that show characteristics associated with blockage-prone areas. The system produces recommendations on where cleaning should be prioritised, allowing maintenance activity to be planned according to predicted risk rather than general assumptions alone. By combining operational data with predictive modelling, the solution supports earlier intervention and better allocation of maintenance capacity. The experience showed that the system can predict blockages effectively and that up to one third of annual sewer blockages could be avoided. The main benefits are reduced disruption, more efficient field operations, lower avoidable maintenance costs and improved reliability of wastewater services across the Helsinki region.
results.memo: Proceed. Sewage - Improving Sewage Pipe Network predicting sewer blockages is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Predicting Heat Energy Consumption
results.proposal: Predicting Heat Energy Consumption. Helen introduced this use case in the City of Helsinki to improve the forecasting of district heat demand, a critical operational task for an energy provider serving an urban environment where consumption fluctuates according to weather, seasonality, building behaviour and customer needs. Accurate heat-demand forecasting is essential for balancing supply and demand, planning production capacity, reducing operational inefficiencies and ensuring reliable service delivery to households, businesses and public facilities. The objective of the use case is to support more precise short-term and medium-term planning by reducing the gap between expected and actual heat consumption. The AI solution uses historical energy-consumption data together with local weather forecasts to predict future heat demand more accurately. At a conceptual level, the model identifies patterns between previous demand levels, meteorological conditions and consumption behaviour, then applies these relationships to forecast upcoming energy needs. This information can be integrated into Helen’s operational planning processes to support production scheduling and resource optimisation. The reported impact is significant: the solution has reduced errors between forecast and actual heat demand by one third. This improves reliability, supports more efficient use of energy-production assets, reduces unnecessary operational costs and strengthens Helsinki’s ability to manage urban energy services in a more data-driven and sustainable way.
results.memo: Proceed. Predicting Heat Energy Consumption is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Kratt Sälli - Organising museum inventory
results.proposal: Kratt Sälli - Organising museum inventory. Kratt Sälli was developed by Estonia’s National Heritage Board to support museums in managing preservation and inventory activities more efficiently. Museum collections require regular monitoring, but traditional inventory work can be labour-intensive, repetitive and difficult to prioritise when institutions hold large numbers of objects with different materials, conditions and preservation needs. The operational challenge is therefore not only to record what is in the collection, but also to identify which objects require attention and when, so that staff time can be used where it creates the greatest preservation value. The objective of Sälli is to make inventory processes faster, more convenient and more need-based. The implementation is described as a prototype using a forecasting model to predict the ageing of museum objects. By analysing available information on collection items and their preservation characteristics, the system can help estimate which objects may be more likely to deteriorate and should therefore be prioritised for inspection. This supports a shift from routine, calendar-based inventory towards targeted monitoring driven by risk and need. The expected benefits include savings in staff hours, better allocation of preservation resources, earlier identification of vulnerable objects and improved planning of museum inventory work. In the longer term, the use case can strengthen cultural-heritage management by helping institutions protect collections more systematically and efficiently.
results.memo: Proceed. Kratt Sälli - Organising museum inventory is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Transcription Kratt 1247 - Transcribing calls to to crisis number 1247
results.proposal: Transcription Kratt 1247 - Transcribing calls to to crisis number 1247. Estonia’s crisis-information services introduced this use case to make better use of the substantial volume of calls handled through the national 1247 crisis number. Spoken interactions often contain valuable information on citizens’ concerns, recurring service needs and operational bottlenecks, yet audio recordings are difficult to analyse at scale and manual review is time-consuming. The service therefore needed a way to convert calls into a format that could support structured analysis, service improvement and the development of additional digital-support tools. The stakeholders include the emergency and crisis-information service, public-sector innovation teams and future service designers working on Estonia’s “kratt” ecosystem. The technological implementation is based on automated speech transcription, which converts spoken conversations from the 1247 line into machine-readable text. Once transcribed, the material can be searched, analysed and reused to identify frequent topics, recurring questions, information gaps and patterns in public demand during crisis situations. The resulting text can also provide a practical evidence base for training or designing future conversational assistants. The main impact is improved reuse of call-centre knowledge, reduced effort in extracting insight from audio material and stronger support for evidence-based service design. More broadly, the solution transforms routine crisis-service interactions into a scalable knowledge resource for public administration.

results.title: Turing - Automatically control Flemish road lighting with local and current data
results.proposal: Turing - Automatically control Flemish road lighting with local and current data. Turing addresses the challenge of managing motorway lighting in Flanders in a way that balances energy efficiency, climate objectives, road safety and operational workload. The Agency for Roads and Traffic had already adopted a lighting strategy in 2011 in response to the European Union’s objective of reducing energy consumption by 20% by 2020, and the number of illuminated road sections has since fallen by almost half. However, the existing control approach relies mainly on historical traffic intensities and weather forecasts at provincial level, which limits the precision of decisions on whether lighting is necessary for a specific road segment. The Turing use case aims to make lighting control more localised, timely and evidence-based. Its implementation combines rule-based algorithms with machine-learning techniques to integrate internal and external data sources into the current road-lighting control system. Local and real-time information on traffic intensity and weather conditions can be processed to determine more accurately when lighting should be switched on or off. This allows the system to move from broad assumptions towards segment-level operational decisions. The anticipated results include lower energy consumption, stronger contribution to climate targets, maintained or improved road safety, and a significant reduction in manual workload for operators. The use case also demonstrates how existing infrastructure-management systems can be upgraded through data-driven automation.
results.memo: Proceed. Turing - Automatically control Flemish road lighting with local and current data is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Capsat - Information from satellite images for a better agricultural policy in Flanders and Europe
results.proposal: Capsat - Information from satellite images for a better agricultural policy in Flanders and Europe. Capsat was developed to support the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries in Flanders in monitoring compliance with agricultural policy requirements linked to the European Common Agricultural Policy. Farmers receiving direct support must respect several climate and environmentally oriented obligations, including crop diversification, grassland maintenance and the creation of ecological focus areas. Traditionally, supervision of these measures has relied on field spot checks, which are resource-intensive, limited in coverage and often unable to provide rapid insight across large agricultural areas. The objective of the use case is therefore to improve follow-up, guidance and control by using remote information that can complement or partially replace manual inspection. The implementation uses high-resolution satellite imagery to map relevant agricultural conditions and detect whether policy measures have been applied correctly and on time. Image-analysis techniques can help identify crops, land use, grassland status or ecological features, while also supporting faster objectification of crop damage caused by drought or flooding. This creates a more systematic evidence base for both compliance monitoring and farmer support. The expected impact is greater efficiency in controls, broader territorial coverage, faster detection of anomalies or damage, and more objective decision-making. In policy terms, Capsat strengthens the administration’s capacity to implement agricultural rules while supporting sustainable, liveable and competitive farming in Flanders and potentially at wider European scale.
results.memo: Proceed. Capsat - Information from satellite images for a better agricultural policy in Flanders and Europe is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Civocracy - Online Platform
results.proposal: Civocracy - Online Platform. Civocracy provides public authorities with an online participation environment designed to improve dialogue between citizens, businesses, civil-society organisations and governments. The use case addresses a recurring challenge in public consultation: traditional participation processes can be fragmented, limited in reach and difficult to analyse systematically once large volumes of feedback are collected. By offering a structured digital space for discussion, debate and idea generation, the platform aims to make consultation more transparent, inclusive and continuous. It has been used by cities in Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, supporting local authorities that want to involve communities in policy development, urban planning or service improvement. Its implementation combines online discussion-board functionality with tools for crowdsourcing ideas, tracking participation, producing statistics and monitoring the impact of engagement activities in real time. Data analytics and machine-learning capabilities support the analysis of group sentiment and help public bodies understand how participants respond to proposals or policy themes. This makes consultation outputs easier to interpret and compare, particularly where feedback is broad or diverse. The platform’s main benefits include wider participation, clearer evidence from citizen input, more transparent follow-up on public discussions and stronger trust-building between institutions and communities. For administrations, it also creates a reusable and scalable channel for managing participatory processes across multiple policy areas.
results.memo: Proceed. Civocracy - Online Platform is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: DBA - Intelligent Control Platform
results.proposal: DBA - Intelligent Control Platform. The Danish Business Authority developed the Intelligent Control Platform to strengthen how public-sector control, supervision and decision-support processes are carried out in areas where large volumes of administrative and operational data must be continuously assessed. The research unit behind the initiative was established in 2017, when the Authority put its first two models into production and integrated them directly with internal control systems. The purpose was to move beyond static checks and enable more dynamic monitoring, where changes in data could be evaluated quickly against defined thresholds and used to support operational decisions. The platform has since evolved through several generations and now includes around 30 models in production. Technically, it combines machine-learning models with internal control-system data, allowing new information to be assessed as it becomes available. The Authority is also working with real-time graph machine learning and fraud-detection methods, supported by a data-platform architecture designed to handle continuous analysis and model deployment. The system therefore functions as an intelligent layer over existing control processes, identifying patterns, risks or threshold breaches that may require attention. Its impact is a more scalable and data-driven approach to supervision, improved capacity to detect irregularities, faster interpretation of changing datasets, and better support for staff responsible for control activities and fraud prevention.

results.title: Kranj Digital Twin - Representation of the city digitally
results.proposal: Kranj Digital Twin - Representation of the city digitally. The City Municipality of Kranj launched this use case in 2021 to explore how a residential district could be managed through more integrated, data-informed urban services. The pilot focused on Mlaka pri Kranju and was carried out with a consortium of local companies, including RIKO d.o.o., 3fs d.o.o., Iskraemeco d.d., Komunala Kranj d.o.o., Domplan d.o.o., Elektro Gorenjska d.d. and Vigred d.o.o. The main operational need was to obtain a clearer, more timely picture of how neighbourhood infrastructure performs, particularly in relation to utilities, environmental conditions, traffic and connectivity. Rather than managing these domains separately, the municipality aimed to create a smart-neighbourhood model that could later be extended to other parts of the city. The technological implementation centres on a digital twin approach, combining data from smart electricity, gas and water meters with environmental and traffic sensors, supported by a telecommunications backbone. These inputs are collected, visualised and analysed to create a digital representation of selected neighbourhood functions and infrastructure conditions. The resulting model can support monitoring, planning and service coordination at local level. Its value lies in giving the municipality and service providers a more coherent operational view, improving evidence for infrastructure decisions, enabling future scalability across Kranj, and establishing a practical foundation for broader smart-city development.
results.memo: Proceed. Kranj Digital Twin - Representation of the city digitally is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: a-z.lu to digitise text documents for Luxembourg's National Library
results.proposal: a-z.lu to digitise text documents for Luxembourg's National Library. The Bibliothèque nationale de Luxembourg implemented this use case to improve the accessibility, usability and long-term management of textual documents held in its collections. National libraries are responsible not only for preserving documentary heritage, but also for making it discoverable and usable for researchers, public institutions and citizens. The operational challenge addressed here concerns the conversion of scanned or image-based materials into structured, searchable and better-organised digital resources. The objective is to enhance the quality of digitised content by correcting errors, identifying meaningful information within texts and improving the organisation of associated image content. The implementation uses optical character recognition as a foundation for transforming scanned documents into machine-readable text, followed by correction processes to improve the reliability of the extracted content. Entity extraction is then applied to identify relevant names, places, organisations or other significant references within the material, while image-content organisation supports better structuring and retrieval of visual components. Together, these techniques make the digitised collections easier to search, classify and reuse. The impact is a stronger digital library service, improved discoverability of national documentary resources, higher-quality metadata and text outputs, and better support for research and public access. Over time, the approach contributes to more scalable digitisation workflows and strengthens the National Library’s capacity to preserve and disseminate Luxembourg’s cultural and documentary heritage.
results.memo: Proceed. a-z.lu to digitise text documents for Luxembourg's National Library is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: AI assisted chat service - Chatbot for tax purposes
results.proposal: AI assisted chat service - Chatbot for tax purposes. OmaVero is a chatbot service that provides the Finnish Tax Administration with a digital channel for answering common tax-related questions from individual taxpayers. The service responds to the recurring need for quick, accessible and low-threshold guidance on tax matters, particularly when users are looking for general clarification rather than case-specific decisions. It allows customers to receive assistance without calling the administration, paying telephone costs or completing identification steps for basic enquiries. During office hours, the interaction can be escalated to a human agent when the automated response is not sufficient, ensuring that more complex issues can still be handled by staff. The technological implementation combines a virtual agent with natural language processing, which converts customer messages into a form that the system can interpret and route towards relevant tax content. The underlying AI-assisted chat solution was developed by a commercial provider, while the Finnish Tax Administration remains responsible for governance, including training, monitoring and content creation through its chat-product team. This arrangement allows the administration to retain control over service quality and accuracy while using external technology to support delivery. The main benefits are faster replies to routine questions, broader service availability regardless of time, reduced demand on telephone and front-office channels, and a more efficient allocation of human agents to cases requiring judgement or personalised assistance.

results.company: Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment
results.title: Job Market Finland - Matching employees with right jobs
results.proposal: Job Market Finland - Matching employees with right jobs. Job Market Finland was developed by the KEHA Centre and the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment to improve how jobseekers, employers and service providers interact within the Finnish labour market. The service addresses a core policy and operational challenge: matching people to suitable vacancies in a context where skills, occupations, training services and employment opportunities are distributed across multiple public and private platforms. Its objective is to create a shared digital environment where jobseekers can present their profiles, employers can identify relevant candidates, and different labour-market services can be connected more coherently. The emerging technology component is centred on an AI-based matching solution that compares jobseeker profiles with vacancies using both structured data, such as skills and occupations, and unstructured natural-language information contained in descriptions. The system scores the degree of fit between candidates and roles and presents matches to both jobseekers and employers. It also assists users in describing the skills they offer or require, helping to improve the quality of profile and vacancy information. The expected impact is a more efficient matching process, better visibility of opportunities, reduced friction in recruitment, and stronger alignment between labour supply and employer demand. By combining public employment services with data-driven matching, the platform supports a more transparent, scalable and user-oriented labour-market infrastructure.

results.title: NeRo Chatbot - Chatbot for clients of maternity services
results.proposal: NeRo Chatbot - Chatbot for clients of maternity services. The City of Helsinki developed NeRo to support parents, expectant parents and carers who need reliable information about pregnancy, infant health and the early development of children. Maternity and child-health services often receive recurring questions on topics such as growth, nutrition, dental care, speech development and everyday health concerns, and users may need guidance outside normal service hours. NeRo responds to this need by offering an around-the-clock digital support channel in Finnish, giving families an accessible source of basic information before they contact health professionals or attend appointments. The chatbot is designed to answer questions related to pregnancy and the health care of babies and small children, covering both preventive guidance and common development-related issues. Technically, it applies conversational technology and language understanding to interpret user questions and match them with curated information from municipal health-service content. The system provides automated responses within a defined service scope and can guide users towards relevant topics without replacing professional medical assessment where individual care is required. Its impact is primarily qualitative: it improves the availability of trusted municipal guidance, helps families obtain answers at any time of day, reduces the burden of repetitive enquiries on maternity and child-health staff, and strengthens the digital service offer of Helsinki’s public health system.

results.title: IMMS (Intelligent Material Management System) for the entire library collection.
results.proposal: IMMS (Intelligent Material Management System) for the entire library collection. Helsinki City Library introduced the Intelligent Material Management System during its transition from separate library-specific collections towards one shared collection serving the whole city network. The operational problem was that materials needed to move more flexibly between branches, while library staff required better visibility over where items were located, how they circulated and how available space could be used. The objective was to support a “floating” collection model, in which books and other materials are no longer tied permanently to a single branch but can circulate according to user demand and operational needs. Implemented in May 2019, IMMS complements the existing library management infrastructure by adding a more detailed layer of collection, space and logistics management. The system uses data collection tools to track materials at granular locations, including shelves, shelving carts, transport bins and storage areas, thereby creating greater transparency across the material flow. It supports decision-making on stock distribution, item movement, collection balance and physical space use across the library network. As a result, Helsinki City Library has been able to move towards a model in which most of the collection floats between libraries. The main benefits include more efficient use of the overall collection, improved staff control over logistics, better alignment between material availability and user demand, and a more scalable approach to managing public library resources across multiple branches.
results.memo: Proceed. IMMS (Intelligent Material Management System) for the entire library collection. is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Chatbot - Social Insurance Institution of Finland
results.proposal: Chatbot - Social Insurance Institution of Finland. The Social Insurance Institution of Finland developed this chatbot to help citizens access information on public welfare matters more easily, particularly in areas where users often require timely clarification, such as family benefits, income support and issues linked to social security. The service responds to the need for a more accessible front door to welfare information, reducing dependence on traditional service channels for routine questions and supporting users who may not immediately know which benefit, allowance or administrative process applies to their situation. The chatbot operates in Finland’s two official languages, Finnish and Swedish, reflecting the institution’s obligation to serve citizens across linguistic groups. While it can understand questions submitted in English, its responses are provided in Finnish or Swedish, ensuring consistency with the language framework of the service. From a technical perspective, the system uses conversational technology and natural language processing to interpret user queries, identify the relevant topic area and return appropriate guidance from structured welfare-service content. Its role is not to replace case-specific decision-making, but to provide first-level information and direct users towards the correct benefit or process. The qualitative impact is improved availability of basic welfare guidance, faster responses to common questions, reduced pressure on staff handling repetitive enquiries, and a more user-friendly digital channel for citizens seeking support from the Finnish social security system.

From a technical perspective, the system uses conversational technology and natural language processing to interpret user queries, identify the relevant topic area and return appropriate guidance from structured welfare-service content.
