results.company: Baden Wurttemberg, Hesse,  Berlin and  North Rhine-Westphalia
results.title: PRECOBS - Predictive policing in German administrations
results.proposal: PRECOBS - Predictive policing in German administrations. PRECOBS and related predictive policing systems in German administrations address the challenge of preventing burglary and other property crime through more targeted operational planning. Several German Länder and cities have tested or deployed tools designed to identify locations where break-ins are more likely to occur, allowing police forces to incorporate forecasts into prevention and patrol strategies. In Bavaria, PRECOBS, developed by the Institut für musterbasierte Prognosetechnik, has been used to calculate areas with higher predicted burglary risk. Similar approaches have been adopted elsewhere: Hesse uses KLB-operativ, Berlin uses KrimPro, North Rhine-Westphalia developed SKALA based on IBM products, and Lower Saxony uses PreMAP. The emerging technology implementation is based on analytical systems that process historical crime data and related contextual variables to identify recurring spatial and temporal patterns. These systems generate forecast areas or hot spots, which police authorities can use in action plans and resource deployment. The impact is intended to be more proactive burglary prevention, better allocation of police capacity and improved operational situational awareness. However, implementation outcomes vary across jurisdictions. In Baden-Württemberg, use of PRECOBS was discontinued in 2019 due to data-quality issues, showing that predictive policing tools depend heavily on the reliability, completeness and suitability of the underlying data. The case therefore illustrates both the operational promise and the governance limitations of algorithmic forecasting in police work.

results.company: Logroño municipality and the La Rioja and Cantabria regional governments
results.title: REACHOUT: Smart Cities: from smart waste to smart tourism
results.proposal: REACHOUT: Smart Cities: from smart waste to smart tourism. The REACHOUT-related Smart Waste example reflects the broader effort of Spanish local and regional authorities to use data-driven tools to improve municipal service planning. Waste management is a complex operational area in which authorities must decide where, when and how services are needed, while responding to changing urban patterns, citizen behaviour and resource constraints. The Smart Waste platform was first piloted in 2018 by Logroño municipality and the regional governments of La Rioja and Cantabria. Its objective was to support more informed waste-management decisions by combining multiple sources of data rather than relying only on fixed collection schedules or fragmented local knowledge. The emerging technology implementation was developed by The Circular Lab, the innovation centre of Ecoembes, with support from Minsait, a division of Indra. The platform gathers data from sensors installed in waste bins and collection trucks, and combines these with information from social media, surveys, census sources and satellite data. At conceptual level, the system supports automated analysis and decision-support outputs that help authorities estimate service needs by location and time. The platform is now described as available to local and regional authorities across Spain. Its potential impact includes improved targeting of waste services, better planning, more efficient resource allocation and increased scalability across municipalities. However, the available information does not explain the software’s internal functioning, the exact outputs it produces, or the concrete decisions adopted by authorities as a result of its use.

results.title: Automated analysis of social media content
results.proposal: Automated analysis of social media content. The automated analysis of social media content in Catalonia was introduced to help public authorities better understand public reactions to policy initiatives and communication campaigns. In January 2018, the regional Government of Catalonia launched a pilot to assess the public impact of STEMcat, a policy initiative aimed at promoting scientific and technological vocations among young people. The objective was to move beyond traditional consultation and survey methods by analysing online conversations at scale, while supporting the SmartCAT strategy to position Catalonia as a smart region. The emerging technology implementation used Citibeats, a text-analysis software developed by Social Coin, a Barcelona-based start-up. During the pilot, the system collected and analysed around 12,000 tweets concerning STEM disciplines in Catalonia, using machine-learning techniques to classify content and identify patterns in public attitudes. Authorities reported insights such as different levels of responsiveness among women to messages on natural sciences compared with technology, which were then used to optimise strategy and propose further initiatives. Citibeats had also been used by Barcelona municipality in December 2017 to analyse around 30,000 comments from more than 15,000 people on public transport and mobility, and by Navarra from March 2019 to detect online hate speech across Facebook, Twitter and Instagram. The main reported value is faster, lower-cost analysis of large volumes of online content, although the representativeness of the samples, methodological transparency, oversight mechanisms and actual policy influence remain unclear.

results.title: Pred Crime Pilot Rivas-Vaciamadrid
results.proposal: Pred Crime Pilot Rivas-Vaciamadrid. The Pred Crime pilot in Rivas-Vaciamadrid addressed the challenge of supporting local police in anticipating where and when common offences and misdemeanours were more likely to occur. In 2016, the local police of Rivas-Vaciamadrid, a municipality of around 86,000 inhabitants in the Madrid region, tested the Pred-Crime software developed by the Spanish company EuroCop. The operational objective was to use historical policing information to support prevention-oriented deployment decisions, particularly in relation to offences such as robberies and traffic violations. The emerging technology implementation relied on analytical software that processed historical crime and incident data to identify spatial and temporal patterns associated with different categories of offences. At conceptual level, the system generated predictions on likely locations and timeframes for future incidents, which could then inform police planning and patrol allocation. The pilot was reportedly intended for full implementation during 2016; however, after nine months of testing, the municipality decided not to continue using the software. The available information therefore points to limited operational impact in this specific municipality. While EuroCop states that it has numerous municipal customers across Spain, it is not clear whether those authorities use Pred-Crime or other non-predictive EuroCop tools. The case is therefore particularly relevant as an example of a tested but discontinued predictive policing application, highlighting issues of adoption, validation and long-term suitability.

results.title: INZNAK Project - Intelligent road signs for adaptive vehicle traffic control
results.proposal: INZNAK Project - Intelligent road signs for adaptive vehicle traffic control. The INZNAK project responds to the need to improve road safety and traffic management by providing drivers with timely, location-specific warnings about hazards, disruptions and recommended speeds. Many highway collisions are linked to speed that is not adapted to current weather, road-surface or traffic conditions, particularly during sudden braking, congestion, fog, storms, blizzards or black ice. In Gdańsk, the project aims to develop a network of autonomous intelligent road signs capable of warning drivers earlier and supporting adaptive traffic control. The emerging technology implementation includes three types of signs: standing, hanging and mobile. Each sign has a display showing text and image messages, including suggested speeds and information on current disruptions. The signs communicate with each other through LoRaWAN and with the traffic control centre through LTE, creating a two-level communication architecture that improves resilience if telecommunications infrastructure fails. Each sign is equipped with sensors such as Doppler radar, lidar, acoustic probes, RGB cameras, Bluetooth receivers and a local weather station. This multimodal approach allows the system to combine different detection methods, for example using lidar when standard cameras are less effective at night. The expected impact is earlier hazard detection, more reliable traffic information and better adaptation of driver behaviour to real-time road conditions, with potential benefits for safety, traffic flow and operational resilience.

results.company: Municipality of Heerlen, CBS, VNG, CoTown, Heerlen Mijn Stad, Brightlands
results.title: W(e). Service.Heerlen (WESH)
results.proposal: W(e). Service.Heerlen (WESH). W(e). Service.Heerlen, or WESH, addresses the challenge of maintaining the public environment while promoting citizen participation and supporting local economic activity. Municipalities often face pressure to keep public spaces clean, safe and well maintained, while citizens may have limited structured opportunities to contribute to neighbourhood improvements. In Heerlen, the municipality and partners including CBS, VNG, CoTown, Heerlen Mijn Stad and Brightlands developed an application that enables citizens to take on maintenance tasks in the public environment. The objective is to create a participatory model in which residents can contribute directly to local upkeep and receive a financial reward that can be spent with local small and medium-sized enterprises. The emerging technology implementation is based on a digital platform that connects available municipal maintenance jobs with citizens willing to complete them. At conceptual level, the app supports task publication, citizen participation, completion confirmation and reward allocation, linking civic engagement with local economic circulation. The solution may also generate useful operational data on maintenance needs, participation patterns and service delivery. Its impact is both operational and social: the municipality can mobilise additional capacity for small-scale public-space maintenance, citizens gain a practical role in improving their environment, and local SMEs benefit from reward spending. The case demonstrates how digital public-service platforms can combine urban maintenance, participation and local value creation.

results.company: Brightlands Techruption, OU (CAROU), UM (BISS), Police NL (iLAB)
results.title: Nexus -  speech-operated expert system
results.proposal: Nexus -  speech-operated expert system. Nexus is designed to support community police officers who require timely, structured and locally relevant information before engaging with neighbourhoods. Officers often need to review recent incidents, local risks and operational context, but conventional briefing processes can be fragmented, time-consuming or dependent on manual searches across different systems. The case involves Brightlands Techruption, the Open University’s CAROU, Maastricht University’s BISS and the Dutch Police iLAB, with the objective of providing officers with an accessible expert system that delivers detailed neighbourhood briefings through speech interaction. The emerging technology implementation consists of a speech-operated expert system that allows officers to request and receive information verbally. At conceptual level, the system combines speech recognition, knowledge retrieval and expert-system logic to transform operational data on recent incidents into a concise briefing tailored to a specific neighbourhood. The interface reduces the need for manual interaction and supports use in operational contexts where officers may benefit from hands-free access to information. The impact is improved situational awareness, more efficient preparation and a better user experience for community police officers. By making local incident information easier to access and interpret, Nexus can support more informed decision-making, strengthen neighbourhood policing and reduce the time spent searching for relevant background information before field activities.

results.title: E-Discovery - automatic classifcation of incoming and outgoing emails
results.proposal: E-Discovery - automatic classifcation of incoming and outgoing emails. The National Archives of the Netherlands and ICTU explored E-Discovery to address a growing information-management challenge within public administration: the increasing volume of incoming and outgoing emails that must be classified, retained, searched and managed in accordance with archival and administrative requirements. Manual classification is time-consuming, inconsistent and difficult to scale, particularly for organisations that handle large volumes of official correspondence. In 2016, the Nationaal Archief launched a study into the potential of E-Discovery methods in information management, with the objective of testing whether automated support could improve the organisation, retrieval and governance of email records. The emerging technology implementation consisted of a prototype capable of classifying emails automatically. At conceptual level, the system used machine-learning techniques to analyse email content and metadata, identify relevant categories, and assign classifications that could support archival processes. The prototype was developed in cooperation with ICTU, linking information-management expertise with technical implementation capacity. The expected impact is a more efficient, consistent and scalable approach to managing public-sector email records. By reducing the burden of manual classification, the solution can support better compliance, faster retrieval of information and more reliable records management. Although described as a study and prototype, the case demonstrates the value of automated classification for public administrations facing rapidly growing volumes of digital correspondence.

results.title: CrossWalk in Smart City Rijswijk
results.proposal: CrossWalk in Smart City Rijswijk. The municipality of Rijswijk tested CrossWalk to address a concrete accessibility and road-safety challenge: standard pedestrian crossing times are often insufficient for older people, people with disabilities or citizens with reduced mobility. This can create unsafe situations at intersections and reduce the autonomy of residents who require more time to cross the road. The pilot involved the Municipality of Rijswijk and Dynniq, with the objective of making pedestrian infrastructure more responsive to the needs of vulnerable road users while avoiding permanent changes to signal timing for all pedestrians. The emerging technology implementation is based on a mobile application connected to traffic signal systems. When a registered user with mobility difficulties approaches or waits at a crossing, the app uses location data to communicate with the traffic control software and signal the user’s presence. The traffic light system can then automatically extend the green phase, allowing additional time for a safe crossing. At conceptual level, the solution integrates mobile positioning, traffic-light control logic and intersection management systems. Its impact lies in improving pedestrian safety, accessibility and user experience for residents who walk more slowly. It also demonstrates how smart-city infrastructure can provide targeted support without redesigning the entire traffic system, making the approach potentially scalable to other intersections and municipalities with similar accessibility objectives.
results.memo: Proceed. CrossWalk in Smart City Rijswijk is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.company: Municipality of Amsterdam and AMS Institute
results.title: CityFlows-Amsterdam
results.proposal: CityFlows-Amsterdam. Busy pedestrian areas in Amsterdam require reliable crowd-management capabilities to safeguard public safety, maintain comfort and support evidence-based operational decisions in high-density urban spaces. The CityFlows initiative, developed as an EIT Urban Mobility flagship project, brought together the Municipality of Amsterdam, AMS Institute and a wider consortium of partners to address the need for better monitoring and management of pedestrian flows, particularly in locations affected by congestion, events, tourism and changing mobility patterns. The objective was to provide public authorities with a decision-support capability that helps them understand crowd dynamics and take timely measures to improve the use of public space. The emerging technology implementation centres on the Crowd Management Decision-Support System, a software-based platform licensed through City Analytics to government authorities. At conceptual level, the system combines pedestrian-flow data, urban analytics and operational decision-support functions to help authorities assess crowding conditions, anticipate risks and select appropriate interventions. Its deployment supports integration between urban data sources, monitoring tools and municipal crowd-management processes. The main impact is improved situational awareness for public authorities, enabling safer, more comfortable and more responsive management of busy pedestrian spaces. The creation of City Analytics as a dedicated start-up also strengthens scalability and reuse, allowing the solution to be offered beyond the original project context and supporting cities seeking reliable tools for managing public space during normal operations and crisis situations.

results.company: Portuguese Public National Health Service (Centro de Controlo e Monitorização do Sistema Nacional de Saúde)
results.title: CCM-SNS - Verification of medical prescriptions
results.proposal: CCM-SNS - Verification of medical prescriptions. Portugal’s National Health Service needed a stronger way to detect irregular prescribing patterns and possible fraud after introducing paperless prescriptions and mandatory electronic medical prescriptions across the public sector in 2016. The operational challenge was to monitor very large volumes of prescription and invoicing data across multiple databases in order to identify suspicious claims without relying on slower, fragmented manual checks. The use case therefore involves the Control and Monitoring Centre of the Portuguese Public National Health Service, healthcare-finance authorities and prosecutors, with the objective of protecting public funds, improving oversight of prescription activity and supporting the investigation of fraud within the health system. The solution is implemented through data integration and analytical controls applied to several health and billing databases. At a conceptual level, the system cross-checks prescription, invoicing and related administrative records to identify anomalies and inconsistencies that may indicate fraudulent or improper activity. These flagged cases can then be escalated for further review or prosecution. The results reported are substantial: during the first seven years, irregularities amounting to hundreds of millions of euros were detected, and in the first half of 2017 alone the Invoice Control Centre processed EUR 356.2 million in prescriptions and flagged EUR 21.1 million to the State Prosecutor. The impact includes major financial-control benefits, improved fraud detection and stronger accountability in public healthcare spending.

results.company: Krajowa Izba Rozliczeniowa S.A (State Clearance Chamber), Krajowa Izba Rozliczeniowa S.A (State Clearance Chamber)
results.title: STIR - System Teleinformatyczny Izby Rozliczeniowej (Clearance Chamber ICT System)
results.proposal: STIR - System Teleinformatyczny Izby Rozliczeniowej (Clearance Chamber ICT System). Polish tax authorities and payment-system institutions needed a stronger mechanism to detect suspicious financial behaviour linked to illegal activity, particularly in a context where unlawful transactions can move quickly through bank accounts before traditional controls can respond. The operational challenge was to assess risk across large volumes of financial information and identify account holders who may be involved in fraud or other illicit conduct, while enabling timely intervention where warranted. The stakeholders include the State Clearance Chamber, tax authorities, banks and the wider financial-control system, with the objective of improving the detection of suspicious activity and strengthening the state’s ability to act before funds are moved or concealed. The solution is implemented through STIR, which compiles a risk indicator from financial data collected from financial institutions. At a conceptual level, the system aggregates and analyses transaction-related and account-level information to generate a risk profile indicating the likelihood that illegal activity may be taking place. Where suspicious activity is identified, tax authorities can request that a bank freeze the account concerned. This embeds the analytical system within the national payment infrastructure and links risk detection directly to enforcement capability. The expected impact is faster identification of high-risk accounts, improved targeting of financial controls and stronger protection of public revenues. More broadly, STIR creates value by increasing the efficiency and reach of financial oversight while supporting a more responsive and coordinated anti-fraud framework.

results.company: Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management of the Netherlands
results.title: RWS - Machine learning for road accident predictions
results.proposal: RWS - Machine learning for road accident predictions. Rijkswaterstaat operates a 24-hour incident-management service in which traffic managers monitor extensive real-time information across more than 15 screens, creating a demanding environment in which accident risks can be difficult to identify early and inspectors may not always be optimally positioned to respond quickly. The operational challenge is not only to detect incidents, but also to anticipate where they are most likely to occur so that patrol deployment can be planned more effectively. This use case therefore involves traffic managers, inspectors and the Netherlands Ministry of Water and Infrastructure Management, with the objective of reducing response times and improving road-safety operations by positioning inspectors where risk is greatest. The solution was developed with Data Science for Social Good using a predictive model trained on incident data from 2012 to 2016, combined with road characteristics, traffic speed and flow data, and weather information. At a conceptual level, the model estimates the probability of an accident occurring within a given time window and road segment, then displays this on a heatmap so that managers can identify high-risk sections and allocate patrols more strategically. The impact is explicitly measurable: the approach delivered a three- to fourfold improvement over a baseline in which inspectors patrolled random road segments. More broadly, the project improves operational efficiency, supports faster incident response and creates value through better use of traffic-management resources.

results.title: SIA - Notifications public space
results.proposal: SIA - Notifications public space. Municipalities receive large numbers of citizen reports about problems in public space, such as damage, nuisance or maintenance issues, and these notifications must be classified and routed to the appropriate department before action can begin. When this sorting is done manually, it can be slow, inconsistent and resource-intensive, especially where incoming reports vary widely in wording and urgency. The SIA use case was developed to address this administrative bottleneck by improving how local authorities process citizen notifications about the public realm. The stakeholders include residents, municipal contact teams and operational departments responsible for public-space maintenance and response, with the objective of speeding up case handling, reducing internal friction and ensuring that reports reach the right team more quickly. The solution is implemented through an automated categorisation tool that analyses incoming citizen notifications and assigns them to the relevant issue type and responsible department. At a conceptual level, the system uses language-processing and classification techniques to interpret the content of free-text reports and connect them with municipal workflows for follow-up. This creates a more consistent and scalable intake process than fully manual routing. The impact includes faster handling of public-space notifications, reduced administrative burden and improved responsiveness for residents reporting problems. More broadly, SIA creates public value by making local-government service delivery more efficient, improving the user experience and supporting a fairer and more reliable way of processing citizen concerns.

results.title: Cameras - Detection holding a phone in car
results.proposal: Cameras - Detection holding a phone in car. The Dutch Public Prosecution Service introduced this use case to strengthen enforcement against drivers holding mobile phones behind the wheel, a behaviour associated with serious road-safety risks and difficult to police consistently through conventional roadside observation alone. Manual enforcement is limited by staff availability and by the practical difficulty of identifying violations reliably in moving traffic. The initiative therefore involves prosecutors, the Central Judicial Collection Agency and road users, with the objective of increasing compliance, improving traffic safety and making enforcement more efficient while preserving a degree of privacy in evidence collection. The solution is implemented through smart enforcement cameras that photograph passing vehicles from above in a way that excludes the driver’s face but captures the vehicle interior and number plate clearly enough to show whether a mobile device is being held. At a conceptual level, the system uses image-analysis techniques to detect likely violations and forwards only those suspected cases to the CJIB, where a staff member performs the final assessment before any sanction is issued. If confirmed, the violation can lead to a fine of EUR 240. The impact includes more targeted and scalable enforcement, reduced reliance on continuous manual observation and improved consistency in identifying offences. More broadly, the system creates value by supporting safer driving behaviour, strengthening operational efficiency and balancing automated detection with human verification in the final decision stage.

results.title: ANPR - Car plate recognition
results.proposal: ANPR - Car plate recognition. Public authorities need reliable ways to monitor vehicle movements and enforce rules across a wide range of operational contexts, including paid parking, traffic management, tax enforcement and environmental regulation. Manual checking is often too slow and resource-intensive to support these activities at scale, particularly when large volumes of vehicles must be processed quickly and accurately. The use case therefore involves local administrations, traffic authorities and enforcement bodies, with the objective of improving operational efficiency, strengthening compliance and enabling more consistent control across transport-related public services. The solution is implemented through automatic number-plate-recognition software that identifies vehicle registration plates from video or photographic footage captured by cameras. At a conceptual level, the system combines image capture, optical character recognition and pattern-detection techniques to isolate number plates, extract alphanumeric characters and match them against relevant administrative or enforcement databases. This makes it possible to automate vehicle identification in real time or near real time across different use cases. According to the source, the system is used in more than 2,000 administrations, indicating broad operational uptake and strong adaptability across service areas. The impact includes faster processing, reduced manual workload and improved enforcement capability, while also supporting scalability across multiple public functions. More broadly, ANPR creates business value by providing a versatile digital-control layer that can be reused across parking, regulation, taxation and environmental monitoring.

results.title: Xomnia - The Burglary Predictor
results.proposal: Xomnia - The Burglary Predictor. Utrecht wanted to strengthen burglary prevention by moving beyond reactive policing and municipal response towards a more anticipatory understanding of where burglary risk was likely to emerge. Burglary patterns are influenced by a mix of temporal, environmental and neighbourhood factors, yet these are difficult to interpret consistently without a structured analytical model. The use case therefore involved the municipality of Utrecht and local safety stakeholders, with the objective of supporting more data-driven decision-making and enabling preventive action at district level before incidents occur. The solution was implemented by Xomnia as a predictive model that estimates the occurrence of burglaries in each district for a given week. At a conceptual level, the model combines burglary date and time information with derived contextual variables such as weather conditions, holidays and special events, and enriches this with sociodemographic neighbourhood statistics and points of interest including street lights, cameras, trees, parks and large rubbish containers. These factors are brought together to generate district-level risk predictions that can inform operational choices and preventive planning. The expected impact is earlier identification of higher-risk areas, better targeting of local prevention measures and more efficient use of municipal and safety resources. More broadly, the Burglary Predictor creates value by improving situational foresight, supporting evidence-based urban safety policy and demonstrating how diverse local data can be combined to strengthen crime-prevention strategies.
results.memo: Proceed. Xomnia - The Burglary Predictor is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Xomnia - Law enforcement optimization system
results.proposal: Xomnia - Law enforcement optimization system. The municipality of Amsterdam needed a better way to coordinate and evaluate law-enforcement activity across a fragmented operational landscape in which relevant information was dispersed across multiple disconnected systems. Enforcement teams were generating valuable data through daily activities, but because these records were stored in separate silos, it was difficult for managers and operational staff to obtain a unified view of what was happening in the field or to use that information effectively for planning and oversight. The use case therefore involved municipal enforcement teams, control-room staff and decision-makers, with the objective of improving operational visibility, supporting more informed deployment decisions and making enforcement management more data-driven and efficient. The solution was implemented by Xomnia through a user-friendly dashboard built on top of an integrated data architecture. At a conceptual level, the system harvested and reconstructed data from seven different municipal sources, including GPS data from walkie-talkies, text data from fines issued through PDAs and reports from the control room, and then interconnected these datasets to allow dynamic exploration. This created a single analytical environment in which previously isolated operational signals could be examined together. The impact includes better situational awareness, improved ability to monitor enforcement activity and stronger support for planning and resource allocation. More broadly, the project creates value by reducing the limits imposed by data silos, improving operational efficiency and enabling a more coordinated and evidence-based approach to municipal law enforcement.

results.title: Amberscript - Automated speech translation for public organisations
results.proposal: Amberscript - Automated speech translation for public organisations. Dutch municipalities such as Staphorst needed a practical way to make council meetings more accessible and transparent, particularly for citizens who are deaf or hard of hearing and may otherwise struggle to follow political debate in real time. Municipal discussions are central to public accountability, yet live accessibility support can be costly and difficult to provide consistently across all meetings. The use case therefore involves local authorities, elected representatives and residents, with the objective of improving access to public decision-making, strengthening civic inclusion and increasing transparency around how municipal decisions are discussed and taken. The solution is implemented through AmberScript’s automated speech-recognition and translation technology, developed for public-sector meeting environments. At a conceptual level, the system was trained on a dataset of more than 1,000 hours of audio recordings and transcriptions from public-sector meetings, which were compiled, cleaned and processed to improve performance on the terminology, speaking styles and formats typical of council proceedings. The platform then converts spoken debate into text that can be followed online by citizens. The impact includes greater accessibility for people with hearing impairments, faster and more scalable production of meeting transcripts and improved visibility of democratic processes. More broadly, the service creates public value by making council proceedings easier to follow, reducing reliance on fully manual transcription and supporting a more open and inclusive model of local governance.

results.title: Wabo assistant - Automated environmental permits
results.proposal: Wabo assistant - Automated environmental permits. The municipality of The Hague needed a more efficient way to manage the intake of environmental-permit applications governed by the Environmental Law General Provisions Act, known as Wabo. Permit procedures in this area can involve large volumes of documents and varied applicant questions, creating an administrative burden at the earliest stages of the process and slowing the movement of cases into proper review channels. The use case therefore focused on improving intake efficiency and reducing repetitive administrative work, while helping the municipality process environmental permits more consistently. The stakeholders include municipal permit teams, applicants and environmental-administration staff, with the objective of automating part of the intake process and improving the speed and quality of early-stage handling. The solution is implemented through a Wabo assistant that uses natural language processing to support permit-related tasks. At a conceptual level, the system analyses incoming textual information, identifies relevant content and helps structure or route permit applications so that initial handling requires less manual intervention. This creates a more standardised intake workflow and allows staff to spend less time on repetitive front-end processing. The expected impact is faster handling of permit submissions, reduced clerical burden and improved efficiency in the administration of environmental permits. More broadly, the Wabo assistant creates value by modernising a document-heavy municipal process, supporting better service for applicants and enabling a more scalable model for managing regulatory intake under environmental law.

results.title: Smart Street Scan really sets up municipal services differently
results.proposal: Smart Street Scan really sets up municipal services differently. Municipalities need to keep public spaces clean, yet litter and other waste in streets and public areas are often detected only after complaints or routine inspections, which can delay action and make municipal services less efficient. Smart Street Scan was developed to address this challenge by enabling faster identification and registration of litter so that waste-collection and street-cleaning operations can be organised more effectively. The stakeholders include municipal service providers, waste-collection teams and residents using public space, with the objective of improving cleanliness, reducing response time and optimising service deployment through better information. The solution is implemented by combining sensor and camera technology with image-recognition methods to scan public space automatically. At a conceptual level, the system detects, classifies and registers litter in the street environment, creating a digital feed of observed waste conditions that can be linked to operational planning. This allows downstream services, such as sweeping and waste collection, to adapt routes and interventions on the basis of current conditions rather than relying solely on fixed schedules or resident reports. The expected impact is quicker detection of litter, more efficient route planning and improved street-cleaning performance. More broadly, the project creates value by changing how municipal services are organised around public-space maintenance, reducing unnecessary effort and supporting a more data-driven, responsive and scalable approach to keeping urban environments clean.

results.proposal: Prediction of young people engagement in undesirable behaviour (Pilot Apeldoorn Youth). The municipality of Apeldoorn explored this pilot to address concerns about youth-related nuisance and other forms of undesirable behaviour in public space, with the aim of identifying where preventive action might be most needed. Municipal authorities often face difficulty in deciding where to direct youth work, supervision and social intervention, especially when risks appear unevenly distributed across locations and groups. The use case therefore involved local authorities and youth-related service actors, with the objective of detecting patterns earlier and supporting more targeted preventive measures rather than relying only on reactive responses once incidents had already occurred. The solution was implemented by linking multiple data sources in order to estimate which groups of young people were more likely to engage in undesirable behaviour and in which locations this was more likely to happen. At a conceptual level, the system used cross-dataset analysis and predictive modelling to generate risk patterns that could inform municipal decision-making about attention, intervention and local policy. This created a data-driven view of behavioural risk across groups and places rather than depending solely on manual observation or isolated reports. The expected impact was earlier visibility of emerging risks, more focused use of local preventive resources and stronger operational support for youth policy. More broadly, the pilot created value by exploring how linked data could help municipalities move towards more anticipatory public-order and youth-support strategies, though such approaches also raise important governance and proportionality questions.

results.title: Artificial inspector - Self-learning system for the inspection of national roads and waterways
results.proposal: Artificial inspector - Self-learning system for the inspection of national roads and waterways. Rijkswaterstaat needed a more efficient and affordable way to inspect national roads and waterways, since traditional inspection approaches often depend on expensive professional camera equipment and limited collection capacity. Routine infrastructure inspection is essential for maintaining safety and service quality, but manual processes and specialist hardware can restrict coverage and raise costs. The use case therefore focused on expanding inspection capability while lowering the barriers to large-scale visual data collection. The stakeholders include Rijkswaterstaat, inspection teams and infrastructure managers, with the objective of automating a larger share of road and waterway inspection and improving the timeliness and consistency of asset monitoring. The solution is implemented through standard Android smartphones mounted on cars and ships, each running an application that captures an image every second. At a conceptual level, these images are combined with geographic data and used to train a cloud-based neural network that can recognise relevant infrastructure conditions and support automated inspection tasks. By using inexpensive, widely available devices instead of specialist cameras, the system creates a more scalable and flexible inspection model. The expected impact is lower equipment cost, broader inspection coverage and faster collection of infrastructure data. More broadly, the project creates value by modernising public-asset monitoring, improving operational efficiency and demonstrating how low-cost sensing combined with cloud-based analysis can reshape large-scale infrastructure inspection.

results.proposal: Auwi SaaS - Real-time AI-run analysis from millions of message. Manual monitoring of such discussions is difficult to sustain at scale and may fail to provide timely insight for communications and policy support. The use case therefore involved ministry teams responsible for analysis and public-information awareness, with the objective of turning high-volume online discussion into actionable intelligence that could support faster interpretation of emerging themes and sentiment. The solution was implemented through the Aiwo Digital platform, a software-as-a-service environment designed to process and analyse millions of messages in real time. At a conceptual level, the platform applies automated language analysis and classification methods to large streams of social-media content, then presents the results through dashboards and structured findings that are intended to support decision-makers directly. In this case, the system was used to analyse coronavirus-related discussions on Twitter and convert dispersed online conversation into clearer analytical outputs. The expected impact includes quicker access to public-discourse insight, reduced manual review effort and more consistent monitoring of high-volume digital communication. More broadly, the use case creates value by improving situational awareness, supporting evidence-based communications and enabling public institutions to interpret online discussion at a scale that would be difficult to manage through conventional methods alone.

The stakeholders include the Tax and Customs Board, tax inspectors and compliant businesses affected by the overall fairness of the system, with the objective of improving inspection targeting, increasing efficiency in tax enforcement and strengthening the board’s ability to detect hidden payroll practices. The solution is implemented as an analytical model built on information already available in tax returns, such as turnover and related reporting patterns. At a conceptual level, the system uses predictive modelling to estimate the probability that a company is paying envelope salaries and to support the selection of suitable inspection targets. This does not replace tax investigators’ judgement, but creates a structured risk signal that can be integrated into enforcement workflows. The expected impact is more focused inspections, better use of enforcement capacity and stronger support for fairer tax collection. More broadly, the project creates value by enabling more evidence-based compliance work and improving the efficiency of public revenue protection.

results.title: Text-to-speech synthesis in Estonian
results.proposal: Text-to-speech synthesis in Estonian. Estonian-language digital services need speech technologies that sound natural and handle linguistic details accurately, yet earlier synthesis methods often produced output that was less convincing in rhythm, intonation and pronunciation. This use case was developed to improve the quality of synthetic speech in Estonian and support applications that require clearer, more human-like spoken output. The stakeholders include language-technology researchers, developers and future users of Estonian speech services, with the objective of producing a more natural-sounding synthesis system that can better handle the specific features of the language. The solution was implemented by the University of Tartu language-technology research group as a neural-network-based speech-synthesis prototype trained on a corpus of Estonian news. At a conceptual level, the model learns speech patterns from recorded data and can currently imitate the voices of six different speakers, allowing it to generate spoken output with more realistic sound and prosody than previous methods. The project reports particular strengths in natural intonation, as well as pronunciation of numbers, symbols and abbreviations. Although the system remains under development and is not yet considered complete, it already marks a qualitative improvement over earlier synthesis approaches. The impact lies in more natural and intelligible Estonian speech generation, stronger technical capability for future voice services and a better basis for accessible digital applications. More broadly, the prototype creates value by advancing language technology for a smaller language community.
results.memo: Proceed. Text-to-speech synthesis in Estonian is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Kratt for analysing customer conversations - Finding the root causes of customer inquiries
results.proposal: Kratt for analysing customer conversations - Finding the root causes of customer inquiries. The Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund needed a better understanding of why customers were contacting its service channels, particularly because recurring enquiry patterns were placing pressure on call volumes and indicated friction in digital services and grant-related communication. From April to August 2019, the organisation worked with Feelingstream on a pilot to identify the root causes of customer calls and use those insights to improve the overall service experience. The stakeholders include the Unemployment Insurance Fund, its customer-service teams and the people using its services, with the objective of reducing unnecessary calls, improving e-environments and addressing the issues most frequently driving customer contact. The solution was implemented through Feelingstream’s multilingual contact-analysis application, which transcribed calls and analysed them in order to detect patterns in customer concerns. At a conceptual level, the system used speech transcription and language-analysis techniques to convert conversations into structured insights, enabling the organisation to see not only what people were asking about, but also when and why certain topics became especially prominent. The pilot showed, for example, that enquiries linked to the receipt of grants rose significantly at the beginning of the month. The impact included actionable insight for service redesign, improvements to digital channels and a stronger basis for reducing avoidable demand, creating value through better customer experience and more efficient service management.
results.memo: Proceed. Kratt for analysing customer conversations - Finding the root causes of customer inquiries is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Kratt Folly - Recognition of museum objects
results.proposal: Kratt Folly - Recognition of museum objects. The National Heritage Board sought to improve how digital objects are described within cultural collections, since manual description is time-consuming, can vary in quality and limits how quickly collections can be made accessible to the public. Heritage institutions increasingly manage large volumes of digital material, yet catalogue enrichment often remains labour-intensive and difficult to scale. Kratt Folly was developed to address this challenge by moving closer to automated description of museum and heritage objects. The stakeholders include the National Heritage Board, memory-institution staff and users of cultural collections, with the objective of increasing data quality, using staff time more intelligently and improving public access to described digital objects. The solution is implemented as a prototype recognition system designed to identify and support description of digital collection items. At a conceptual level, the system applies image-recognition and object-description techniques to digital heritage material so that descriptive metadata can be generated or suggested automatically, reducing the need for fully manual catalogue creation. This creates a workflow in which automation supports curatorial work rather than replacing institutional expertise. The expected impact includes richer and more consistent object descriptions, more efficient use of staff capacity and better accessibility of collections for end users. More broadly, Kratt Folly creates value by supporting scalable digital heritage management and by helping cultural institutions make their collections more searchable, understandable and usable.

results.title: Chatbot Vesta - Estonian National Library

The stakeholders include library staff, users seeking information and the institution responsible for maintaining access to knowledge services, with the objective of improving efficiency, reducing routine workload and ensuring that common questions can be handled more quickly. The solution was implemented through a prototype chatbot application capable of classifying incoming questions by topic and responding automatically to repetitive first-level enquiries. At a conceptual level, the system analyses question content, identifies topical patterns and either routes or answers the request on the basis of recurring structures already known to the library. This allows staff attention to be concentrated on more complex requests that still require human expertise. The impact includes faster handling of standard enquiries, better sorting of incoming messages and reduced pressure on library staff. More broadly, Vesta creates value by modernising user support in a high-volume cultural institution and by providing a scalable approach to repetitive information requests in library services.

results.title: Automatic border control - Facial Recognition at border controls

The stakeholders include border guards, travellers and the authorities responsible for border management, with the objective of speeding up crossings, reducing the risk of identity fraud and strengthening the overall reliability of entry checks. The solution is implemented through biometric ABC gates that use facial-recognition-based identification algorithms alongside document verification. At a conceptual level, the system compares the traveller’s biometric data with the information in the travel document and supports the border guard by automating core identity and eligibility checks before human intervention where needed. The reported performance is notable: initial testing showed that a person could pass through the gates in an average of 15 seconds. The impact includes faster border processing, improved operational efficiency and lower risk of crossing with the wrong document. results.title: Mapping of flooded areas from satellite images
results.proposal: Mapping of flooded areas from satellite images. Authorities responsible for flood response and environmental monitoring need a dependable way to identify inundated areas quickly, yet flood mapping can be difficult because water detection varies depending on weather, vegetation cover and sensor type. This use case focused on finding the most suitable operational methodology for mapping flooded areas under different conditions, with the objective of improving the reliability and timeliness of flood detection from satellite data. The stakeholders include environmental analysts, emergency-management actors and organisations working with Earth-observation data, all of whom benefit from more consistent flood mapping. The solution was implemented through an evaluation of Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery and the development of a prototype processing workflow. At a conceptual level, the work compared the suitability of radar and optical satellite data, identified the necessary preprocessing steps and selected the most appropriate vegetation index for characterising open water. These elements were then combined into an operational prototype capable of processing Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 data for flood-area mapping. By structuring the method in this way, the project moved beyond ad hoc interpretation towards a repeatable analytical workflow. The impact includes a clearer methodological basis for flood detection, improved operational readiness for mapping inundation and better use of satellite resources under varying environmental conditions. More broadly, the prototype creates value by supporting faster, more systematic flood monitoring and by enabling scalable geospatial analysis for hazard assessment and response planning.

results.title: Crop detection from Sentinel-1 and -2 time series using deep learning methods
results.proposal: Crop detection from Sentinel-1 and -2 time series using deep learning methods. Estonia needed a more objective and scalable way to identify agricultural crops for official monitoring and statistics, as traditional methods can be labour-intensive and difficult to apply uniformly across the country. The operational challenge was to create a methodology suited specifically to Estonian conditions and capable of supporting both agricultural administration and the production of consistent national statistics. The stakeholders include Estonian universities, agricultural authorities such as PRIA and the wider state administration, with the objective of improving crop identification, strengthening the quality of agricultural statistics and providing a more standardised evidence base for public-sector use. The solution was implemented through a methodology that combines Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 time-series data with contextual variables including soil type, average daily air temperature and precipitation. At a conceptual level, deep-learning techniques were used to model crop classes from these multi-source inputs and distinguish between different agricultural patterns over time. The results showed that several crop categories could be identified with over 90% accuracy, including potatoes, field peas and beans, summer and winter rapeseed, maize, rye, winter wheat and barley, while berry and fruit plantations, as well as carrot and beetroot plantations, could not yet be classified with sufficient reliability. The impact is a more uniform and objective basis for agricultural statistics, better support for monitoring and a scalable method that can be integrated into PRIA and wider state use.
results.memo: Proceed. Crop detection from Sentinel-1 and -2 time series using deep learning methods is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Analysis of customer calls at the Estonian Social Insurance Board
results.proposal: Analysis of customer calls at the Estonian Social Insurance Board. The Estonian Social Insurance Board needed a better understanding of why customers were contacting its service channels and what recurring issues were driving calls and online chats. Routine contact analysis can be difficult to perform manually at scale, especially when interactions take place across multiple channels and in more than one language. This pilot was therefore designed to help the organisation detect patterns in customer appeals and use those insights to improve service design and communication. The stakeholders include the Social Insurance Board, service managers, call-centre staff and citizens using social-insurance services, with the objective of identifying the most common concerns more precisely and supporting more informed managerial decisions. The solution was implemented in cooperation with Feelingstream, whose application transcribed customer calls and chats over a three-month period from May to August 2020 in both Estonian and Russian. At a conceptual level, the system converted spoken and written interactions into analysable text and then examined these data to identify themes, recurring problems and patterns in customer needs. This provided a more detailed basis for service insight than high-level contact statistics alone. The impact includes better understanding of why citizens contact the organisation, improved potential to redesign problematic service areas and stronger evidence for decision-making. More broadly, the pilot creates value by turning everyday customer interactions into a usable source of operational intelligence and by supporting more responsive and efficient social-insurance services.
results.memo: Proceed. Analysis of customer calls at the Estonian Social Insurance Board is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Statistical characterization of the sea ice extent in the Gulf of Riga (Baltic Sea) using optical remote-sensing imagery
results.proposal: Statistical characterization of the sea ice extent in the Gulf of Riga (Baltic Sea) using optical remote-sensing imagery. Monitoring sea-ice conditions in the Gulf of Riga is important for understanding winter dynamics, environmental conditions and maritime risks, yet consistent large-scale observation is difficult to achieve through field methods alone. This use case addressed the need for a more systematic way to characterise ice extent, ice occurrence probability and ice-season length across different winter scenarios in the Baltic Sea. The stakeholders include researchers, environmental analysts and organisations concerned with marine observation, with the objective of generating a reliable statistical picture of sea-ice behaviour over time and across locations. The solution was implemented using optical remote-sensing data from the MODIS instrument at 250 m resolution, covering the period from 2002 to 2011. At a conceptual level, the method relied on bimodal histogram analysis of remote-sensing reflectance data to distinguish ice from water, then used the resulting classifications to calculate sea-ice extent, occurrence probability and season length. The outputs were compared with official ice charts and multi-sensor products, showing strong agreement with reference data, with R² values above 0.83. The study found large year-to-year variation: the ice season ranged from 68 to 146 days and maximum ice extent from 329 to 15,350 km², with higher ice occurrence in waters shallower than 15 m. More broadly, the work creates value by providing a robust analytical basis for regional ice monitoring and winter-scenario classification.
results.memo: Proceed. Statistical characterization of the sea ice extent in the Gulf of Riga (Baltic Sea) using optical remote-sensing imagery is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Salme - Speech recognition in courts
results.proposal: Salme - Speech recognition in courts. Estonia’s courts needed a faster and more efficient way to produce hearing transcripts, since manual transcription of court sessions is slow, labour-intensive and places a heavy burden on clerks. According to the Estonian courts, a single criminal case containing about 14 hours of hearings could require an average of 112 working hours to transcribe manually. The use case therefore involved the courts, the Centre of Registers and Information Systems and judicial staff, with the objective of reducing transcription effort, speeding up protocolling and improving the handling of spoken courtroom data in both physical and remote hearings. The solution is implemented through Salme, a speech-recognition tool developed with CGI Estonia and Tilde and integrated into the Court Information System via X-Road. At a conceptual level, Salme supports both real-time and offline transcription, assigns microphones to speakers, returns transcript text with only a short delay and links recordings, transcripts and notes back into court workflows. The system was trained using more than 800 hours of transcribed audio for acoustic models and over 800 million words of textual data for the custom language model, producing reported word-error rates between 8% and 15% and overall precision of about 92%. The impact includes major time savings, faster transcript production and better integration of courtroom recordings into digital judicial processes, creating value through efficiency, accuracy and secure operation on authorised court infrastructure.

results.title: Marakratt - Personal learning path infrastructure
results.proposal: Marakratt - Personal learning path infrastructure. Education systems increasingly need to support learners whose interests, prior knowledge and abilities differ widely, yet standardised content delivery can make it difficult to provide genuinely individual learning pathways. Marakratt was developed to explore how students could be supported more effectively through educational content and activities that are better matched to their personal learning needs. The use case therefore involved students, educators and digital-learning stakeholders, with the objective of testing whether recommendation models and automation could help build more individualised study paths and improve the relevance of educational material. Rather than redesigning the entire education process, the project focused on creating a proof-of-concept infrastructure able to personalise parts of the learner experience. The solution was implemented through machine-learning experimentation aimed at recommending educational materials and automating the personalisation of learning activities. At a conceptual level, the prototype used learner-related information such as interests, knowledge and abilities to generate recommendations and adapt content pathways, creating models that could serve as the basis for more personalised digital learning environments. This allowed the project to test how recommendation systems might support both educational planning and learner engagement. The impact is primarily exploratory, but it includes a clearer technical basis for individual study-path support, improved understanding of how recommendation models can function in education and a prototype framework for future scaling. More broadly, Marakratt creates value by laying the groundwork for more adaptive and learner-centred digital education services.
results.memo: Proceed. Marakratt - Personal learning path infrastructure is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Water level monitoring in coastal seas and lakes using satellite altimetry
results.proposal: Water level monitoring in coastal seas and lakes using satellite altimetry. Hydrological monitoring traditionally depends on in situ measurements of water levels and flows at national stations, but these observations do not always provide the spatial coverage needed for large lakes and coastal seas. This creates a challenge for flood monitoring and marine forecasting, where broader and more continuous visibility of water conditions can improve both warning and planning. The use case was developed to enhance water-level observation by combining conventional monitoring with remote methods, with the objective of improving hydrological information available to authorities and the public. The stakeholders include hydrological-monitoring services, marine forecasters and users of water-level information, with the broader aim of strengthening operational flood monitoring and sea-level prediction. The solution is implemented through prototypes that combine radar remote-sensing data, satellite altimetry, forecasting models and analytical methods. At a conceptual level, the platform integrates remote water-level observations with existing hydrometric data and modelling workflows so that water conditions can be observed over a wider area than is possible through ground stations alone. This is particularly relevant for improving observation coverage over the Great Lakes and for feeding better data into forecasting systems. The expected impact is improved spatial coverage, more accurate sea-level forecasts and stronger flood-monitoring capability. More broadly, the project creates value by making hydrological services more comprehensive and by supporting a more resilient, data-rich approach to water-level monitoring in coastal and inland waters.
results.memo: Proceed. Water level monitoring in coastal seas and lakes using satellite altimetry is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Calculation of forest resources by remote sensing methods
results.proposal: Calculation of forest resources by remote sensing methods. Estonia’s forest monitoring system relies on annual field measurements from 5,600 plots, which provide the basis for national reporting and forest policy, but translating those point measurements into broader, map-based resource estimates remains a difficult and labour-intensive task. The operational challenge is to extend detailed statistical inventory information across large forest areas in a way that improves spatial coverage and supports both monitoring and stand-level economic decisions. This use case therefore involves forest-monitoring authorities, policy planners and users of national forest-resource data, with the objective of developing a methodology that can turn inventory data into maps of species composition, stand height and trunk volume. The solution is implemented by combining multispectral satellite imagery, airborne laser-scanning data and accurate tree measurements from sample plots. At a conceptual level, the system uses the plot-based measurements as model inputs and links them with remote-sensing variables in order to estimate forest characteristics spatially and produce map-based resource assessments. This moves the inventory system from pure sampling towards a hybrid model that supports both national reporting and more operationally detailed forest analysis. The expected impact is better spatial representation of forest resources, improved support for monitoring and stronger evidence for policy and economic planning. More broadly, the project creates value by increasing the usefulness of Estonia’s forest inventory, supporting smarter forest management and enabling more scalable environmental analysis through remote sensing.
results.memo: Proceed. Calculation of forest resources by remote sensing methods is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Appearance - Identification of objects at the Estonian National Archives
results.proposal: Appearance - Identification of objects at the Estonian National Archives. The Estonian National Archives wanted to make its vast photographic holdings more accessible by allowing users to search not only through metadata, but also through visual similarity in faces. Historical image collections are rich in public value yet often difficult to navigate when names are unknown, records are incomplete or users are trying to identify ancestors or historical figures from a single photograph. This use case therefore involved the National Archives, researchers, family historians and the wider public, with the objective of improving discoverability and opening new ways of engaging with archival photo collections. The solution is implemented through Ilme, a facial-recognition-based search service linked to Fotis, the National Archives’ photo database. At a conceptual level, users upload a photo, faces are detected and compared against more than half a million archive photographs spanning back to the 1840s, representing around three million faces in total, and the most similar matches are returned by email within 24 hours as a PDF. This creates a visual retrieval workflow that complements conventional catalogue search. The expected impact is easier access to archival imagery, improved usability of large photo collections and new opportunities for users to identify individuals across historical materials. More broadly, the system creates value by making cultural heritage more searchable, more personal and more meaningful for both specialist and public audiences.

results.title: Transcription Kratt 112 - Transcribing emergency calls dialed to the emergency number 112
results.proposal: Transcription Kratt 112 - Transcribing emergency calls dialed to the emergency number 112. Emergency-call centres handle high volumes of urgent voice data, yet spoken calls are difficult to search, analyse or reuse unless they are converted into text. Estonia introduced this use case to support the handling of 112 emergency calls by beginning the systematic transcription of those conversations. The operational challenge is that emergency communication must be processed instantly for response purposes, but afterwards authorities also need a usable record for review, quality improvement and possible integration into future support systems. The stakeholders include the emergency centre, call operators and related public-safety services, with the objective of making emergency-call content more accessible for analysis and process improvement while supporting a more modern digital workflow around voice data. The solution is implemented through automated transcription of calls to 112. At a conceptual level, the system applies speech-recognition technology to transform emergency conversations into text, allowing spoken interactions to become searchable, analysable and suitable for downstream use in training, quality monitoring or future decision-support development. Even where the immediate use is modest, the transcription layer creates a reusable digital asset from otherwise transient audio. The expected impact is improved access to operational information, better conditions for service analysis and stronger foundations for future emergency-support tools. More broadly, the project creates value by enabling voice-based public-safety interactions to be incorporated into broader data-driven improvement and digital-service development.

results.title: Alarm Center Assistant for Risk Assessment
results.proposal: Alarm Center Assistant for Risk Assessment. Estonia’s emergency notification process is highly time-critical and operationally complex: rescue operators must assess threats within roughly a minute while taking into account the information needs and resource rules of at least three different agencies. Under such pressure, mistakes in risk assessment or delays in gathering the right details can directly affect response quality. This use case was developed to support operators in one of the most demanding parts of emergency-call handling, with the objective of reducing error, speeding up assessment and improving the consistency of resource deployment. The stakeholders include the emergency centre, rescue operators and the agencies that depend on accurate threat classification, with the wider goal of making emergency call processing more reliable under severe time constraints. The solution is implemented through software that transcribes the incoming call and analyses it in light of previous actions in order to suggest the most likely event type and a typical case profile for the operator. At a conceptual level, the system combines real-time transcription, contextual analysis and historical pattern support to assist rather than replace the human operator during risk assessment. This allows critical information to be surfaced more quickly while keeping the operator in control of the final judgement. The expected impact is faster and more consistent threat assessment, reduced cognitive burden and better coordination of emergency resources, creating value through higher reliability in high-pressure public-safety operations.

results.title: PPA Information Phone call transcription for customers analysis different languages
results.proposal: PPA Information Phone call transcription for customers analysis different languages. The Police and Border Guard Board needed a better understanding of why customers were contacting its information lines and how service bottlenecks were affecting the uptake of digital channels. Calls concerning the issuance of documents had already been identified as the largest category of enquiries, yet the organisation needed richer insight into customer difficulties, especially across different languages and over long service cycles in which people may only renew documents every five to ten years. The use case therefore focused on improving service design, encouraging greater use of e-channels and refining the content and presentation of customer information. The stakeholders include the Police and Border Guard Board, customer-service teams and citizens interacting with document-issuance services, with the objective of reducing avoidable calls and making digital services easier to use. The pilot showed that customers often forgot the correct steps because document requests are infrequent, and it identified specific bottlenecks hindering smoother digital use. results.title: ESTNLTK - Open source tools for Estonian natural language processing
results.proposal: ESTNLTK - Open source tools for Estonian natural language processing. Estonia’s digital ecosystem depends on high-quality language tools to support public services, research and software development in Estonian, yet language-technology resources for smaller languages often remain fragmented or incomplete. ESTNLTK was created to address this challenge by making existing Estonian language-technology tools easier to access and by developing new ones where gaps remain. The stakeholders include researchers, developers, public institutions and organisations working with Estonian-language data, with the objective of strengthening the technical foundation for processing Estonian texts and enabling wider reuse of language resources across different domains. The solution is implemented as an open-source toolkit, written mainly in Python, for analysing and editing Estonian text. At a conceptual level, the collection acts both as an integration layer for existing language-technology components and as a development framework for new tools, allowing users to perform a range of text-processing tasks within one extensible environment. Because it is open source and funded through the Estonian National Language Technology Programme, it supports both practical deployment and broader ecosystem building. The expected impact is improved availability of language-processing tools, lower barriers for developers and researchers, and better support for Estonian-language applications. More broadly, ESTNLTK creates value by reinforcing digital capability in a smaller language market, enabling innovation and reuse, and providing shared infrastructure that can support public-sector, academic and commercial work on Estonian text.

results.title: Kama - Multilingual multidisciplinary neuroma machine translation
results.proposal: Kama - Multilingual multidisciplinary neuroma machine translation. In multilingual public and professional environments, the need to translate accurately across a range of languages and subject areas is essential for communication, cooperation and access to information. The operational problem addressed by Kama is that multilingual translation often requires separate tools, uneven language coverage or manual effort that reduces efficiency and consistency. This use case therefore focuses on providing a broader, more flexible translation capability that can support different domains and users working across several languages. Its objective is to enable reliable translation between multiple language pairs in a single system, making multilingual communication more practical and accessible. The solution is implemented as a multilingual neural machine translation system supporting seven input and output languages: Estonian, Latvian, Lithuanian, English, Russian, German and Finnish. At a conceptual level, the platform uses neural translation models trained to operate across multiple language directions, allowing users to move between different linguistic contexts within one shared architecture rather than relying on isolated bilingual tools. This design supports more efficient maintenance and broader applicability across disciplines and use cases. The expected impact is improved translation availability, greater consistency across languages and reduced dependence on manual translation for routine needs. In operational and business terms, Kama offers scalability, supports multilingual service delivery and creates value by widening access to information and collaboration across language communities.

results.title: UiPath - AI to help farmers get EU funding
results.proposal: UiPath - AI to help farmers get EU funding. Romania’s Agency for Financing Rural Investments needed to simplify and speed up the process through which farmers access EU funding, a process that traditionally involves collecting multiple documents and authorisations from different public sources. This administrative complexity can create delays, increase processing costs and discourage applicants, particularly where rural beneficiaries have limited time or resources to navigate public procedures. The use case therefore involves AFIR, farmers and the state institutions whose documents are needed for funding applications, with the objective of making access to EU support quicker, less burdensome and more efficient at scale.
