results.title: URBANITE - AI-driven insights to optimise public transport systems
results.proposal: URBANITE - AI-driven insights to optimise public transport systems. Public-transport planning has often depended on surveys and interviews, which are valuable but slow, expensive and limited in their ability to capture real, constantly changing mobility patterns across a city. As a result, transport authorities and operators may lack the detailed and timely evidence needed to understand current demand, anticipate future shifts and optimise multimodal services effectively. URBANITE addresses this challenge by providing cities and transport organisations with a richer, more dynamic understanding of how people actually move. The stakeholders include municipalities, public transport authorities and public transport operators, with the objective of improving operational planning, anticipating future demand and supporting the creation of safer and more sustainable urban mobility systems. The solution is implemented through the integration of historical data, GPS traces, mobile-network information and passenger data, analysed using advanced modelling techniques to reconstruct and predict mobility demand across buses, trams, trains and bicycles. At a conceptual level, the platform combines data fusion, predictive analytics and movement modelling to produce actionable insights into both present and future transport needs. These outputs can then support network design, service planning and operational adjustment. The expected impact is more precise planning, better alignment between services and demand, and reduced reliance on costly traditional data collection. More broadly, URBANITE improves scalability in mobility analysis, enhances decision quality and creates value through more efficient, sustainable and user-responsive public transport systems.
results.memo: Proceed. URBANITE - AI-driven insights to optimise public transport systems is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: AI MOVE - AI mobility optimisation and vehicle efficiency for public transport
results.proposal: AI MOVE - AI mobility optimisation and vehicle efficiency for public transport. Many public-transport-priority systems still rely on transponders installed on vehicles communicating with traffic lights, a set-up that typically benefits only municipal operators and excludes other high-occupancy services. This limits the effectiveness of traffic prioritisation in increasingly mixed mobility environments where demand-responsive transport and other non-municipal providers also play an important role. AI MOVE addresses this gap by seeking to make urban traffic management more inclusive and efficient across a broader set of public and shared transport vehicles. The stakeholders include transport authorities, public-transport operators, demand-responsive providers and city traffic managers, with the objective of reducing congestion and improving journey efficiency by extending priority mechanisms beyond traditional municipal fleets. The solution is implemented through enhanced CCTV systems deployed at intersections and transit zones, using computer vision to recognise high-occupancy vehicles and support dynamic prioritisation through existing infrastructure. At a conceptual level, the system combines video analytics, vehicle-recognition models and traffic-signal integration to identify eligible vehicles in real time and adapt signal behaviour accordingly. This approach avoids the limitations of hardware installed only on selected vehicles and creates a more flexible foundation for priority management. The expected impact is improved traffic flow for public transport, more cost-effective use of existing infrastructure and broader coverage across transport providers. More broadly, the project enhances urban mobility efficiency, supports scalable traffic management and creates value through reduced congestion and more equitable prioritisation.

results.title: ROSE - Route optimisation module for waste logistic platforms - Cascais (PT) pilot
results.proposal: ROSE - Route optimisation module for waste logistic platforms - Cascais (PT) pilot. Waste collection services face constant pressure to reduce costs, emissions and congestion while maintaining reliable collection standards across urban areas. Traditional collection routes can be inefficient when they do not reflect the actual fill levels of containers or the most suitable deployment of available vehicles, leading to unnecessary mileage, wasted time and avoidable fuel consumption. ROSE addresses this operational problem by helping municipalities organise waste collection more intelligently and only when necessary. The stakeholders include city authorities, waste-management operators and logistics planners, with the objective of improving the efficiency and sustainability of collection operations through smarter route design and scheduling. The solution is implemented as an advanced logistics routing engine that clusters waste containers on the basis of historical fill-rate patterns, assigns the most appropriate vehicles to each cluster and optimises collection schedules using transport data. At a conceptual level, the module combines route optimisation, demand forecasting and vehicle-assignment logic, building on Theoremus’ experience with Digital Waste Monitoring Platforms and integrating with broader waste-logistics workflows. The system is being deployed in Cascais and Montana, demonstrating its applicability across different urban contexts. The expected impact is fewer vehicle miles travelled, lower operational time and reduced costs, together with lower fuel consumption, emissions and traffic burden. More broadly, ROSE improves scalability, supports cleaner urban operations and creates value through more data-driven and sustainable waste-management practices.

results.title: PILLAR Robots - a project to increase the autonomy of AI-based robots
results.proposal: PILLAR Robots - a project to increase the autonomy of AI-based robots. PILLAR Robots addresses a fundamental operational challenge in robotics: enabling robots to function with greater autonomy across different domains while ensuring that what they learn remains relevant to real deployment contexts. Many autonomous systems can acquire behaviours through training, yet they often struggle to generalise beyond narrow environments or to focus learning on what truly matters for practical applications. This use case therefore involves robotics researchers, developers and application-oriented stakeholders seeking to improve the adaptability and usefulness of autonomous machines in real-world settings. Its objective is to help robots acquire the knowledge and capabilities needed for target applications more efficiently by giving them a stronger internal basis for selecting, prioritising and acting on relevant goals. The solution is implemented by operationalising the concept of “purpose”, drawn from cognitive science, within robotic cognitive architectures. At a conceptual level, the project develops algorithms for purpose acquisition, mechanisms to bias perceptual, motivational and decision systems towards purposeful behaviour, and learning strategies for representations, skills and models that support both deliberative and reactive decision-making. These elements are designed to work together so that learning is not only autonomous but also better aligned with task relevance. The expected impact is increased robot autonomy, stronger domain independence and more effective acquisition of usable skills. More broadly, the project creates value by improving the transferability, reliability and practical utility of autonomous robots in applied settings.

evidence.quote: PILLAR Robots addresses a fundamental operational challenge in robotics: enabling robots to function with greater autonomy across different domains while ensuring that what they learn remains relevant to real deployment contexts.

results.title: OpenGPT-X project to create a LLM "Made in Germany"
results.proposal: OpenGPT-X project to create a LLM "Made in Germany". OpenGPT-X was launched to strengthen Europe’s capacity in generative-language technologies by developing a large language model ecosystem rooted in German and European research, industrial capability and trusted data environments. The broader challenge is that advanced generative models are increasingly important for business applications and digital transformation, yet strategic dependence on non-European solutions may limit sovereignty, transparency and local innovation capacity. This use case therefore brings together partners from industry, research and media across the generative AI value chain, with the objective of advancing cutting-edge research while driving practical adoption in the German economy. The solution is implemented as a collaborative Gaia-X-related project funded by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action, with total funding of around EUR 14 million and a project timeline spanning January 2022 to March 2025. At a conceptual level, the initiative develops large language model capabilities, supporting infrastructure and practical application pathways that connect foundational research with real business use cases. This includes work across model development, data spaces and deployment-oriented innovation within a trusted digital ecosystem. The expected impact is stronger domestic capability in generative-language technologies, greater readiness for enterprise adoption and improved alignment between research and market application. More broadly, OpenGPT-X supports technological sovereignty, boosts innovation capacity and creates long-term value by establishing a European foundation for advanced language-model development and use.

results.title: Better match between unemployed citizens and companies
results.proposal: Better match between unemployed citizens and companies. Even where employers are actively seeking staff, matching unemployed citizens to suitable vacancies can remain difficult because the fit between a person’s experience, transferable skills and available roles is not always obvious from standard job titles or sector boundaries. As a result, case workers may struggle to guide citizens towards realistic opportunities, especially where alternative occupations or industries could offer a viable route back into employment. This use case addresses that challenge by improving how unemployed citizens are matched with company demand and by supporting more targeted job-search strategies. The stakeholders include case workers, job-ready unemployed citizens and employers, with the objective of increasing the effectiveness of employment programmes and improving the connection between labour supply and labour demand. The solution is implemented through a matching tool that compares the professional and personal capabilities described in citizens’ CVs with the requirements listed in current job openings. At a conceptual level, the system uses skills-matching and recommendation techniques to identify suitable vacancies, including alternatives in other industries or job types that may not have been considered initially. These results support the case worker in guiding the citizen towards a broader and more realistic search strategy. The expected impact is better job matching, a more focused job-search process and improved employment outcomes. In practical terms, the approach enhances service quality, increases the utility of available vacancy data and creates value through more efficient and responsive labour-market intermediation.

results.title: Targeted employment programmes for unemployed citizens
results.proposal: Targeted employment programmes for unemployed citizens. Employment services often need to decide which programme or activity is most likely to help a job-ready unemployed citizen return to work quickly, yet this is difficult to do consistently without clear evidence on what interventions deliver the strongest results for different profiles. The challenge is not simply to offer support, but to direct each individual towards the activities most likely to shorten unemployment and improve outcomes. This use case responds to that need by helping case workers design more targeted employment programmes for unemployed citizens. The stakeholders include employment advisers, case workers, programme managers and citizens seeking work, with the objective of reducing unemployment duration and improving the relevance and benefit of employment services. The solution is implemented as a decision-support tool that uses individual citizen information to propose specific activities expected to reduce the likely period of unemployment. At a conceptual level, the system combines predictive modelling with recommendation logic, drawing on patterns from previous programme outcomes and citizen characteristics to identify interventions with the greatest expected effect. These suggestions are then incorporated into the case worker’s planning process. The expected impact is more personalised employment support, faster transitions back into work and better use of programme resources. More broadly, the approach strengthens the effectiveness of labour-market services, improves the citizen experience and creates value by aligning support measures more closely with individual needs and likely outcomes.

evidence.quote: Employment services often need to decide which programme or activity is most likely to help a job-ready unemployed citizen return to work quickly, yet this is difficult to do consistently without clear evidence on what interventions deliver the strongest results for different profiles.

results.title: Correct and uniform case management when sanctioning unemployed citizens
results.proposal: Correct and uniform case management when sanctioning unemployed citizens. Deciding whether an unemployed citizen should be subject to an economic sanction is a difficult and sensitive task, as case workers must consider not only the triggering event, such as absence from an interview or activation offer, but also whether a sanction is likely to have the intended effect on the person’s availability for work. In practice, these judgements are not always applied uniformly, which can lead to inconsistency in case handling and uncertainty for both staff and citizens. This use case addresses the need for more consistent and evidence-informed decision-making in employment services. The stakeholders include case workers, employment-service managers and unemployed citizens, with the objective of supporting fairer and more uniform assessments while helping staff distinguish between cases in which sanctions may be effective and those in which they may not. The solution is implemented through a decision-support tool that analyses factors associated with positive or negative effects on a citizen’s likelihood of becoming more available for employment. At a conceptual level, the system evaluates adverse events and broader citizen characteristics to support judgements on whether a sanction should be triggered. These analytical outputs are integrated into the case worker’s decision process rather than replacing professional discretion. The expected impact is more consistent case management, better-targeted use of sanctions and improved transparency in decision-making. In operational terms, the approach enhances fairness, reliability and resource efficiency across municipal employment services.
results.memo: Proceed. Correct and uniform case management when sanctioning unemployed citizens is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Shorter response time to construction applications and help submitting correct documents
results.proposal: Shorter response time to construction applications and help submitting correct documents. Municipal construction applications often take a long time to process, not only because of the complexity of planning and compliance checks, but also because many submissions are incomplete or incorrectly prepared from the outset. This creates delays for applicants and additional workload for case workers, who must spend time identifying errors, requesting further documentation and comparing the case with similar precedents. The use case therefore focuses on improving the efficiency and consistency of construction-application handling, with the objective of reducing response times and supporting better-quality submissions. The stakeholders include applicants, municipal planning officers and case workers, all of whom benefit when straightforward errors can be identified early and previous comparable decisions are easier to consult. The solution is implemented as a decision-support tool that screens applications for likely errors and retrieves relevant decisions from earlier similar cases. At a conceptual level, the system uses document analysis and case-comparison techniques to highlight missing or problematic elements and present precedent information within the case worker’s assessment process. This helps staff make more informed and consistent decisions while also improving the quality of the material under review. The expected impact is shorter case-processing times, fewer avoidable delays caused by incorrect documentation and greater consistency in planning decisions. More broadly, the approach improves the applicant experience, reduces administrative effort and creates value through more efficient municipal permitting processes.
results.memo: Proceed. Shorter response time to construction applications and help submitting correct documents is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Intelligent sorting and filing of mail to provide citizens with faster case processing
results.proposal: Intelligent sorting and filing of mail to provide citizens with faster case processing. Norddjurs Municipality receives substantial volumes of digital mail and emails every day through a central inbox, and each message must be sorted, routed to the correct case worker and filed appropriately before any substantive action can begin. These are routine but resource-intensive administrative tasks that consume staff time and can delay the start of case processing for citizens. This use case addresses that operational bottleneck by aiming to streamline intake management and reduce the manual burden associated with handling incoming correspondence. The stakeholders include administrative staff, case workers and citizens, with the objective of accelerating distribution, improving filing accuracy and ensuring that enquiries reach the right destination more quickly. The solution is implemented through an automated mail-handling system that classifies incoming digital mail and email, distributes it to the relevant recipients and files it in the appropriate location. At a conceptual level, the system combines text classification, routing logic and document-management integration to interpret message content and connect it with the municipality’s internal case-processing structure. This enables intake tasks to be handled with greater speed and consistency than purely manual processing. The expected impact is reduced administrative workload, quicker initiation of citizen cases and improved reliability in document handling. In practical terms, the use case supports faster case processing, better internal efficiency and a more scalable way to manage growing communication volumes in municipal administration.
results.memo: Proceed. Intelligent sorting and filing of mail to provide citizens with faster case processing is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Faster case processing when granting cleaning services using new technology
results.proposal: Faster case processing when granting cleaning services using new technology. Assessing whether a citizen should receive municipal cleaning assistance can vary considerably in complexity, as case workers must evaluate individual need on the basis of health, living conditions and household circumstances. This variation creates uneven workloads and can slow down decision-making, particularly where straightforward cases consume time that could otherwise be devoted to more complex assessments. The purpose of this use case is therefore to improve the quality and speed of case processing for citizens while releasing capacity for staff to focus on cases requiring greater professional attention. The stakeholders include municipal case workers, social-care administrators and citizens applying for support, all of whom benefit from a more consistent and efficient assessment process. The solution is implemented through a decision-support tool that uses structured data on the citizen’s condition, housing situation and possible cohabitants to inform recommendations on eligibility for cleaning services. At a conceptual level, the system applies classification and pattern-recognition techniques to comparable historical cases and integrates the resulting output into the case worker’s existing workflow. This allows routine applications to be assessed more efficiently while preserving human oversight in the final decision. The expected impact is shorter processing times, improved consistency in eligibility assessments and better use of staff resources. More broadly, the approach strengthens service quality, improves the citizen experience and supports a more scalable model for handling municipal care applications.

results.title: AI-Rehabilitering (AIR) - Intelligent rehabilitation and targeted healthcare services for citizens
results.proposal: AI-Rehabilitering (AIR) - Intelligent rehabilitation and targeted healthcare services for citizens. In municipal rehabilitation services, one recurring challenge is that citizens who could benefit from physical exercise or preventive support are not always identified or referred at the most appropriate time. This can delay intervention, reduce the likelihood of successful outcomes and limit the efficient use of rehabilitation resources, assistive aids and fall-prevention measures. The AIR use case, anchored in the Municipality of Aalborg, addresses this problem by supporting case workers who must decide which rehabilitation pathway best matches an individual citizen’s needs and prospects. Its objective is to improve the consistency and timing of referrals, strengthen professional judgement and ensure that citizens are directed towards the course of action most likely to deliver benefit. The solution is implemented as a decision-support tool built on statistical modelling and predictive analytics. At a conceptual level, it analyses citizen-level data to estimate current eligibility for a rehabilitation course, the likelihood of completing it successfully and the expected level of benefit from participation. These outputs are designed to complement, rather than replace, the case worker’s assessment and can also support decisions on specific interventions, assistive-device use and fall prevention. The expected impact is more targeted rehabilitation, earlier and better-informed intervention and improved allocation of municipal care resources. In practice, this can enhance service quality, increase consistency in decision-making and create value through more efficient and personalised support for citizens.

results.title: Reduction of radiation dose in relation to scans used in cancer treatment
results.proposal: Reduction of radiation dose in relation to scans used in cancer treatment. PET imaging is an important tool in cancer diagnosis and treatment planning, but it requires the injection of a radioactive tracer, and higher tracer doses generally produce clearer images. The operational challenge is therefore to maintain diagnostic image quality while reducing the radiation exposure faced by patients, particularly when repeated scans may be required over time. The stakeholders include radiologists, nuclear-medicine specialists, oncology teams and patients, with the objective of making imaging safer and more cost-effective without undermining its clinical usefulness. The solution is implemented through image-processing models that work on scans acquired using a reduced radiation dose. At a conceptual level, the system addresses the increased noise created by lower-dose imaging by applying denoising and reconstruction techniques that enhance image clarity sufficiently for diagnostic use. This allows the scan to retain its practical value while lowering the quantity of tracer administered. The expected impact is a reduction in radiation exposure and, consequently, a lower long-term risk associated with imaging, alongside savings linked to reduced use of radioactive tracer. In broader terms, the use case improves patient safety, supports more sustainable imaging practice and enhances service efficiency by preserving diagnostic quality while lowering both clinical risk and material cost.

results.title: Artificial Intelligence to prevent complications after bowel cancer surgery
results.proposal: Artificial Intelligence to prevent complications after bowel cancer surgery. Bowel cancer surgery carries substantial risk: around one in four patients develops complications after the operation, and roughly one in three experiences relapse. This creates a pressing need for earlier identification of patients who are most vulnerable to poor outcomes so that treatment plans can be adjusted before surgery and postoperative care can be better targeted. The use case therefore addresses the challenge of improving risk assessment in bowel cancer pathways, with the aim of reducing complications, mortality and recurrence. The stakeholders include surgeons, oncologists, perioperative teams and patients, all of whom benefit from more precise information when deciding how treatment and follow-up should be organised. The solution is implemented through a predictive model trained on health-registry data relating to bowel cancer patients and embedded in a software module for clinical use. At a conceptual level, the system analyses individual patient data to estimate the risk of death, complications, readmission, re-operation and relapse, providing structured support for preoperative and postoperative planning. This allows clinicians to identify higher-risk cases earlier and adapt treatment plans accordingly. The expected impact is more proactive care, fewer preventable adverse outcomes and stronger support for personalised surgical pathways. In practical and economic terms, the approach can improve patient safety, reduce avoidable readmissions and complications, and generate business value through better resource use and more efficient management of complex cancer care.

results.title: Artificial Intelligence for better planning of cancer treatments
results.proposal: Artificial Intelligence for better planning of cancer treatments. Cancer services must balance clinical complexity, finite resources and the need to tailor treatment to the individual patient’s likely trajectory. A major operational challenge is to identify which patients are at greater risk and therefore need more intensive treatment or closer monitoring, and which may be managed through less demanding pathways without compromising outcomes. This use case focuses on stratifying cancer patients into meaningful risk groups so that care plans can be better aligned with individual needs and clinical resources can be deployed more effectively. The stakeholders include oncologists, cancer-care teams, hospital planners and patients, with the objective of supporting more personalised treatment planning and improving the overall efficiency of care delivery. The solution is implemented through predictive models that divide patients into high-risk and low-risk groups on the basis of relevant clinical data and disease characteristics. At a conceptual level, the system combines risk stratification, pattern recognition and decision-support integration so that treatment pathways can be adapted according to the patient’s expected level of need. This enables clinicians to supplement their judgement with structured analytical insight when planning therapies and follow-up. The expected impact is better adaptation of treatment plans, improved use of healthcare resources and more consistent targeting of intensive care to those most likely to benefit. More broadly, the approach supports scalability, strengthens clinical precision and enhances patient value through more individualised cancer treatment.

results.title: Better diagnosis of prostate cancer
results.proposal: Better diagnosis of prostate cancer. Prostate cancer is frequently identified at an early stage, when the disease has not yet spread beyond the prostate, yet many patients still undergo surgery that may later prove unnecessary and can cause complications or long-term discomfort. This use case addresses the clinical and operational challenge of determining which patients genuinely need intervention and which can be managed more conservatively without compromising outcomes. The stakeholders include urologists, oncologists, multidisciplinary cancer teams and patients, with the objective of improving treatment decisions, reducing overtreatment and ensuring that surgery is reserved for cases where the risk of progression is sufficiently high. The solution is implemented through a risk-assessment model trained on historical disease patterns and clinical outcome data to estimate the likelihood that the cancer will spread from the prostate. At a conceptual level, the system analyses patterns in previous patient trajectories and produces an individualised risk estimate that can be incorporated into medical assessment and treatment planning. This supports clinicians in distinguishing patients who may require surgery to prevent metastases from those who may safely avoid surgical treatment. The expected impact is more precise diagnosis-related decision-making, fewer unnecessary operations and a better balance between clinical benefit and treatment burden. In practical terms, the use case improves patient experience, supports more efficient use of surgical resources and creates value through more personalised and proportionate cancer care.

results.title: Real-time predictions and essential information for clinicians
results.proposal: Real-time predictions and essential information for clinicians. Hospitals need timely and accurate information on ward occupancy, discharges and likely patient returns in order to plan staffing, organise patient pathways and make the best possible use of available beds. Without a current picture of capacity, operational decisions can become reactive, leading to bottlenecks, inefficient resource allocation and pressure on both patients and staff. This use case addresses that challenge by equipping health professionals with real-time insight into hospital capacity and expected patient movement. The stakeholders include ward managers, clinicians, discharge planners and hospital operations teams, with the objective of improving day-to-day planning and supporting smoother patient flow across the organisation. The solution is implemented through predictive models that estimate bed-occupancy rates, the expected number of discharges and the risk of patient readmission. At a conceptual level, the system combines hospital activity data with forecasting techniques to generate a live operational view of capacity, which can be integrated into existing planning and coordination processes. This allows staff to anticipate pressure points rather than simply react to them once they occur. The expected impact is better use of hospital capacity, more efficient organisation of patient pathways and improved staff planning. In operational and business terms, the approach increases scalability, supports more reliable decision-making and enhances the patient experience by reducing avoidable delays and improving the coordination of care delivery.

results.title: Artificial Intelligence in general practice
results.proposal: Artificial Intelligence in general practice. General practitioners routinely receive large volumes of clinical information, including laboratory results, many of which do not require immediate medical action but still demand time and attention to review. This creates an administrative burden that can reduce the time available for direct patient care and increase the risk that urgent findings are not prioritised as quickly as they should be. The use case therefore focuses on supporting physicians in general practice by improving the handling of incoming test results and helping surgeries manage clinical information more efficiently. The stakeholders include GPs, practice staff and patients, with the objective of reducing routine workload, sharpening clinical prioritisation and freeing up professional capacity for treatment and patient interaction. The solution is implemented through algorithms that automatically process selected test results, sort blood-test outputs and flag results requiring immediate physician attention. At a conceptual level, the system uses classification and prioritisation techniques applied to structured clinical data, embedded within the practice’s existing information flows so that incoming results can be routed, filtered and escalated appropriately. This means routine or low-risk results can be handled more efficiently, while urgent cases are surfaced promptly for review. The impact is expected to include lower administrative effort, quicker response to clinically significant findings and better use of time in primary care. More broadly, the approach improves reliability, enhances workflow efficiency and strengthens the overall quality and responsiveness of general-practice services.

results.title: Artificial Intelligence for faster and better diagnosis of emergency patients
results.proposal: Artificial Intelligence for faster and better diagnosis of emergency patients. In emergency departments, clinicians must decide quickly whether a patient can be safely discharged or needs immediate admission, often while facing incomplete information, time pressure and high patient volumes. This use case addresses the operational need for faster, more reliable early assessment of emergency patients, particularly in distinguishing non-critical cases from those requiring urgent hospital care. The stakeholders include emergency physicians, nurses, laboratory services and hospital managers, all of whom need better decision support to improve triage, reduce delays and allocate beds and clinical attention more effectively. The objective is to strengthen the initial diagnostic process so that patients receive the right level of care sooner and hospital resources are directed where they are most needed. The solution is implemented through a diagnostic-support tool that analyses blood and urine samples and applies predictive models to identify the 15 most common acute illnesses and infections seen in emergency settings. At a conceptual level, the system combines laboratory data, probabilistic ranking methods and workflow integration to produce a prioritised list of likely diagnoses within 60 minutes of the patient’s arrival. This enables clinicians to incorporate rapid analytical insight into admission and treatment decisions. The expected impact is quicker diagnosis, more accurate triage and improved use of emergency capacity. In practice, the tool supports better patient flow, a more consistent clinical response and greater value through safer, more efficient acute-care delivery.

results.title: Prediction of heart failure from exacerbations in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients
results.proposal: Prediction of heart failure from exacerbations in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients. The use case therefore involves patients, clinicians and remote-monitoring teams, with the objective of detecting elevated risk before a serious event occurs and enabling earlier, more targeted clinical action. The solution is implemented through a predictive algorithm that analyses patient-reported measurements such as blood pressure, oxygen saturation and heart rate. At a conceptual level, these physiological data are captured through monitoring processes, assessed for risk patterns associated with exacerbation or heart failure, and translated into alerts that notify healthcare professionals when a patient’s condition appears to be deteriorating. This allows preventive treatment to be initiated before the event fully develops and integrates monitoring with clinical decision support. The expected impact is fewer admissions, better prevention of deterioration and a more proactive model of care for vulnerable patients. More broadly, the use case improves service responsiveness, enhances patient safety and experience, and creates business value through more efficient use of healthcare resources and better continuity of care.

results.title: Loting illegally buried cadavers with drones -  Use of drones to detect illegaly buried cadavers
results.proposal: Loting illegally buried cadavers with drones -  Use of drones to detect illegaly buried cadavers. The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority needed a faster and more accurate way to identify sites where animal cadavers may have been buried illegally, since manual inspection over large areas is resource-intensive and can delay enforcement action. Illegal burial may alter surface vegetation and create subtle irregularities that are difficult to spot consistently from the ground. The use case therefore involves inspectors and regulatory authorities seeking to target investigations more effectively, with the objective of obtaining an early and reliable picture of suspicious locations so that field resources can be deployed where they are most needed. The solution uses drones to collect aerial data and analytical models to detect anomalies associated with disturbed vegetation patterns. At a conceptual level, the implementation combines remote sensing, machine-learning-based irregularity detection and inspection triage, allowing broad areas to be screened quickly and suspect zones to be flagged for human follow-up. Rather than replacing inspectors, the system acts as an early-warning layer that narrows the search area and improves the efficiency of site verification. The expected impact is faster localisation of suspicious burial sites, reduced manual search effort and better prioritisation of inspections. In operational terms, the approach improves scalability, strengthens responsiveness and delivers business value through more efficient environmental and public-health enforcement.

results.title: Project ROMATRIS
results.proposal: Project ROMATRIS. Project ROMATRIS responds to a practical problem in emergency response: transporting essential materials through difficult or obstructed terrain during rescue operations. In scenarios such as collapsed buildings, rail accidents, road incidents or off-road emergencies, responders often need to carry equipment across gravel, slopes or obstacles, which slows interventions and increases physical strain. The use case therefore involves rescue teams and emergency-service organisations, with the objective of improving field logistics, reducing responder burden and supporting faster, safer access to critical equipment in demanding environments. The solution is based on a partially automated mobile assistance robot designed to accompany a person through impassable terrain while carrying materials needed for the operation. At a conceptual level, the robot combines autonomous mobility, terrain adaptation, person-following capabilities, gesture recognition and feedback mechanisms so that it can remain aligned with the user and respond appropriately in dynamic rescue conditions. By integrating transport support with human guidance, the system is intended to fit into operational workflows without replacing the rescuer’s judgement. The expected impact is greater efficiency in material transport, reduced physical effort for responders and improved continuity of operations in hazardous settings. More broadly, the project offers scalable support for emergency logistics, enhances reliability under difficult field conditions and contributes to safer, more effective rescue missions.
results.memo: Proceed. Project ROMATRIS is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Machine Learning in Text Classification Projects -  Relieving staff from coding tasks
results.proposal: Machine Learning in Text Classification Projects -  Relieving staff from coding tasks. Across many official statistics processes, large amounts of text information must be coded into predefined categories before the data can be analysed and published. This coding work is repetitive, labour-intensive and increasingly difficult to sustain as digitisation expands the volume of incoming textual material. The use case at the Federal Statistical Office of Germany addresses this bottleneck by supporting teams responsible for statistical coding and production, with the objective of reducing manual effort, improving turnaround times and enabling staff to focus on the most complex cases rather than routine assignments. The solution is implemented through text-classification models trained on previously coded examples and embedded within statistical production workflows. At a conceptual level, the system uses machine-learning techniques to detect patterns in textual responses, assign likely categories and pre-sort or directly code new records against the required classification schemes. Human review can then be concentrated on ambiguous or higher-risk cases, allowing the overall process to operate more efficiently. The expected impact is improved timeliness of statistical results, reduced pressure on coding staff and greater consistency in the handling of textual information. In operational terms, the approach offers stronger scalability, better use of limited personnel capacity and a more sustainable way to manage growing data volumes while maintaining quality in official statistical production.
results.memo: Proceed. Machine Learning in Text Classification Projects -  Relieving staff from coding tasks is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Machine Learning in Editing and Imputation - Automated editing and correcting of data
results.proposal: Machine Learning in Editing and Imputation - Automated editing and correcting of data. A key operational issue in official statistics is the need to correct missing, implausible or inconsistent observations quickly enough to keep production cycles on schedule without overloading staff. At the Federal Statistical Office of Germany, editing and imputation are essential steps in data processing, yet manual treatment becomes increasingly difficult as digitisation produces larger and more complex datasets. The use case therefore involves statistical production teams and data-quality specialists, with the objective of reducing routine manual work while preserving the quality and timeliness of published results. The implementation uses observed values, plausibility rules and machine-learning techniques to support automated editing and imputation within the statistical workflow. Conceptually, the system analyses historical and current data patterns, applies prediction methods to infer likely corrections or substitute values, and combines these outputs with existing validation logic so that suspect observations can be treated more consistently and at scale. This creates a more adaptive alternative to purely manual intervention and helps incorporate automation into established statistical processes. The impact is expected to include lower administrative effort, quicker processing of large datasets and improved timeliness of statistical outputs. More broadly, the use case increases scalability, strengthens consistency in data treatment and delivers business value by enabling statistical offices to manage growing data volumes more efficiently without proportionate increases in staffing.
results.memo: Proceed. Machine Learning in Editing and Imputation - Automated editing and correcting of data is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: CERTH-MUKA - Public Organizations Multi-factor Misinformation Handling
results.proposal: CERTH-MUKA - Public Organizations Multi-factor Misinformation Handling. In the municipality of Katerini, the challenge addressed by this use case is the growing need to identify misleading information quickly and to prioritise emerging issues before they create operational, reputational or social harm. Public authorities must respond in an environment where inaccurate online content can spread rapidly, undermine trust and complicate communication with citizens. The use case therefore involves municipal decision-makers, communication teams and public-sector organisations seeking to manage information risks more effectively, with the objective of detecting problematic content early and handling it in a way that is operationally useful and socially responsible. The solution combines misinformation-detection and issue-prioritisation capabilities with the ETAPAS framework, which is used to assess deployment risks and define mitigation actions. At a conceptual level, the implementation analyses content and signals associated with potentially false or harmful narratives, prioritises relevant issues for attention and embeds an ethical and social impact assessment around the operational system. This allows the municipality to evaluate not only technical performance but also governance risks, unintended consequences and required safeguards. The expected impact is improved responsiveness to misinformation, better prioritisation of public communication efforts and stronger institutional trust. In business and public-value terms, the approach enhances reliability, reduces the risk of harmful side effects and supports scalable adoption through structured risk management.

results.title: Kari - Chatbot for local governments
results.proposal: Kari - Chatbot for local governments. Kari was created to help local municipalities manage large volumes of citizen enquiries about public services in a faster and more consistent way. In many councils, residents need clear answers on procedures, rights and local services, yet frontline teams often face repetitive requests that absorb time and slow response delivery. The use case therefore involves municipal administrations and citizens, with the objective of improving access to information, reducing pressure on service staff and strengthening the quality of digital interaction with local government. The solution is implemented through a virtual-agent platform integrated into municipal service channels and supported by a knowledge base containing more than 6,000 intents, covering a very broad range of local-government questions. At a conceptual level, the system uses conversational language-processing and intent-recognition techniques to interpret citizen requests, match them to the relevant service information and return standardised answers that can be maintained centrally and reused across municipalities. Kari is currently available in 80 Norwegian municipalities, covering about 30% of the Norwegian population, and is being introduced in Sweden, Finland and Denmark. The result is improved user experience, faster access to information and greater scalability in handling routine enquiries, while municipalities benefit from more efficient service delivery, better consistency of responses and reduced administrative workload.

The objective is to strengthen emergency preparedness and improve the speed and quality of response by combining operational, geographic and contextual information in a more systematic way. The implementation integrates INEM’s internal information systems with external datasets such as meteorology, epidemic indicators, demography and forest-fire information, and uses historical records to build predictive models for emergency vehicle demand in each geographic area. These forecasts then inform optimisation models that support resource allocation and deployment decisions. At a conceptual level, the solution combines data integration, demand prediction and operational optimisation within emergency-management workflows. The expected impact is faster response to medical emergencies, more efficient use of vehicles and personnel, and improved scalability in managing fluctuating demand. results.title: EPISA - Entity and property inference for semantic archives
results.proposal: EPISA - Entity and property inference for semantic archives. EPISA addresses a core challenge in the archival domain: how to improve the accessibility, structure and interoperability of Portuguese cultural heritage records so that archives can be more easily searched, connected and reused. Traditional archival descriptions often contain rich information, but much of it is difficult to process automatically or integrate into broader digital ecosystems. The use case therefore involves archivists, cultural-heritage institutions and information-management stakeholders seeking to create a richer and more machine-readable description model for archival material. Its objective is to support the semi-automatic creation of metadata, improve the quality and consistency of archival descriptions and connect national archives to the wider network of semantic linked data. The implementation uses natural language processing, named-entity recognition and machine-learning methods to analyse archival descriptions and, where available, the digital documents themselves. Conceptually, the system extracts entities, relationships and relevant properties from texts and uses them to populate a semantic description model that is more expressive and more suitable for automated processing than conventional archival structures. The impact is improved discoverability, stronger interoperability and reduced manual effort in metadata creation. More broadly, the project increases the accessibility and long-term value of archival collections, supports digital transformation in the cultural sector and enables more scalable management of documentary heritage.

results.title: Failstopper - Study the compressed air system of the vehicle
results.proposal: Failstopper - Study the compressed air system of the vehicle. Metro do Porto faces a significant operational reliability issue, with around 3,000 journeys cancelled each year due to breakdowns in MP vehicles, many of which are linked to critical onboard systems such as compressed air. The use case focuses on supporting maintenance teams by improving visibility over asset condition and enabling earlier intervention before faults disrupt service. In this context, operators, maintenance engineers and fleet managers require a more timely and data-driven understanding of vehicle behaviour in order to reduce cancellations, improve service continuity and strengthen maintenance planning. The objective is therefore to monitor the compressed air system in operation and provide actionable alerts that help maintenance teams prevent failures rather than react to them after disruption has already occurred. The implementation relies on sensors installed in vehicles to capture operational data from the compressed air system, which is then analysed in real time to detect patterns associated with degradation or emerging faults. At a conceptual level, the solution combines continuous data acquisition, condition-monitoring models and alerting mechanisms that integrate with maintenance workflows so that anomalies can be identified and escalated promptly. The expected impact is improved fleet reliability, fewer cancelled trips, better-targeted maintenance activity and more efficient use of technical resources. In business terms, the project supports service quality, reduces disruption-related costs and creates a scalable predictive-maintenance capability for public transport operations.

results.proposal: Predicting long term unemployment in Portugal. The context was an existing risk-categorisation framework that provided a starting point but lacked the ability to reflect changes in an individual’s circumstances over time. The use case involved employment-service teams, caseworkers and programme managers, with the objective of creating a more responsive assessment process that could better flag high-risk individuals and support more tailored intervention. The implementation introduced a dynamic predictive model that updated each individual’s risk score over time rather than relying on a static classification. At a conceptual level, the solution used longitudinal administrative and service data, predictive modelling and score recalculation to reflect evolving employment risk and integrate updated assessments into operational decision-making. This allowed the system to support more precise targeting of services and better coordination of case-management activity. The impact was improved prioritisation of individuals most in need, more efficient allocation of public employment resources and stronger potential for earlier intervention. Qualitatively, the approach improves service personalisation, enhances the responsiveness of employment support and increases the overall effectiveness of delivery by aligning scarce resources with changing levels of risk across the beneficiary population.

results.title: Canard - Speed camera system to flag potential traffic rules infringement
results.proposal: Canard - Speed camera system to flag potential traffic rules infringement. Canard's speed-camera system was developed to improve the efficiency of traffic-rule enforcement at road junctions by helping staff process large volumes of photographic evidence more quickly and consistently. The operational challenge was not simply capturing images, but extracting usable information from them so that potential infringements could be identified and prioritised without requiring every case to be reviewed from scratch. The use case involved road-enforcement personnel and administrative teams responsible for case handling, with the objective of creating an initial sorting mechanism that would support, rather than replace, human decision-making on fines and infringements. The implementation used image-processing and analytical techniques to derive relevant information from photographs captured by cameras installed at junctions. At a conceptual level, the system analysed vehicle images and event data to flag cases that appeared to indicate potential breaches of traffic rules, feeding these into a human review workflow. The final enforcement decision remained non-automatic, ensuring human oversight and procedural control. The impact was greater operational efficiency for CANARD staff, reduced manual effort in first-line case screening and improved scalability of enforcement processes as camera coverage expanded. In practice, the system supports faster triage, more consistent handling of potential cases and better use of public enforcement resources, while preserving reliability and accountability in the final decision process.

results.title: PRORAIL: Rail trespassers prediction
results.proposal: PRORAIL: Rail trespassers prediction. ProRail aimed to improve the safety and efficiency of the Dutch rail network by using operational data to anticipate risks and optimise infrastructure management. One important challenge was understanding when and where trespassers might enter railway tracks, alongside broader needs such as preventive maintenance and more reliable scheduling. The use case involved asset-management teams, operational planners and safety stakeholders, with the objective of turning continuously generated infrastructure data into practical insight for safer operations and better network performance. The implementation relied on Internet of Things sensor data collected from the rail system, including track-monitoring information used to assess infrastructure condition on different routes. At a conceptual level, predictive algorithms were applied to identify correlations, estimate likely events and support decision-making beyond the limits of manual analysis. These models were integrated into operational processes to inform maintenance planning, improve schedule optimisation and identify locations or circumstances in which trespassing risk might be higher. The impact was greater visibility over infrastructure conditions, stronger preventive maintenance capability and improved support for safety-related interventions. Qualitatively, this enhances network reliability, reduces operational disruption and helps protect the physical rail environment. More broadly, the use case demonstrates how data-driven forecasting can improve both efficiency and public safety across a large-scale transport system.
results.memo: Proceed. PRORAIL: Rail trespassers prediction is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Rotterdam – Improving the usage of rooftops
results.proposal: Rotterdam – Improving the usage of rooftops. The Municipality of Rotterdam needed a better understanding of how the city’s extensive stock of flat rooftops could contribute to urban sustainability goals, including water storage, green space creation and energy generation. With around 14.5 km² of flat roofs across a dense and modern urban environment, the challenge was to move from fragmented visual assessment to a city-wide evidence base that could support planning, prioritisation and investment decisions. The use case involved municipal departments and urban-planning stakeholders, with the objective of identifying current rooftop use and uncovering opportunities for more sustainable and productive deployment of roof space across the city. The implementation used computer-vision techniques applied to aerial and satellite imagery to classify rooftops and infer their current characteristics and use. At a conceptual level, the approach combined image data, geospatial analysis and classification models to create a scalable mapping layer that could be integrated with municipal planning processes and related environmental datasets. This provided a structured basis for evaluating where roofs might support climate adaptation or energy initiatives. The expected impact was improved decision quality, greater scalability than manual inspection and a stronger ability to prioritise interventions across the city. In business terms, the use case supports more efficient urban planning, better use of public resources and a more informed pathway towards environmental resilience.

results.title: CAS - Crime anticipation system
results.proposal: CAS - Crime anticipation system. The Crime Anticipation System was designed to help police allocate limited resources more effectively by identifying where and when specific categories of crime were more likely to occur. Operating in a context of recurrent local crime patterns, the use case brought together police forces, local operational teams and public-data providers to improve weekly planning and deployment decisions. It addressed the practical challenge of turning large volumes of local, time-sensitive information into actionable operational insight, with the objective of anticipating patterns such as repeated offences in particular neighbourhoods or at particular times and enabling a more focused preventive presence. The implementation combined predictive analytics with regular ingestion of local and current data, including police records, neighbourhood and resident data, contextual information on local conditions and statistics from Statistics Netherlands. At a conceptual level, the system used pattern-recognition and spatio-temporal analysis techniques to detect recurring crime behaviours and generate weekly forecasts that could be integrated into policing workflows and resource-planning processes. The impact lay in more targeted deployment of officers, improved responsiveness to recurring crime trends and better use of available capacity. Qualitatively, this increased operational efficiency, supported evidence-based planning and strengthened the police’s ability to intervene earlier and more effectively in areas of elevated risk.

results.title: FCIS - Machine learning to identify suspicious patterns (trade, financial flows)
results.proposal: FCIS - Machine learning to identify suspicious patterns (trade, financial flows). Financial Crime Investigation Service under Lithuanian Customs sought to strengthen its ability to detect suspicious trade and financial-flow patterns across fragmented and high-volume datasets, in a context where investigators and other law-enforcement units needed faster, better-prioritised intelligence to support operational decisions. The use case focused on improving the linking, filtering and analysis of information gathered from multiple internal and external sources so that relevant cases could be identified earlier and assessed more consistently. The objective was to support analysts and decision-makers with a targeted data-processing and analysis capability able to surface anomalies, relationships and priorities that would otherwise remain difficult to detect manually. The solution was implemented within a Horizon 2020 research and innovation project using machine-learning methods, data-analysis techniques and visual analytics to process heterogeneous datasets conceptually spanning trade records, financial flows and other investigative information. The system combined pattern-detection models, data integration and analytical workflows to help users connect entities, rank leads and explore evidence in a more structured way. The result was a more scalable and informed investigative process, with improved analytical depth, faster triage of complex information and stronger support for operational decision-making across the organisational units involved.

results.title: Robot-mediated rehabilitation (IIT-FDG)
results.proposal: Robot-mediated rehabilitation (IIT-FDG). This use case addresses the need to extend rehabilitation support beyond conventional clinical sessions by introducing an assistive robot that can complement therapists’ work in hospitals, rehabilitation gyms and patients’ homes. The context is one in which patients recovering from injury or managing long-term functional limitations often require frequent support with exercises, daily activities and safety monitoring, while clinical staff must balance intensive care needs with limited time and resources. The stakeholders include patients, rehabilitation professionals, ward staff and carers, with the objective of improving continuity of support, reinforcing therapy routines and assisting with everyday tasks that help preserve autonomy and safety. The implementation uses the humanoid robot R1, developed as part of the ETAPAS H2020 project, combining advanced mechanics, sensors and intelligent control capabilities to operate as a low-cost assistive-rehabilitation platform. At a conceptual level, the system supports traditional rehabilitation treatments, assists staff in clinical environments and provides in-home functions such as fetching or locating objects, reminding patients about appointments or medication, and detecting falls to support emergency management. The expected impact includes improved continuity of care, better patient experience and stronger support for independent living. More broadly, the solution offers scalability through lower-cost deployment, reduces pressure on clinical staff and strengthens rehabilitation outcomes by extending assistance into everyday environments.

results.title: AI against pornography - Analysis of suspicious material
results.proposal: AI against pornography - Analysis of suspicious material. Public prosecutors and investigators face the operational challenge of reviewing very large volumes of seized digital material in cases involving the distribution, acquisition or possession of child and youth sexual abuse imagery. Much of this material may be entirely irrelevant to the offence under investigation, yet it must still be assessed carefully to identify evidential content. The use case was therefore designed to support case workers by accelerating the initial sorting of suspicious images so that the most potentially relevant material could be prioritised for detailed review. Its objective was to reduce the burden of manual screening, improve consistency in the handling of digital evidence and support more efficient investigative and prosecutorial workflows while preserving human judgement in the final assessment. The implementation used automated image-recognition techniques to analyse visual material and identify items most likely to depict illegal content involving children or adolescents. At a conceptual level, the system functioned as a triage mechanism, separating likely irrelevant material from images requiring closer investigation and forwarding flagged content to case handlers and, where appropriate, to the public prosecutor for decision. The impact was faster evidence screening, reduced manual effort and improved focus of investigative resources on the most relevant material. In operational terms, the approach enhanced scalability, supported reliability in evidence handling and improved the efficiency of highly sensitive prosecutorial work.

results.company: Federal Ministry of Transport and Digital Infrastructure (BMVI)
results.title: Indoor Robot - Making a 3D model of a new building
results.proposal: Indoor Robot - Making a 3D model of a new building. This use case was created to improve accessibility and navigation in public buildings by generating more detailed and practical spatial information than conventional building plans typically provide. The problem was especially significant for people who need barrier-free navigation, including blind people and wheelchair users, because standard plans often lack the information required for independent movement through complex indoor environments. The use case therefore involved public-building managers, accessibility stakeholders and end users requiring reliable orientation information, with the objective of producing accurate indoor models that could support inclusive navigation and better user autonomy. The implementation used a robot equipped with a laser scanner and object camera to measure the entire building and capture detailed spatial data. At a conceptual level, the solution transformed individual measurement points into a 3D vector model of the building through automated modelling techniques, creating a digital representation that could then support orientation maps and display on mobile devices. This provided a richer and more usable description of the indoor environment than static architectural drawings alone. The expected impact was improved accessibility, better navigation support and a stronger basis for inclusive public-space design. More broadly, the use case offers a scalable way to capture building information and translate it into practical guidance tools that enhance independence and user experience for people with disabilities.
results.memo: Proceed. Indoor Robot - Making a 3D model of a new building is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Trade statistics - Classification system that automatically new data points as relevant
results.proposal: Trade statistics - Classification system that automatically new data points as relevant. This use case was developed to improve the production of official trade statistics by automating the initial classification of incoming units, such as craft enterprises, as relevant or not relevant for inclusion in the statistical process. Previously, this task had been performed manually, which consumed significant staff time, was vulnerable to inconsistency and error, and placed pressure on already limited personnel resources. The use case therefore involved statistical case handlers and official statistics teams seeking to maintain processing quality while increasing efficiency in the treatment of new data points. Its objective was to pre-sort cases more effectively so that staff could focus their effort within the same operational time window but on a more intelligently ordered set of records. The implementation used previously identified classification patterns for units, drawing on information from business registers, to train a classification system that could assess the likely relevance of new cases. At a conceptual level, the solution applied supervised learning to historical administrative patterns and fed the resulting predictions into the case-handling workflow as a prioritisation layer. The impact was a more efficient and reliable screening process, reduced manual burden and better use of scarce staffing capacity. In practical terms, the approach improved throughput, supported more consistent statistical production and created a scalable mechanism for handling growing volumes of administrative data.
results.memo: Proceed. Trade statistics - Classification system that automatically new data points as relevant is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.company: BMVI, Autobahn GmbH of the Federal Government
results.title: ARC-D - Automatic Road Condition Detection
results.proposal: ARC-D - Automatic Road Condition Detection. ARC-D addresses the lack of automated, up-to-date condition monitoring across the federal motorway network, a gap that makes it harder for road authorities to detect deterioration early and to plan timely maintenance before defects become more severe and more expensive to repair. The use case involves transport infrastructure authorities and maintenance planners who need consistent, network-wide visibility of road quality in order to prioritise interventions and manage public assets more effectively. Its objective is to create a more systematic and scalable basis for assessing the condition of individual motorway sections, replacing a fragmented approach with one that supports earlier action and better long-term maintenance planning. The implementation uses image data previously classified by experts to train a system capable of partially automating the evaluation of road video footage and classifying stretches of road according to their condition. At a conceptual level, the solution combines supervised classification methods with image-based inspection workflows, with the longer-term intention of integrating additional sensor data to broaden and strengthen detection capability. The expected impact is earlier identification of road degradation, more efficient maintenance targeting and reduced risk of cost-intensive long-term damage. In operational terms, the system improves scalability, enhances the timeliness of infrastructure monitoring and supports more reliable, data-informed management of motorway assets.
results.memo: Proceed. ARC-D - Automatic Road Condition Detection is classified as minimal. No prohibited practice, no Annex I or III ground and no transparency trigger found: minimal risk, voluntary codes only.

results.title: Misty II - Robot for elderly people
results.proposal: Misty II - Robot for elderly people. This use case was designed to explore whether a social robot could improve the daily lives of older people living alone by providing practical support, companionship and routine assistance in the home. The pilot involved twenty older residents already supported by the City Council’s Area for Social Rights and was launched in the context of a broader challenge focused on improving quality of life for senior citizens through technology. The operational problem was social isolation and the difficulty of maintaining regular reminders, wellbeing monitoring and day-to-day support for people who may be vulnerable but still living independently. The objective was therefore to assess whether a domestic assistive solution could reduce loneliness, support adherence to medication and appointments, and contribute to safer and more confident independent living. The implementation used the Misty II social robot as an in-home interaction platform, capable of providing reminders, supporting simple monitoring functions and engaging users in daily routines. At a conceptual level, the solution combined conversational interaction, scheduling support and basic assistive features within a real-world pilot setting so that user acceptance and practical value could be evaluated directly. The expected impact included better user experience, reduced feelings of isolation and improved support for routine health and wellbeing tasks. More broadly, the pilot explored a scalable model for complementing social-care services and extending support for older people living alone.

results.title: Stockholm3 - Diagnosing prostate cancer with OncoWatch
results.proposal: Stockholm3 - Diagnosing prostate cancer with OncoWatch. This use case focuses on improving the diagnosis of prostate cancer by strengthening the consistency, accuracy and scalability of pathology assessment across laboratories and clinical settings. Diagnosing prostate cancer can be complex, and variability in interpretation may affect both efficiency and quality of care. The use case therefore involved pathology laboratories, clinicians, diagnostic innovators and health-system stakeholders seeking to improve diagnostic support and broaden access to reliable assessment tools. Its objective was to accelerate the development and implementation of Stockholm3 together with OncoWatch, so that diagnostic workflows could benefit from more standardised and scalable support. The implementation involved the development and validation of OncoWatch as a diagnostic system for use in pathology contexts, supported by EIT Health through funding and network access. At a conceptual level, the solution was tested in a nine-country multicentre study to assess performance across different laboratories and a wider range of digital pathology scanners, ensuring that the system could operate effectively in heterogeneous real-world environments. This emphasis on cross-site validation supported readiness for broader deployment, with a first CE-marked product expected to launch by the end of the year referenced. The impact includes improved confidence in diagnostic consistency, stronger interoperability across lab settings and better scalability of prostate-cancer diagnostics. More broadly, the use case supports faster translation of innovation into clinical practice and creates business value through improved efficiency, standardisation and potential expansion across multiple healthcare markets.

results.company: Uppsala, Umeå, Linköping, Malmö/Lund, Gothenburg and Stockholm Hospitals
results.title: SCAPIS - Prevention of heart- and lung-diseases
results.proposal: SCAPIS - Prevention of heart- and lung-diseases. SCAPIS was established to strengthen prevention and risk assessment for cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases through a large-scale population study capable of generating deeper insight into how these conditions develop and how they might be prevented or delayed. Heart and lung diseases place a major burden on health systems, yet earlier and more individualised risk identification requires data on a scale and depth that routine care alone cannot easily provide. The use case brought together all six Swedish healthcare regions, university hospitals and a broad group of scientific stakeholders, with the objective of building a national evidence base to improve understanding of cardiovascular, pulmonary, epidemiological and genetic risk factors. The implementation was centred on the Swedish CardioPulmonary bioImage Study, a population-based initiative involving 30,000 participants. At a conceptual level, the programme integrated imaging, clinical, epidemiological and genetic data in order to support the development of more individualised risk assessments and preventive strategies. The study began with a pilot in 2012 to confirm feasibility, followed by the major study launch in 2014, building on work initiated in 2007. The impact lies in creating a world-leading research resource that supports earlier prevention, more precise risk stratification and stronger scientific understanding of heart and lung disease. In broader terms, SCAPIS improves the foundation for long-term public-health planning, supports clinical innovation and strengthens the ability of the health system to move from reactive treatment towards prevention.
